docs.label: Not draining / won't empty
symptoms: wont spin with water in the drum
makes a noise but no water comes out
it drains but water comes back up
sink backs up when it drains
discriminators: If you can HEAR THE PUMP HUMMING/straining but little or no water leaves, the drain pump is blocked or failing (or the filter/hose is blocked). Prioritise this over the motor even if it also won't spin - it won't spin until it has drained.
Won't drain AND won't spin: almost always the drain pump or a blocked pump filter (the machine won't spin until it has drained).
Drains slowly or noisily: partial blockage in the filter, or a worn pump impeller.
Drains fine but won't spin: this is NOT a drain fault - see motor/brushes/belt (motor-drum).

WON'T SPIN + WATER STILL IN THE DRUM = investigate DRAINAGE first (spin is inhibited until emptied); do NOT jump to motor/belt/spin parts. WON'T SPIN + NO retained water = not a drainage fault, see motor-drum.

FREE FIX FIRST: the most common cause is a BLOCKED PUMP FILTER or a trapped foreign object (coins, hair grips, buttons, lint) - clear/clean the filter and accessible pump path before condemning the drain pump. This is a CHECK, not a part.
PUMP HUMMING + NO DRAINAGE does NOT automatically mean replace the pump: a blocked filter/hose/sump or a jammed impeller gives the same sound. Exclude blockages first.

If filter, hose, waste and any trapped object are all clear and the pump hums-but-moves-nothing or is silent when commanded, THEN it's the drain pump (jammed/failed) or, with abnormal level behaviour, the pressure system.
Slow/progressive drainage or a recent house move points to a hose/waste restriction rather than a failed pump.

DRAINS OK BUT DIRTY WATER BACKS UP / RETURNS (into the drum, or up through the sink or standpipe), especially with a DRAIN or SEWER SMELL: the machine IS pumping out - the fault is in the HOUSEHOLD WASTE PLUMBING (a blocked standpipe, waste trap/U-bend, or the kitchen sink waste the drain hose empties into), NOT the appliance pump, filter or hose. Advise checking/clearing the standpipe and household waste plumbing; do not condemn or sell a drain pump for this. A machine that simply WON'T EMPTY at all is still the appliance - see the filter/pump above.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is there still water sitting in the drum, and when it tries to drain can you hear the pump running or humming?

- won't pump out = replace the drain pump: A pump that hums or is noisy does NOT prove a failed pump. docs.label: Fill / water inlet fault (incl. overfill)
symptoms: fills with water when switched off
discriminators: A machine that FILLS with water while switched OFF is a water inlet valve stuck/not closing (mains pressure passes the failed valve) - route to the inlet valve; the anti-flood may trigger as a knock-on effect.
A loud buzz/hum only while FILLING is usually a restricted inlet (blocked inlet filter/kinked hose making the valve strain) or a failing water inlet valve. Check/clean the inlet filter first.
SPLIT THE COMPLAINT FIRST: no fill vs slow/insufficient fill vs genuine overfill vs continuous filling with the level not rising - these need different reasoning, not one static component order.

NO FILL: establish external supply FIRST - are the other cold taps in the property normal? If other taps are affected, strongly down-rank an appliance part. Then tap open -> hose unkinked -> inlet mesh clear -> THEN the inlet valve. The machine may also refuse to fill until the door has locked (sequencing), which is not a fill-system failure.

SLOW FILL: move the inlet mesh/filter and supply/pressure checks UP; a gradually worsening trickle with good supply elsewhere is usually a restriction (mesh/hose/tap), not a dead valve. Do NOT encode one manufacturer's flow/pressure threshold as a universal spec.

OVERFILL (level gets too high): use the switched-off test - if water keeps entering with the machine SWITCHED OFF, strongly suspect a mechanically passing/stuck inlet valve; if it stops when off, the level-sensing/pressure path is more likely (see pressure-switch).

CONTINUOUS FILLING BUT LEVEL NOT RISING: if water keeps entering but the level stays low, suspect water leaving at the same time - siphoning from drain-hose installation (often after a move), NOT genuine overfill or the inlet valve. (No dedicated taxonomy node yet - see the Story-10 taxonomy report.)
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does no water come in at all, does it fill very slowly, or does it keep filling until the water level gets too high?

docs.label: Pressure switch / water level fault
symptoms: fills then drains over and over
discriminators: Repeatedly filling then draining over and over = the machine can't sense the water level, so it keeps correcting. Usual cause is a faulty pressure switch/sensor or a blocked/split pressure chamber (air-trap) hose.

SWITCHED-OFF TEST is the highest-value overfill discriminator: water still entering with the machine OFF = mechanically passing/stuck inlet valve; entry stops when OFF = level-sensing/pressure path (chamber/hose/sensor).

Treat the pressure sensing path as a SYSTEM - do NOT jump straight to 'replace the pressure switch'. Check the pressure chamber and small-bore hose (contamination/restriction/damage/disconnection) before condemning the sensor.

HARD-WATER (environmental, supporting evidence ONLY): in hard-water areas limescale residue in the pressure chamber or small-bore pressure hose can block the rising-level signal. A hard-water area + genuine overfill (valve closes when off) increases suspicion of the pressure PATH - but location alone does NOT diagnose a pressure-system fault, and do not assume/fabricate the local water hardness.
LEVEL NOT RISING despite continuous entry = siphoning/drain-hose installation, not overfill (see inlet-valve continuous-fill note and the taxonomy report).
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does water keep coming into the machine even when it's switched off?

components.name: inlet valve mechanically stuck open / passing
supports: water continues entering while the machine is SWITCHED OFF
filling continues with no active programme
water gradually appears in the drum while idle
against: water stops immediately when the control stops requesting fill
overfill only occurs during active programme control (points to level sensing)

components.name: pressure chamber / small-bore pressure hose (sensing path)
supports: overfills while powered/running but the inlet valve closes when switched off
restriction/contamination in the pressure path
pressure hose blocked, kinked, split, disconnected or leaking
hard-water area/history with genuine overfill (supporting evidence)
against: inlet valve keeps passing water with the machine switched off
pressure path confirmed clear/intact and behaving correctly

components.name: pressure switch / electronic level sensor
supports: pressure chamber and hose confirmed clear/intact
overfill only while the machine is actively controlling fill
level-sensor error, with the valve closing correctly when the command is removed
against: pressure chamber/hose restriction still plausible
inlet valve mechanically passes with the machine switched off

components.name: wiring / control PCB
supports: inlet valve sound AND pressure path sound AND sensor verified
incorrect electrical command to the valve
wiring/connector evidence
against: simpler valve or pressure-system explanations remain

commonConfusion.name: pressure switch (as the automatic answer to overfill)
commonConfusion.note: Overfill does NOT automatically mean a failed pressure switch. The pressure chamber and small-bore pressure hose can stop correct level information reaching an otherwise-good sensor. Treat the sensing path as a system: chamber contamination -> hose restriction -> hose damage/leak/disconnection -> sensor -> wiring.
wouldApplyIf: genuine overfill, inlet valve closes when switched off, and the pressure chamber/hose is confirmed clear and intact

commonConfusion.name: genuine overfilling (vs siphoning)
commonConfusion.note: 'Keeps filling' is not always overfilling. If water enters continuously but the LEVEL does not rise, water may be siphoning away (drain-hose installation, often after a move) - not an overfill/level-sensing fault.
wouldApplyIf: the water level actually rises too high (not merely continuous entry with a low level)

docs.secondaryQuestion: Is the water level actually getting too high, or does it keep taking water without the level rising much?
adviceBeforeReplacement: do the switched-off test (does water keep entering with the machine off?) before choosing between the valve and the sensing path
check/clean the pressure chamber and the small-bore pressure hose - especially in hard-water areas
check the pressure hose isn't split, blocked, kinked or disconnected before replacing the pressure switch/level sensor

Fault: Pressure switch / water level fault
Customer phrases: level fault; not filling right; won't spin with water; pressure sensor; keeps filling and draining; fills and drains repeatedly; constantly filling and draining; fills then drains over and over; keeps filling and emptying; cycles between fill and drain; keeps filling; too much water; water level gets too high; doesn't stop taking water; fills right up; overfilling; water level fault; level sensor fault
Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. inlet valve mechanically stuck open / passing [PART]
   More likely if: water continues entering while the machine is SWITCHED OFF; filling continues with no active programme; water gradually appears in the drum while idle.
   Less likely if: water stops immediately when the control stops requesting fill; overfill only occurs during active programme control (points to level sensing).
2. pressure chamber / small-bore pressure hose (sensing path) [CHECK]
   More likely if: overfills while powered/running but the inlet valve closes when switched off; restriction/contamination in the pressure path; pressure hose blocked, kinked, split, disconnected or leaking; hard-water area/history with genuine overfill (supporting evidence).

   More likely if: pressure chamber and hose confirmed clear/intact; overfill only while the machine is actively controlling fill; level-sensor error, with the valve closing correctly when the command is removed.

4. wiring / control PCB [PART]
   More likely if: inlet valve sound AND pressure path sound AND sensor verified; incorrect electrical command to the valve; wiring/connector evidence.
   Less likely if: simpler valve or pressure-system explanations remain.

- pressure switch (as the automatic answer to overfill): Overfill does NOT automatically mean a failed pressure switch. The pressure chamber and small-bore pressure hose can stop correct level information reaching an otherwise-good sensor. Treat the sensing path as a system: chamber contamination -> hose restriction -> hose damage/leak/disconnection -> sensor -> wiring.
   Only consider if: genuine overfill, inlet valve closes when switched off, and the pressure chamber/hose is confirmed clear and intact.

Usual cause is a faulty pressure switch/sensor or a blocked/split pressure chamber (air-trap) hose. SWITCHED-OFF TEST is the highest-value overfill discriminator: water still entering with the machine OFF = mechanically passing/stuck inlet valve; entry stops when OFF = level-sensing/pressure path (chamber/hose/sensor). Treat the pressure sensing path as a SYSTEM - do NOT jump straight to 'replace the pressure switch'. Check the pressure chamber and small-bore hose (contamination/restriction/damage/disconnection) before condemning the sensor. HARD-WATER (environmental, supporting evidence ONLY): in hard-water areas limescale residue in the pressure chamber or small-bore pressure hose can block the rising-level signal. docs.label: Temperature sensor (NTC) fault
discriminators: NTC = temperature FEEDBACK, not heat generation. Suspect it when the heater looks serviceable but temperature is wrong/intermittent or the programme won't progress on temperature. Confirm the element isn't simply open-circuit first.
No universal NTC resistance value - characteristics are component/model/platform specific.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does the heater itself seem okay, but the temperature reads wrong or the programme won't move on from the wash?

components.name: NTC / thermistor (temperature sensor)
supports: heater appears serviceable but temperature is wrong/implausible/intermittent
temperature-related error appropriate to the model
wrong progression suggesting target temperature isn't detected
against: heating element conclusively failed
never reaches the heating stage

components.name: NTC wiring / connector
supports: intermittent/implausible readings with a good sensor
loose/damaged connector
against: sensor itself faulty
element failure explains it

components.name: control PCB
supports: sensor and wiring serviceable but temperature handling wrong
against: simpler sensor/wiring cause remains

commonConfusion.name: the NTC heats the water
commonConfusion.note: It doesn't. The NTC is a negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor - resistance falls as temperature rises - providing FEEDBACK to the controller. Faults cause no/incorrect heat, overheating or stalled progression via wrong feedback. Do NOT assume a universal resistance value; it is component/model specific.
wouldApplyIf: temperature feedback is implausible while the heater is serviceable

docs.label: Heater / heating fault
discriminators: Washes but stays cold / long cycles: heater element or the NTC temperature sensor.
Trips the electrics when it should heat: heater element earthing/shorting.

SUSPECTED vs CONFIRMED: cold laundry or a cool door/glass alone is WEAK evidence (cold rinses, eco/low-temp, judged at the wrong point) - clarify programme/temperature first, do not recommend a heater. Genuine no-heat needs evidence it should be heating and isn't.

STUCK ON WASH: fills normally + tumbles normally + stays in wash abnormally long / won't progress => strongly raise the HEATING SYSTEM (the controller is typically waiting for a target temperature it isn't reaching). Common programme behaviour, not universal - and rule out slow fill / drainage delay / load first.

ELEMENT vs NTC: the ELEMENT produces heat; the NTC only SENSES it. Dead-cold on a genuine hot wash => element; implausible/incorrect/intermittent temperature or wrong progression with a serviceable heater => NTC. Do not assume a universal NTC resistance value - it is component/model specific.

SEQUENCE: don't diagnose the heating system just because the water isn't hot if the machine hasn't reached the heating stage - inadequate fill / water level / early abort can be upstream (see inlet-valve / pressure-switch).

HEATER BRACKET [front-entry designs only]: a physically damaged heater (contacted the drum, mechanical noise, repeated failures) means inspect the retaining support/bracket to find why - don't just fit another heater.

HOT/COLD-FILL [older architecture only]: separate hot+cold inlets can mask a failed internal heater on warmer cycles, so intermittent progression does not exclude the heater. Not applicable to cold-fill-only machines.
SAFETY: serious burning smell, melted insulation or smoke at the heater/terminals => stop-use, not continued operation.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: What makes you think it isn't heating - does the programme finish normally but the washing seems cold, or does it stop / take much longer / show an error?

components.name: programme / temperature selection & how the customer judged it
supports: only evidence is cold laundry after the cycle, or a cool door/glass
low-temperature or eco programme
customer checked during/after cold rinses
small amount of heated water
against: objective evidence it should be heating and isn't (stalls in wash, error, clearly cold on a genuine hot programme)

components.name: water level / fill established (upstream sequence)
supports: no heat accompanied by abnormal filling / incorrect water level
machine may not have reached the heating stage
against: fill and level are completely normal and the machine clearly reaches the heating stage

components.name: heating element
supports: genuine hot programme, fills/tumbles normally, target temperature not reached
remains in the heating/wash phase abnormally long
element electrically confirmed failed by competent testing
against: only evidence is cold laundry after rinse / low-temp programme
hasn't reached the heating stage
temperature-sensing evidence is stronger
element known electrically sound

components.name: NTC / thermistor / temperature sensor
supports: heater itself appears serviceable
implausible/incorrect temperature feedback
heating incorrect/intermittent
programme progression suggests target temperature isn't being detected
against: heating element conclusively failed
never reaches the heating stage
NTC behaviour known correct

components.name: heater wiring / connectors
supports: heater tests correct but heating is intermittent
loose/burnt/discoloured/heat-damaged terminal
continuity problem despite a serviceable heater
against: heater itself conclusively failed
NTC/temperature sensing clearly explains it

components.name: heater support / bracket [front-entry-heater designs ONLY]
supports: design uses a front-entry heater with a retaining support
heater physically damaged / has contacted the drum/tub
mechanical contact noise
repeated heater failure
against: design does not use a heater support/bracket
no mechanical damage - a plain electrical element failure

components.name: heater relay / control PCB
supports: heater, NTC, wiring serviceable AND correct water level AND reaches heating stage, but the heater isn't switched/energised
relay/control evidence
against: simpler heater/NTC/wiring cause remains
hasn't reached the heating stage
upstream fill/level problem remains

commonConfusion.name: heating element (as the automatic answer to 'not heating')
commonConfusion.note: 'Not heating = element' is too simplistic. The element produces heat, but sensing (NTC), switching (relay/control), wiring and the machine's sequence all determine whether it actually heats. Confirm a genuine no-heat first.
wouldApplyIf: genuine hot programme, fills/tumbles normally, reaches heating stage, target temperature not reached, and the NTC/wiring are not the stronger explanation

commonConfusion.name: cold laundry / cool door = heater failed
commonConfusion.note: Weak evidence on its own: final rinses are cold, eco/low-temp programmes heat little, and finished laundry naturally feels cool. Clarify the programme/temperature and how they judged it before recommending a part.
wouldApplyIf: there is objective evidence beyond cool laundry/door (stalls in wash, error, cold on a genuine hot wash)

commonConfusion.name: machine stuck on wash = control PCB
commonConfusion.note: On programme logic that waits for the target wash temperature, a heating failure often makes the machine REMAIN in wash (waiting for a temperature it never reaches). Fills+tumbles normally but washes for hours => raise the heating system, do not default to the PCB. (Common, not universal across platforms.)
wouldApplyIf: fill normal, tumble normal, drainage not blocking, stuck specifically in wash/heating at a consistent point

commonConfusion.name: the NTC heats the water
commonConfusion.note: It does not. The NTC is a negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor whose resistance changes with temperature; it provides temperature FEEDBACK to the controller. A faulty NTC can cause no/incorrect heat, overheating, or failure to progress - via wrong feedback, not by heating.
wouldApplyIf: heater appears serviceable but temperature feedback/behaviour is implausible or intermittent

commonConfusion.name: broken heater = just replace the heater
commonConfusion.note: On front-entry-heater designs a broken heater SUPPORT/BRACKET lets the heater move and contact the drum/tub, damaging it. If mechanically damaged, inspect the support and find WHY - otherwise a replacement heater may be damaged again.
wouldApplyIf: front-entry-heater design with mechanical damage to the heater

commonConfusion.name: sometimes completes so the heater must work (hot/cold-fill machines)
commonConfusion.note: On OLDER machines with SEPARATE hot and cold inlets, incoming hot water can occasionally be warm enough to reach the progression threshold despite a failed internal heater; on cooler cycles it sticks. Intermittent progression does NOT exclude a failed heater on hot/cold-fill machines. Do not apply to modern cold-fill-only machines.
wouldApplyIf: architecture confirmed as separate hot-and-cold fill, with variable progression and a suspected heater

docs.secondaryQuestion: What temperature and programme are you using, and does the machine have both a hot and a cold water inlet or only a cold one?
adviceBeforeReplacement: establish it should genuinely be heating (programme/temperature; not just cold rinses) before suspecting the heater
confirm it fills to the correct level and actually reaches the heating stage
on a front-entry-heater design with a physically damaged heater, inspect the heater support/bracket and find why it was damaged
if there is a serious burning smell, melted insulation or smoke, stop using the machine

docs.label: Overheating / unexpected heating
symptoms: gets hot on a cool wash
discriminators: Overheating is usually a SENSING or SWITCHING fault, not the element: implausible/incorrect temperature feedback => NTC; correct feedback but heater stays energised past target => relay/control stuck; element only with specific evidence.
SAFETY: excessive/abnormal heating is safety-relevant - do not encourage repeatedly running the machine just to reproduce severe overheating.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is it getting much hotter than the temperature you selected, even on a cooler wash?

components.name: NTC / temperature sensor
supports: much hotter than selected / hot on a cool wash
implausible temperature feedback
heating continues beyond the requested temperature
temperature-sensor error
against: temperature feedback appears correct (points to switching/relay)

components.name: temperature-sensor wiring
supports: intermittent/implausible readings from a loose/damaged NTC connector
against: sensor or control clearly explains it

components.name: heater relay / control stuck on
supports: temperature feedback appears correct but the heater stays energised past the target
relay/switching evidence
against: NTC feedback is implausible (sensor first)

components.name: heating element
supports: specific evidence implicates the element itself
against: the element makes heat fine - the fault is measuring/stopping the heat (NTC/relay)

commonConfusion.name: overheating = heating element
commonConfusion.note: Not necessarily. The element's ability to PRODUCE heat is usually fine; overheating is normally a failure to MEASURE (NTC) or STOP (relay/control) the heat. Lead with sensing/switching, not the element.
wouldApplyIf: specific evidence implicates the element itself

adviceBeforeReplacement: excessive heating is safety-relevant - avoid repeatedly reproducing it; if the door/water is dangerously hot, stop using the machine

docs.label: Door lock / interlock fault
symptoms: nothing happens when i press start
only starts if i push the door
starts if i lift the door
door still locked after the wash
discriminators: A door that stays LOCKED after a cycle was interrupted or didn't finish is usually a CONSEQUENCE of the cycle not completing (often a drain or heater fault leaving it mid-programme) - not a failed lock. Only suspect the lock itself if the cycle completed normally but the door still won't release, or it won't lock to start.

Won't start when you press start: if it STILL HAS power/lights, the usual cause is the door interlock not confirming the door is shut (or a failed door lock / start switch). If it's COMPLETELY DEAD with no lights, look at the mains/fuse or PCB instead (main-pcb).

There are TWO separate systems: a mechanical spring-loaded latch/catch that holds the door physically shut, and a SEPARATE electrical interlock that locks it during operation. Match the candidate to which one the evidence points at.
WATER IN DRUM + LOCKED => drainage / water-level FIRST (Story 9); the lock is likely protecting the customer. Do not force it or replace the lock.
JUST FINISHED / STILL HOT => a normal timed safety/unlock delay can hold it for a minute or two - wait before diagnosing a part. (Don't encode one maker's exact timing.)
EMPTY + COOL + HANDLE FLOPPY/BROKEN => MECHANICAL release/handle/catch/linkage leads; the electrical interlock is down-ranked.
PHYSICALLY WON'T CLOSE => obstruction/trapped clothing/overload/alignment/catch/hinge first, not the electrical lock.
CLOSES NORMALLY + POWERED + PROGRAMMABLE + WON'T START => electrical interlock / start-permission (NOT dead/no-power, Story 15).
STARTS ONLY IF THE DOOR IS PUSHED/LIFTED => hinge/alignment / worn catch / poor interlock engagement - argues AGAINST a generic PCB or power fault.
EMPTY but the controller behaves as though WATER REMAINS => a pressure/water-level false signal can hold the lock (see pressure-switch) - consider before replacing the lock.
Only once retained water, unlock delay, mechanical handle/catch and control-lock are excluded is a failed interlock/lock the answer.

ALREADY REPLACED the door lock / interlock and it STILL won't start? The new lock is proven, so move to the WIRING / loom to the interlock and the MAIN PCB (the control isn't sending or confirming the lock signal). Do NOT re-blame the lock, and do NOT default to the 'cycle didn't complete' explanation - that is for a door that won't OPEN after a wash, not a won't-START.

Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. retained water / not drained (lock correctly held) [CHECK]

2. normal unlock delay / still hot / programme not complete [CHECK]
   More likely if: wash has just finished (a timed safety lock holds it briefly); machine/water still hot; programme interrupted/not fully complete.

   More likely if: door physically fine, interlock and wiring proven good, water/level normal, but the lock isn't commanded.
   Less likely if: any physical/interlock/wiring/water cause remains (do not lead with the PCB).

   Only consider if: door physically fine, interlock and wiring proven good, but the lock isn't commanded.
- door seal because the complaint mentions 'door': A door seal is not normally why a machine electrically refuses to start. Trapped clothing or a badly displaced seal can physically prevent closure, but don't let the word 'door' over-rank the seal (see leak-flood for seal leaks).
   Only consider if: clothing/displaced seal is physically stopping the door closing.

Only suspect the lock itself if the cycle completed normally but the door still won't release, or it won't lock to start. Won't start when you press start: if it STILL HAS power/lights, the usual cause is the door interlock not confirming the door is shut (or a failed door lock / start switch). There are TWO separate systems: a mechanical spring-loaded latch/catch that holds the door physically shut, and a SEPARATE electrical interlock that locks it during operation. Do not force it or replace the lock. JUST FINISHED / STILL HOT => a normal timed safety/unlock delay can hold it for a minute or two - wait before diagnosing a part. (Don't encode one maker's exact timing.) EMPTY + COOL + HANDLE FLOPPY/BROKEN => MECHANICAL release/handle/catch/linkage leads; the electrical interlock is down-ranked. PHYSICALLY WON'T CLOSE => obstruction/trapped clothing/overload/alignment/catch/hinge first, not the electrical lock. CLOSES NORMALLY + POWERED + PROGRAMMABLE + WON'T START => electrical interlock / start-permission (NOT dead/no-power, Story 15). STARTS ONLY IF THE DOOR IS PUSHED/LIFTED => hinge/alignment / worn catch / poor interlock engagement - argues AGAINST a generic PCB or power fault. Likely parts in order: door handle, door catch, door hinge, door interlock, wiring harness, main pcb
Confused with: not-draining, pressure-switch, low-voltage, leak-flood, control-panel, main-pcb

docs.label: Motor / drum fault
symptoms: fills but drum just sits there
motor runs but drum doesnt turn
i can hear the motor but the drum isnt moving
drum stiff to turn by hand
washing still wet at the end
drum dropped and it's catching the clothes
clothes catching because the drum has dropped
door seal ripped because the drum has dropped
greasy black marks on my clothes and a rumble on spin
black oily marks on the washing with rumbling
discriminators: NOISE BY TIMING: a noise ONLY while DRAINING is the drain pump (see not-draining), not the drum. Motor can be heard but the drum doesn't turn = drive belt. Drum jerks / struggles to reach speed = motor or control/inverter (carbon brushes on brushed motors). Grinding/rumbling that worsens at high-speed spin = drum bearings.

A screech/squeal on spin = drum bearings or a glazed/slipping drive belt, NOT carbon brushes. A burning-rubber smell = a slipping/perished drive belt or a seized pump/motor - unplug it if the smell is strong.
Won't spin but drains fine and the drum turns freely by hand: carbon brushes (brushed motors) or a snapped/slipped drive belt.
Won't spin because water is left in the drum: it's a drain fault first (not-draining), not the motor.
Loud grinding/rumbling on spin with drum movement: drum bearings.
Brushless brands (LG/Samsung, newer Bosch): no carbon brushes - suspect the hall sensor or inverter PCB.

MODE SPLIT FIRST: (A) wash tumble works and only the FAST SPIN fails => spin-management: retained water (drainage), unbalanced load, overload, or reduced/no-spin programme - not a dead motor. (B) drum NEVER turns in wash or spin => genuine drive/drum fault.

PHYSICAL HAND-TURN (power off): drum STIFF/JAMMED/part-rotation => mechanical (foreign object / bearings / seizure) rises before any electronics. Drum turns FREELY => drive system (belt/brushes/capacitor/motor per architecture).
MOTOR HEARD, DRUM STATIONARY: on a belt-driven machine the drive belt/transmission rises sharply; on direct-drive the belt is absent and diagnosis follows the actual drive architecture.

ARCHITECTURE-AWARE (constrain candidates by the model where known): offer a DRIVE BELT only on belt-driven machines; CARBON BRUSHES only on brushed universal motors; a START/RUN CAPACITOR only on capacitor-start motors. Do not recommend a part the architecture doesn't have.
RETAINED WATER: no-spin with water left in the drum is a drainage route (see not-draining), NOT the motor. Empty drum => continue spin/drive diagnosis.

Existing engineer noise guide: deep RUMBLING/grinding worsening on spin = worn DRUM BEARINGS (rock the inner drum for up/down play); TICKING/knocking with paddles snapping = a trapped FOREIGN OBJECT; WHIPPING/slapping = a worn DRIVE BELT; the drain pump is the LAST suspect for noise.

CLOTHES DAMAGE + MECHANICAL EVIDENCE: if clothes are marked/caught/torn AND the drum has dropped/sagged, wobbles, or rumbles/roars on spin, the ROOT CAUSE is the worn drum bearing/spider (motor-drum) — the dropped drum fouls the seal/cabinet. GREASY or BLACK/OILY marks on washing = bearing grease driven past the tub seal. Ground motor-drum (or excessive-vibration when noise/instability dominates), NOT damaging-clothes.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does the drum turn normally during the wash and only fail on the fast spin, or does it not turn at all?

commonConfusion.name: won't spin = motor fault
commonConfusion.note: If wash tumble still works, first consider retained water (drainage), unbalanced load, overload and reduced/no-spin programme before any motor/drive part.
wouldApplyIf: drum is empty AND drains fully AND a balanced load on a full-spin programme still won't spin AND the drum turns freely by hand

commonConfusion.name: drum doesn't turn = drive belt
commonConfusion.note: Only valid on belt-driven machines. On direct-drive there is no belt - it must not be recommended. Confirm the drive architecture from the model.
wouldApplyIf: belt-driven architecture confirmed, motor heard running, drum free by hand

commonConfusion.name: burning smell / older machine = PCB or automatic carbon brushes
commonConfusion.note: On a confirmed BRUSHED motor, severely worn carbon brushes cause sparking, a burning/electrical smell and intermittent operation - so brushes rise there. But don't assume brushes on a brushless motor, and don't default to the PCB. Significant burning/smoke means stop-use first (see safety).
wouldApplyIf: confirmed brushed motor with sparking/burning-smell and intermittent rotation

commonConfusion.name: repeated slow drum movements / violent abort = failing motor
commonConfusion.note: Slow back-and-forth is deliberate load redistribution (drive works). Accelerate-then-violent-bang-then-abort is imbalance/levelling/suspension. Neither is automatically a motor fault.
wouldApplyIf: drum never turns at all, or the same failure repeats with a sensible balanced load

commonConfusion.name: clothes too wet / poor spin = motor or brushes
commonConfusion.note: Poor-spin is a ROUTER: rule out retained water (not-draining), load imbalance (unbalanced-load), spin-speed/programme selection, and excessive foam (foam-suds) BEFORE motor/brushes/tacho. Slow back-and-forth redistribution means the drive works.
wouldApplyIf: the drum drains fully, the load is balanced and full-spin is selected, yet it still won't reach spin speed

commonConfusion.name: direct-drive won't spin = motor/brushes
commonConfusion.note: On a direct-drive/brushless machine there are NO carbon brushes and NO belt; abnormal powered movement with a free drum points to hall/rotor-position sensing or the inverter (see hall-sensor), after ruling out retained water/imbalance/jam.
wouldApplyIf: confirmed direct-drive, drum free by hand, abnormal powered twitching

docs.secondaryQuestion: With the machine switched off does the drum turn freely by hand, and is all the water gone before it tries to spin?
adviceBeforeReplacement: confirm all the water has drained before treating it as a spin fault
try a normal, evenly-distributed load (and check the spin/programme setting isn't reduced/off)
with the power off, turn the drum by hand to tell mechanical (stiff) from drive (free)
identify the drive architecture (belt-driven vs direct-drive; brushed vs brushless; capacitor-equipped) before recommending a drive part
if there is significant burning smell, smoke or heavy sparking, stop using the machine and do not keep power-testing it

2. unbalanced load / overload / spin-setting [CHECK]
   More likely if: wash tumble works, drum empty, but fast spin is refused; single heavy item / bath mat / very full or tiny load; keeps turning slowly to redistribute; reduced/no-spin programme selected; spins fine with a sensible balanced load.
   Less likely if: drum does not rotate during wash either; same failure with a balanced load on a full-spin programme.
3. foreign object / mechanical obstruction [CHECK]
   More likely if: drum stiff/jammed or only part-rotates by hand; scraping/ticking/knocking, paddles snapping off; sudden mechanical restriction (bra wire, coin between drums).
   Less likely if: drum turns freely and smoothly by hand.
4. drum bearings [PART]
   More likely if: drum rough/stiff by hand with up/down play when rocked; deep rumbling/grinding that worsens on spin; progressively worsening mechanical noise independent of the motor.
   Less likely if: drum turns freely/smoothly; motor heard running while drum stays still and drive transmission explains it.
5. drive belt [belt-driven machines ONLY] [PART]
   More likely if: belt-driven architecture; motor can be heard running but drum stays still; drum turns freely by hand; sudden failure / prior belt slip or whipping noise.
   Less likely if: DIRECT-DRIVE architecture (no belt) - do NOT recommend; drum mechanically seized; motor itself not operating.
6. carbon brushes [brushed universal motor ONLY] [PART]
   More likely if: confirmed brushed/universal motor; intermittent/weak/hesitant rotation worsening over time; sparking around the motor and/or a motor-area burning smell on a brushed motor; significant brush wear for the age/use.
   Less likely if: brushless/inverter/direct-drive motor with no replaceable brushes - do NOT recommend; motor runs normally but drum stationary (belt/transmission); drum mechanically seized.
7. motor thermal fuse / cut-out [PART]
   More likely if: brushed motor where worn brushes have sparked and tripped the cut-out; motor dead after overheat/sparking.
   Less likely if: mechanical seizure or belt explains it; non-brushed architecture where this isn't fitted.
8. start / run capacitor [capacitor-start motors ONLY] [PART]
   More likely if: confirmed capacitor-equipped motor architecture; drum free by hand, belt intact; motor HUMS but fails to start / can't develop starting torque.
   Less likely if: motor architecture does not use a capacitor - do NOT recommend; drum seized; broken belt explains motor-runs/drum-still; motor runs normally during wash.
9. drive motor [PART]
   More likely if: drum free, belt intact where applicable, brushes/capacitor not applicable or excluded; motor fails during both wash and spin; motor-specific error where available.
   Less likely if: drum rotates normally in wash (imbalance-only); retained water explains it; belt/brush/capacitor/mechanical cause better explains it.
10. motor control / inverter module [where architecture uses one] [PART]
   More likely if: correct architecture; mechanical drive intact, motor not obviously failed; drive-control error / motor not being driven correctly.
   Less likely if: simpler mechanical/load/water cause remains; belt/brush/capacitor cause applicable and unexcluded.
11. wiring / main PCB [PART]
   More likely if: mechanical drive confirmed good and architecture-specific motor parts excluded; motor not commanded/supplied correctly with wiring/connector evidence.
   Less likely if: drainage/load/programme cause remains; belt/brush/capacitor/mechanical cause remains; drive architecture not yet established.
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- won't spin = motor fault: If wash tumble still works, first consider retained water (drainage), unbalanced load, overload and reduced/no-spin programme before any motor/drive part.
   Only consider if: drum is empty AND drains fully AND a balanced load on a full-spin programme still won't spin AND the drum turns freely by hand.
- drum doesn't turn = drive belt: Only valid on belt-driven machines. On direct-drive there is no belt - it must not be recommended. Confirm the drive architecture from the model.
   Only consider if: belt-driven architecture confirmed, motor heard running, drum free by hand.
- burning smell / older machine = PCB or automatic carbon brushes: On a confirmed BRUSHED motor, severely worn carbon brushes cause sparking, a burning/electrical smell and intermittent operation - so brushes rise there. But don't assume brushes on a brushless motor, and don't default to the PCB. Significant burning/smoke means stop-use first (see safety).
   Only consider if: confirmed brushed motor with sparking/burning-smell and intermittent rotation.
- repeated slow drum movements / violent abort = failing motor: Slow back-and-forth is deliberate load redistribution (drive works). Accelerate-then-violent-bang-then-abort is imbalance/levelling/suspension. Neither is automatically a motor fault.
   Only consider if: drum never turns at all, or the same failure repeats with a sensible balanced load.
- clothes too wet / poor spin = motor or brushes: Poor-spin is a ROUTER: rule out retained water (not-draining), load imbalance (unbalanced-load), spin-speed/programme selection, and excessive foam (foam-suds) BEFORE motor/brushes/tacho. Slow back-and-forth redistribution means the drive works.
   Only consider if: the drum drains fully, the load is balanced and full-spin is selected, yet it still won't reach spin speed.
- direct-drive won't spin = motor/brushes: On a direct-drive/brushless machine there are NO carbon brushes and NO belt; abnormal powered movement with a free drum points to hall/rotor-position sensing or the inverter (see hall-sensor), after ruling out retained water/imbalance/jam.
   Only consider if: confirmed direct-drive, drum free by hand, abnormal powered twitching.
Engineering notes: NOISE BY TIMING: a noise ONLY while DRAINING is the drain pump (see not-draining), not the drum. Motor can be heard but the drum doesn't turn = drive belt. Drum jerks / struggles to reach speed = motor or control/inverter (carbon brushes on brushed motors). Grinding/rumbling that worsens at high-speed spin = drum bearings. A screech/squeal on spin = drum bearings or a glazed/slipping drive belt, NOT carbon brushes. A burning-rubber smell = a slipping/perished drive belt or a seized pump/motor - unplug it if the smell is strong. Won't spin but drains fine and the drum turns freely by hand: carbon brushes (brushed motors) or a snapped/slipped drive belt. Won't spin because water is left in the drum: it's a drain fault first (not-draining), not the motor. Loud grinding/rumbling on spin with drum movement: drum bearings. Brushless brands (LG/Samsung, newer Bosch): no carbon brushes - suspect the hall sensor or inverter PCB. MODE SPLIT FIRST: (A) wash tumble works and only the FAST SPIN fails => spin-management: retained water (drainage), unbalanced load, overload, or reduced/no-spin programme - not a dead motor. (B) drum NEVER turns in wash or spin => genuine drive/drum fault. PHYSICAL HAND-TURN (power off): drum STIFF/JAMMED/part-rotation => mechanical (foreign object / bearings / seizure) rises before any electronics. Drum turns FREELY => drive system (belt/brushes/capacitor/motor per architecture). MOTOR HEARD, DRUM STATIONARY: on a belt-driven machine the drive belt/transmission rises sharply; on direct-drive the belt is absent and diagnosis follows the actual drive architecture. ARCHITECTURE-AWARE (constrain candidates by the model where known): offer a DRIVE BELT only on belt-driven machines; CARBON BRUSHES only on brushed universal motors; a START/RUN CAPACITOR only on capacitor-start motors. Do not recommend a part the architecture doesn't have. RETAINED WATER: no-spin with water left in the drum is a drainage route (see not-draining), NOT the motor. Empty drum => continue spin/drive diagnosis. Existing engineer noise guide: deep RUMBLING/grinding worsening on spin = worn DRUM BEARINGS (rock the inner drum for up/down play); TICKING/knocking with paddles snapping = a trapped FOREIGN OBJECT; WHIPPING/slapping = a worn DRIVE BELT; the drain pump is the LAST suspect for noise. CLOTHES DAMAGE + MECHANICAL EVIDENCE: if clothes are marked/caught/torn AND the drum has dropped/sagged, wobbles, or rumbles/roars on spin, the ROOT CAUSE is the worn drum bearing/spider (motor-drum) — the dropped drum fouls the seal/cabinet. GREASY or BLACK/OILY marks on washing = bearing grease driven past the tub seal. Ground motor-drum (or excessive-vibration when noise/instability dominates), NOT damaging-clothes.
Likely parts in order: drum bearing, drive belt, carbon brushes, motor thermal fuse, start capacitor, drive motor, motor module, main pcb
Confused with: not-draining, unbalanced-load, motor-triac, drain-pump, excessive-vibration, foam-suds, tacho, hall-sensor
Advice before replacing parts: confirm all the water has drained before treating it as a spin fault; try a normal, evenly-distributed load (and check the spin/programme setting isn't reduced/off); with the power off, turn the drum by hand to tell mechanical (stiff) from drive (free); identify the drive architecture (belt-driven vs direct-drive; brushed vs brushless; capacitor-equipped) before recommending a drive part; if there is significant burning smell, smoke or heavy sparking, stop using the machine and do not keep power-testing it
Best question to ask if unsure: Does the drum turn normally during the wash and only fail on the fast spin, or does it not turn at all?
Follow-up question if still unclear: With the machine switched off does the drum turn freely by hand, and is all the water gone before it tries to spin?

docs.label: Motor speed sensor (tachometer) fault
symptoms: motor revs up really fast then stops
spins too fast then cuts out
drum spins very fast then stops
discriminators: ARCHITECTURE FIRST: brushed/universal motor => tacho coil + magnet on the shaft AND carbon brushes exist (check brushes before the tacho). Brushless/direct-drive => hall/rotor-position sensing (see hall-sensor), NO brushes.

Distinguish the failure MODE: motor doesn't run at all vs runs intermittently vs over-speeds vs speed hunts vs fails only at high-speed spin vs obvious brush symptoms (arcing/burning). Worn brushes commonly cause intermittent/erratic operation and can trigger speed-sensor error codes.
Error codes are evidence WITH make/model context, NOT universal mappings — do not encode 'code = tacho' across brands.
REPLACEMENT ORDER: rule out a jammed drum (turn by hand) and worn brushes before condemning the tacho coil or the control board.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does the motor race/over-speed and then cut out, or fail to build up spin at all — and is it an older machine with a carbon-brush motor?

supports: drum stiff or won't turn by hand with the power off
something obstructing the drum
against: drum turns freely and smoothly by hand

components.name: carbon brushes [brushed / universal motor ONLY]
supports: older brushed-motor machine
arcing/sparking or a burning smell from the motor
erratic or over-speed then cut-out
intermittent running or gradual loss of power
against: brushless / inverter / direct-drive motor (no brushes) — do NOT recommend
brushes inspected and still long

components.name: tacho coil / magnet + connector
supports: speed-sensor symptom with brushes proven good (or a brushless machine)
tacho coil open-circuit or dislodged magnet on the motor shaft
no speed feedback / over-speed with a free-turning drum
against: carbon brushes not yet checked on a brushed machine
the drum is mechanically jammed

components.name: wiring / connector motor to control
supports: intermittent speed error
chafed or loose loom to the motor

commonConfusion.name: speed error = replace the tacho
commonConfusion.note: NOT acceptable as a default. On a brushed motor, badly worn carbon brushes cause the same speed-feedback/erratic-speed symptoms — check brushes FIRST where the architecture has them.

commonConfusion.note: Manufacturer error codes are NOT portable across brands/generations, and the same number means different things on brush vs brushless motors — interpret only with make/model context.
wouldApplyIf: make/model is known and its own documentation maps the code to the speed sensor

commonConfusion.note: Direct-drive/brushless machines have no carbon brushes and use hall/rotor-position sensing instead (see hall-sensor); don't recommend brushes.
wouldApplyIf: a confirmed brushless / direct-drive architecture

docs.label: Hall / rotor position sensor fault (direct-drive)
discriminators: ARCHITECTURE FIRST: BRUSHED => carbon brushes + commutator + conventional tacho (see tacho); BRUSHLESS/INVERTER/DIRECT-DRIVE => hall/rotor-position + stator/rotor + inverter, NO brushes, NO conventional belt. With the machine OFF, hand-rotate the drum: STIFF/locked => mechanical path (jam/bearing/foreign object); FREE + abnormal powered movement (twitch/judder, can't establish speed) => motor/sensing/control path becomes plausible.

docs.label: Control board / PCB fault (incl. EEPROM/config)
discriminators: If it went 'dead'/stuck RIGHT AFTER washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet), that's almost certainly an unbalanced load, not this - the machine is stalled trying to rebalance. Redistribute/add smaller items and re-run before suspecting a part (see unbalanced-load).
For DEAD/no-power, route to low-voltage first (supply -> filter -> wiring -> PCB last). The PCB is the right answer only once the cheaper incoming-power causes are excluded.
The PCB's own domain is erratic/random behaviour, config/EEPROM faults and module comms - not 'the machine is dead so it must be the board'.

supports: erratic/random programme behaviour, settings not saving, config/EEPROM error, unexplained control faults with the machine otherwise powered
against: a single specific symptom better explained by a sensor/actuator

components.name: wiring / connectors to the board
supports: intermittent/erratic behaviour that responds to disturbance
burnt/loose connector

commonConfusion.name: dead / no power = replace the PCB
commonConfusion.note: For a DEAD machine, exclude the external supply, plug/lead, mains filter and incoming wiring first (see low-voltage). The PCB power-supply is a last, evidence-based conclusion - don't lead with it.

Fault: Control board / PCB fault (incl. EEPROM/config)
Customer phrases: dead; no power; erratic behaviour; eeprom fault; software error; control board fault; programme behaviour random; settings not saving; board fault
Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. control PCB (power-supply section) [for a DEAD machine] [PART]
   More likely if: truly dead AND external supply, plug/lead, mains filter and incoming wiring all confirmed good.
   Less likely if: supply/lead/filter/wiring not excluded (see low-voltage); machine powers up but won't start (see door-lock).
2. control PCB / EEPROM / config [erratic behaviour] [PART]
   More likely if: erratic/random programme behaviour, settings not saving, config/EEPROM error, unexplained control faults with the machine otherwise powered.
   Less likely if: a single specific symptom better explained by a sensor/actuator.
3. wiring / connectors to the board [CHECK]
   More likely if: intermittent/erratic behaviour that responds to disturbance; burnt/loose connector.
   Less likely if: board clearly faulty with sound wiring.
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- dead / no power = replace the PCB: For a DEAD machine, exclude the external supply, plug/lead, mains filter and incoming wiring first (see low-voltage). The PCB power-supply is a last, evidence-based conclusion - don't lead with it.
   Only consider if: dead with supply/lead/filter/wiring all confirmed good.
Engineering notes: If it went 'dead'/stuck RIGHT AFTER washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet), that's almost certainly an unbalanced load, not this - the machine is stalled trying to rebalance. Redistribute/add smaller items and re-run before suspecting a part (see unbalanced-load). For DEAD/no-power, route to low-voltage first (supply -> filter -> wiring -> PCB last). The PCB is the right answer only once the cheaper incoming-power causes are excluded. The PCB's own domain is erratic/random behaviour, config/EEPROM faults and module comms - not 'the machine is dead so it must be the board'.
Likely parts in order: main pcb, wiring harness
Confused with: low-voltage, comms, control-panel
Best question to ask if unsure: Is the machine completely dead, or does it power up but behave erratically / not save settings?

docs.label: Water leak / anti-flood (water in the base)
discriminators: A DARK, greasy/oily leak (not clear water) usually means the DRUM BEARINGS have failed - the bearing seal lets water past and dark residue out - or an oil-filled shock absorber is leaking. Listen for a grinding/rumbling on spin (bearings). Do NOT tell the customer the machine has no oil; front-loaders do have greased bearings and oil-damped absorbers. Clear-water leaks are the door seal, sump hose, pump or inlet valve.

Only say the anti-flood/Aquastop has TRIGGERED if the customer actually reports water in the base tray, a machine that has locked with a flood warning, or an anti-flood/LE/LC code - not for a plain 'it's leaking'.
If the customer can say WHERE the water appears (front/door, drawer, underneath, rear) or WHEN (fill, wash, drain/spin), use the matching leak-source node for a more specific diagnosis.

COMMIT-FIRST: an explicit report of external water pooling/escaping - 'leaking underneath', 'water/puddle on the floor', 'leaks water', 'water pouring out' - is enough on its own to COMMIT the leak-flood route; do not withhold the route or ask whether it is really a leak. (Water specifically from the DETERGENT DRAWER/soap dispenser still belongs to the dispenser route, not generic leak-flood.) THEN DIAGNOSE BY WHERE + WHEN + APPEARANCE: location (front/back/underneath, left/right), cycle stage (fill / wash / drain-spin / while off), and water appearance (clean / soapy-dirty / oily-dirty) pin the part far better than 'leak' alone. Use these ONLY to narrow the source component (door seal, sump hose, drain pump, dispenser, inlet valve, tub/bearing) as a follow-up refinement - not as a precondition for routing.
DURING FILL: dispenser path first (drawer residue/oversudsing = CHECK), then dispenser-to-tub hose; external rear fill hose rises mainly after a recent move/disturbance or visible damage.
LEFT SIDE + DURING FILL => strongly consider the dispenser-to-tub hose/path WHERE THE MODEL LAYOUT SUPPORTS IT - not a universal rule; use the actual architecture if known.

DRAIN/SPIN + RIGHT SIDE + relatively CLEAN water => pump/pump-housing/filter area rises WHERE THE MODEL LAYOUT SUPPORTS IT - again not universal. But if it started after a filter clean, check the filter cap/seal seating BEFORE the pump.
DIRTY/OILY water underneath across the front + rumbling/drum play/dropped drum => drum bearings / tub seal (a multi-observation call, not 'water underneath = pump').
BIG sudden leak + loud banging/impact => loose counterweight cracking the tub; don't reduce to 'split hose'.
WHILE OFF: CLEAN water still ENTERING => mechanically passing inlet valve (Story-10); DIRTY water backing in => waste plumbing/backflow, not an appliance part.

OVERFILL masquerade: if the water level goes abnormally high and THEN it leaks, diagnose the overfill cause (pressure chamber/hose/level sensing/passing valve) - the escape point may be a consequence, not the fault.

CAUSAL CHAINS: (A) bearing/drum-drop -> seal ripped; (B) loose counterweight -> tub cracked; (C) overfill -> secondary escape; (D) oversudsing -> foam escapes. Address the underlying cause, not just the escape point.
SAFETY: a large uncontrolled leak or water reaching electrical parts is a stop-use situation, not continued operation.

leak only while the pump is discharging
clear door-seal source

leak far larger than hose seepage

clear minor hose/seal source

against: DIRTY waste water appears while off (waste plumbing/backflow, not an appliance part)

commonConfusion.name: the leaking component is the failed component
commonConfusion.note: Often the component water escapes through is the VICTIM, not the cause. A ripped door seal can be caused by a dropped drum/bearing; a cracked tub by a loose counterweight; an escape point by an overfill or oversudsing event. Ask WHY it leaked.
wouldApplyIf: there is supporting evidence of an underlying mechanical/level/dosing cause

commonConfusion.name: door seal ripped = just replace the seal
commonConfusion.note: If the boot is badly ripped, check for abnormal drum play / a dropped drum / bearing noise first - a rotating drum contacting the seal tears it, and a new seal will be destroyed too if the drum fault isn't fixed.
wouldApplyIf: seal torn AND drum has up/down play, sits low, or rumbles on spin

commonConfusion.name: water at the front = door seal
commonConfusion.note: It can equally be the dispenser above (down the front), the filter/pump area, or oversudsing. Locate the true source first.
wouldApplyIf: water is clearly seen passing THROUGH the door seal, not from above or below

commonConfusion.name: foam coming out = a failed seal/pump
commonConfusion.note: Excessive foam (too much/unsuitable detergent) can push water/foam out of the drawer/door/vent with NO failed part. Check dosing/oversudsing first.
wouldApplyIf: a genuine leak persists with correct detergent and no excess foam

commonConfusion.name: leaks during fill = external inlet hose
commonConfusion.note: A fill hose spontaneously leaking is relatively uncommon unless the machine was recently moved/disturbed or is visibly damaged. During fill, also strongly consider the dispenser path and dispenser-to-tub hose.
wouldApplyIf: leak clearly at the rear connection, or the machine was recently moved/reconnected

commonConfusion.name: large leak = split hose
commonConfusion.note: A big leak WITH severe mechanical banging can be a loose counterweight cracking the tub - not a simple hose.
wouldApplyIf: large sudden leak accompanied by loud banging / severe vibration

commonConfusion.name: foam from the drawer/door = a leak
commonConfusion.note: Excess foam escaping is over-sudsing (foam-suds), not a hydraulic leak — the escape point is a consequence. Clear or dirty WATER escaping is a real leak.
wouldApplyIf: actual water (not foam) is escaping the machine

docs.secondaryQuestion: Is the leaking water clean, soapy/dirty wash water, or dirty/oily-looking water?
adviceBeforeReplacement: establish WHERE the water appears, WHEN in the cycle, and what it LOOKS like before choosing a part
if it started after cleaning the filter, re-seat the filter cap/seal and check the sealing face before suspecting the pump

likelyComponents: check the door seal folds for trapped debris or coins

docs.label: Unbalanced load (spin aborted / stops mid-cycle)
symptoms: keeps trying to spin then stops
discriminators: Started right after washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet, blanket): that's an unbalanced load, not a fault. The item soaks up water and sticks to one side, so the machine keeps trying to redistribute and won't spin up (can look 'stuck' or 'dead' mid-cycle). Pause, open the door, redistribute or add a few smaller items, then re-run - no part needed.
Happens on EVERY load with normal mixed washing, and the machine bangs/walks: then suspect worn shock absorbers or suspension, or (with a grinding/rumbling noise) drum bearings.
Won't spin AND water is left in the drum: that's a drain fault (see not-draining), not balance.

Distinguish: slow back-and-forth REDISTRIBUTION (load/imbalance; drive is fine) vs accelerate-then-VIOLENT-bang-and-abort (levelling/installation, or suspension if repeatable with balanced loads) vs NEVER turns (drive/mechanical - see motor-drum).
A machine that aborts spin only with a bath mat/heavy single item/duvet and spins fine with a normal balanced load is load/imbalance, NOT a fault - do not recommend a part.
Retained water inhibits spin too: if water remains, that is a drainage route (see not-draining), not imbalance.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does it keep turning slowly backwards and forwards as if trying to balance the load, and does it spin fine with a different, evenly-spread load?

docs.label: Excess foam / suds detected
symptoms: foam coming out of the drawer
foam coming out of the door
wont spin because of the foam
discriminators: Excess foam is almost always too much detergent or the wrong (non-HE) type - reduce the dose and run a rinse/spin to clear the suds FIRST; this is a free fix, not a part. Only if it keeps happening at the correct dose does the pressure chamber/switch (false suds/level sensing) warrant checking.
Foam pushing water out of the drawer or door is a consequence of the suds, not a failed drawer or seal.

3-WAY BOUNDARY (Story-18 D-class #1 + Story-19): obvious FOAM/suds dominant => foam-suds (advice). WATER pouring from the drawer WITHOUT excessive foam => dispenser / blocked flow path. Genuine WATER leak (split hose/seal/pump/tub/bearing seal) => leak-flood. Foam escaping the drawer/door is a consequence, not a failed drawer/seal.
Strongly CHECK/advice-first: reduce dose, use the correct HE / 'for automatic machines' detergent, run rinse/drain cycles without detergent, and let suds settle before draining.
SUDS-LOCK: heavy foam can clog the pump/hoses and stop drain/spin — don't force-drain; let it settle (cross-link not-draining).
AUTO-DOSE (where fitted): check the dose setting/concentration before any pump/control part.

docs.label: Mains supply / voltage / frequency fault
symptoms: keeps going dead then comes back
cuts out then comes back on
discriminators: If it went 'dead'/stuck RIGHT AFTER washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet), that's almost certainly an unbalanced load, not this - the machine is stalled trying to rebalance. Redistribute/add smaller items and re-run before suspecting a part (see unbalanced-load).

ESTABLISH TRULY DEAD FIRST: absolutely no lights/display/response = dead/no-power family; powers up and lets you select a programme but won't Start = door-lock/start-permission (see door-lock), NOT dead.

EXTERNAL SUPPLY FIRST for a truly dead machine: does the socket work with another device, is any switched/fused spur on, is the plug/lead seated? Recent house move / machine move raises supply/installation strongly. These are CHECKS, not appliance parts.

CONFIRMED SUPPLY + STILL DEAD: work the incoming-power path - mains interference suppressor/filter (first component powered) -> incoming wiring/connector -> power switch (if fitted) -> PCB low-voltage power-supply LAST. Do not rank the PCB first.

BLOWN FUSE = ask WHY it blew (evidence, not the fix). Do not instruct repeated fuse replacement, live testing, insulation/earth-leakage testing or bypassing protection - that's beyond WhichPart; advise professional electrical diagnosis if needed.

TIMING (use already-observed behaviour, don't ask them to reproduce an electrical fault): dead from the outset => incoming supply/filter/wiring/PCB; died around the HEATING stage => the heater circuit deserves strong consideration (high-current, in contact with water) but not certainty - cross-ref heater/tripping-electrics; died when the MOTOR/drum started => motor/drive electrical path (motor-drum); died at another repeatable stage => the component active at that stage.

INTERMITTENTLY DEAD (comes back later, responds to disturbing the plug/lead) => loose/burnt connection, mains lead, filter, power switch or a thermal/intermittent PCB power fault - distinct from permanently dead. Do NOT tell the customer to manipulate wiring/connections while powered.

BURNING SMELL / POP / BANG then dead => mains filter, burnt connector/wiring, PCB/power electronics, or another component causing secondary electrical damage - do NOT equate a burning smell with the PCB. Stop-use safety applies.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is it completely dead with no lights or display at all, or does it power up and let you choose a programme but then not start?

components.name: property socket / supply / switched fused spur
supports: recently moved home or the machine recently moved/installed
the socket may be dead
there may be a separate switched/fused spur controlling the socket that has been switched off
another appliance also has no power from that supply
against: the socket is confirmed working with another device AND any switched spur is on

components.name: power cord / plug / lead seated and undamaged
supports: vibration can work the plug loose from the socket over time
damaged/pinched lead or plug
responds when the plug/lead is reseated
against: plug firmly seated and lead undamaged

components.name: mains interference suppressor / mains filter
supports: socket/supply/lead confirmed good but the machine is completely dead
the filter is the first component powered when plugged in
a pop/bang/burning smell preceded going dead
failure after a power cut/surge
against: external supply not yet confirmed
the machine actually powers up (not truly dead)

components.name: incoming wiring / burnt connector
supports: burnt/discoloured connector or open wiring in the incoming path
intermittent power that responds to disturbance
burning smell
against: incoming wiring intact; the fault is clearly the filter or PCB power section

components.name: power switch [architectures that use a distinct on/off switch]
supports: the design uses a mechanical/electronic mains power switch and it is faulty/intermittent
against: touch-control machine with no separate power switch

components.name: control PCB low-voltage power-supply section
supports: external supply, lead, mains filter and incoming wiring all confirmed good, machine still completely dead
the low-voltage power-supply section of the board has failed
against: supply/lead/filter/wiring NOT yet excluded (do not lead with the PCB for a dead machine)
machine powers up (not dead)

commonConfusion.name: powered-but-won't-start = dead
commonConfusion.note: If the display/lights work and a programme can be selected but pressing Start does nothing, the machine is NOT dead - the door interlock / start-permission / control-lock path is the leading route (see door-lock). Don't let 'won't start' become 'dead/no power'.
wouldApplyIf: there are genuinely NO lights/display/response at all

commonConfusion.name: display dead but the machine still responds/runs = total power loss
commonConfusion.note: A failed display/UI module or its connection can leave the display blank while the rest of the machine still works - that is a UI/display fault (see control-panel/comms), not a loss of appliance power.
wouldApplyIf: there is truly no power anywhere (no response at all)

commonConfusion.name: dead = replace the control PCB
commonConfusion.note: Do not lead with the PCB because the machine is dead. Exclude the external supply, plug/lead, mains filter and incoming wiring first; the PCB power-supply section is an evidence-based last conclusion.
wouldApplyIf: supply, lead, mains filter and wiring are all confirmed good and it's still dead

commonConfusion.name: blown plug fuse = replace the fuse and it's fixed
commonConfusion.note: A blown fuse is EVIDENCE, not automatically the fault - ask WHY it blew. Replacing it may restore power without addressing the cause. A healthy fuse doesn't prove there's no fault (RCD/MCB may operate first). Do NOT repeatedly replace fuses or carry out electrical testing.
wouldApplyIf: the fuse blew with no underlying electrical fault (e.g. a genuinely one-off event) - which cannot be assumed

if there was a pop/bang/burning smell, or any sign of burnt wiring, stop using it and unplug it
