Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- powered-but-won't-start = dead: If the display/lights work and a programme can be selected but pressing Start does nothing, the machine is NOT dead - the door interlock / start-permission / control-lock path is the leading route (see door-lock). Don't let 'won't start' become 'dead/no power'.
   Only consider if: there are genuinely NO lights/display/response at all.
- display dead but the machine still responds/runs = total power loss: A failed display/UI module or its connection can leave the display blank while the rest of the machine still works - that is a UI/display fault (see control-panel/comms), not a loss of appliance power.
   Only consider if: there is truly no power anywhere (no response at all).
- dead = replace the control PCB: Do not lead with the PCB because the machine is dead. Exclude the external supply, plug/lead, mains filter and incoming wiring first; the PCB power-supply section is an evidence-based last conclusion.
   Only consider if: supply, lead, mains filter and wiring are all confirmed good and it's still dead.
- blown plug fuse = replace the fuse and it's fixed: A blown fuse is EVIDENCE, not automatically the fault - ask WHY it blew. Replacing it may restore power without addressing the cause. A healthy fuse doesn't prove there's no fault (RCD/MCB may operate first). Do NOT repeatedly replace fuses or carry out electrical testing.
   Only consider if: the fuse blew with no underlying electrical fault (e.g. a genuinely one-off event) - which cannot be assumed.
Engineering notes: If it went 'dead'/stuck RIGHT AFTER washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet), that's almost certainly an unbalanced load, not this - the machine is stalled trying to rebalance. Redistribute/add smaller items and re-run before suspecting a part (see unbalanced-load). ESTABLISH TRULY DEAD FIRST: absolutely no lights/display/response = dead/no-power family; powers up and lets you select a programme but won't Start = door-lock/start-permission (see door-lock), NOT dead. EXTERNAL SUPPLY FIRST for a truly dead machine: does the socket work with another device, is any switched/fused spur on, is the plug/lead seated? Recent house move / machine move raises supply/installation strongly. These are CHECKS, not appliance parts. CONFIRMED SUPPLY + STILL DEAD: work the incoming-power path - mains interference suppressor/filter (first component powered) -> incoming wiring/connector -> power switch (if fitted) -> PCB low-voltage power-supply LAST. Do not rank the PCB first. BLOWN FUSE = ask WHY it blew (evidence, not the fix). Do not instruct repeated fuse replacement, live testing, insulation/earth-leakage testing or bypassing protection - that's beyond WhichPart; advise professional electrical diagnosis if needed. TIMING (use already-observed behaviour, don't ask them to reproduce an electrical fault): dead from the outset => incoming supply/filter/wiring/PCB; died around the HEATING stage => the heater circuit deserves strong consideration (high-current, in contact with water) but not certainty - cross-ref heater/tripping-electrics; died when the MOTOR/drum started => motor/drive electrical path (motor-drum); died at another repeatable stage => the component active at that stage. INTERMITTENTLY DEAD (comes back later, responds to disturbing the plug/lead) => loose/burnt connection, mains lead, filter, power switch or a thermal/intermittent PCB power fault - distinct from permanently dead. Do NOT tell the customer to manipulate wiring/connections while powered. BURNING SMELL / POP / BANG then dead => mains filter, burnt connector/wiring, PCB/power electronics, or another component causing secondary electrical damage - do NOT equate a burning smell with the PCB. Stop-use safety applies.
Likely parts in order: mains lead, mains filter, wiring harness, power switch, main pcb
Confused with: door-lock, main-pcb, heater, tripping-electrics, control-panel
Advice before replacing parts: check the socket works with another appliance and that any separate switched/fused spur controlling it is on (especially after a recent move); check the plug is fully seated and the lead undamaged - vibration can work a plug loose over time; if there was a pop/bang/burning smell, or any sign of burnt wiring, stop using it and unplug it; a blown plug fuse is a clue - the underlying cause needs finding; do not just keep replacing fuses, and leave electrical testing to a professional
Best question to ask if unsure: Is it completely dead with no lights or display at all, or does it power up and let you choose a programme but then not start?
Follow-up question if still unclear: Do other nearby sockets have power, and has the machine or your home recently been moved or had a power cut?

docs.label: Detergent dispenser fault
symptoms: water only trickles into the drawer
water down the front from the drawer
discriminators: WATER-DELIVERY CHAIN: is there adequate incoming water? -> is it reaching the dispenser? -> is the correct compartment getting adequate flow? -> can that water/product leave? Only THEN a failed valve/distributor/dispenser part.
KEY: when it should take detergent/conditioner, does PLENTY of water enter that compartment, just a TRICKLE, or NONE? (adequate-but-not-emptying vs low-flow vs no-flow).
ALL compartments weak / trickle => property pressure -> isolation tap/hose -> inlet filter -> partially-opening inlet valve (Story-10), BEFORE local dispenser faults.
ONE compartment fails, others work => local jet/channel/siphon or an architecture-specific distributor/diverter/valve path; generic property pressure moves DOWN.

CONDITIONER remains BUT water entered => siphon cap/insert/channel/jets, residue, softener above MAX / too thick - NOT the inlet valve (water demonstrably reached it). Conditioner is siphon-drawn on the final rinse.
CONDITIONER gets NO water (others fine) => the water-delivery path to that compartment (jet/channel/diverter).
POWDER remains: little/no water => delivery path; good water but powder remains => caking / too much / wrong or liquid detergent / blocked drawer.

OVERFLOW / down the front => direction matters: no water IN = upstream supply/valve/channel; water IN but can't LEAVE = drawer/siphon/dispenser-to-tub path. Cross-ref leak-flood; loads of foam => foam-suds.
LIQUID detergent in the drawer can cake/congeal - establish powder vs liquid, correct compartment, and any liquid insert/flap; clean, don't replace.

AUTO-DOSE (architecture): first establish conventional-drawer vs auto-dose. Auto-dose CHECKS: enabled / dose set (often OFF by default or after a power cut), reservoir has the right product, concentration set to match, congealed detergent, air-pocket, needs cleaning/self-clean - pump/control only if the architecture confirms one and checks fail.
PCB / dispenser assembly are NOT default fallbacks - exclude physical/hydraulic/use causes first.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: When it should take the detergent or conditioner, does plenty of water enter that compartment, just a trickle, or no water at all?

components.name: property water pressure / cold supply
supports: ALL compartments flush weakly / water only trickles in
fill is generally slow
poor supply or recent supply change
against: only ONE compartment affected (others flush fine)
water clearly enters the compartment but product remains

components.name: isolation tap / inlet hose restriction
supports: tap only part-open or hose kinked/crushed (all-compartment weak flow)
machine recently moved
against: good flow demonstrated and only one compartment affected

components.name: inlet-valve inlet filter / strainer
supports: property pressure good and hose clear but flow into the drawer is weak (all compartments)
silted inlet strainer
against: filter clear and poor flow remains (valve)
single-compartment problem

components.name: detergent use — type / amount / compartment / liquid insert / congealed
supports: good water enters but powder/detergent remains
liquid detergent used in the drawer, sticky/caked
wrong compartment or missing liquid-detergent insert/flap
too much detergent
against: no/low water is actually reaching the compartment (delivery path)

components.name: conditioner siphon cap / insert / channel / jets
supports: WATER ENTERS the conditioner compartment but conditioner/water REMAINS afterwards
siphon cap/insert missing or misfitted
blocked jets/channel or residue/congealed softener
softener above the MAX line or too thick
against: NO water reaches the conditioner compartment (water-delivery path to it)

components.name: drawer / dispenser roof jets & channels (clean; replace only if damaged)
supports: visible residue/limescale/mould blocking drawer passages or roof jets
product remains despite adequate water
against: drawer clean and clear but flow still poor (upstream) or won't discharge (dispenser-to-tub)

components.name: auto-dose settings / reservoir / concentration / cleaning [auto-dose machines ONLY]
supports: auto-dosing machine
auto-dose turned off / dose-per-wash not set (often OFF by default or after a power cut)
reservoir empty / wrong or congealed product
concentration setting doesn't match the product
needs a dispenser clean / self-clean
against: conventional drawer machine with no auto-dose system

components.name: inlet valve (partially opening / restricted / one coil-path)
supports: property pressure good AND hose/inlet filter clear but flow still weak (a valve can partly open and pass only a trickle)
long fill time
on a multi-coil valve one compartment path is weak while another is fine
against: upstream restriction (tap/hose/filter) not excluded
water clearly reaches the compartment but product remains (siphon/jets/use)

components.name: dispenser-to-tub hose / discharge path
supports: water REACHES the drawer but can't discharge - drawer overflows / backs up / leaks down the front during fill
split/displaced/blocked discharge path
against: problem is getting water INTO the drawer (upstream supply/valve/channel)

components.name: water distributor / diverter [architectures that use one]
supports: one compartment gets NO water while others work AND the design uses a mechanical/electronic distributor/diverter
distributor not directing water to that compartment
against: no such distributor on this design (single/multi-coil valve feeds fixed channels)
local jet/channel blockage explains it

components.name: auto-dose pump [auto-dose machines ONLY]
supports: confirmed auto-dose machine, settings/reservoir/cleaning all good, but product still not dosed
against: conventional machine with no auto-dose pump - do NOT recommend
settings/reservoir/concentration/cleaning not yet checked

components.name: dispenser assembly (damaged)
supports: drawer/dispenser physically cracked/damaged and cleaning won't restore it
against: a clean/use/blockage cause not yet excluded

components.name: wiring / control PCB
supports: supply good, passages clear, architecture known, and the expected valve/diverter is not being commanded/operated
against: any physical/hydraulic/use cause remains

commonConfusion.name: soap-drawer problem = replace the dispenser
commonConfusion.note: The dispenser is part of a water-delivery system. Exclude incoming water/pressure, the delivery path, blockages, siphon and detergent use before recommending a dispenser/valve/PCB part.
wouldApplyIf: the drawer/dispenser is physically damaged and cleaning won't restore it

commonConfusion.name: conditioner remains = inlet valve / no water
commonConfusion.note: If water clearly ENTERED the conditioner compartment but it remains, the incoming supply is LESS suspicious - raise the siphon cap/insert, blocked jets/channel, residue, or softener above MAX / too thick. Conditioner is drawn by a siphon on the final rinse.
wouldApplyIf: NO water reaches the conditioner compartment at all (then investigate the delivery path to it)

commonConfusion.name: all compartments weak = dispenser fault
commonConfusion.note: General weak flow across the whole drawer points to incoming water (property pressure -> tap/hose -> inlet filter -> a partially-opening inlet valve), not a local dispenser fault (cross-ref Story-10 filling).
wouldApplyIf: only one compartment is affected while others flush normally

commonConfusion.name: loads of foam from the drawer = failed dispenser
commonConfusion.note: Excess foam out of the drawer is usually a detergent-use/oversudsing issue - cross-ref foam-suds, not a broken dispenser.
wouldApplyIf: a genuine dispensing/flow fault persists with correct detergent and no excess foam

commonConfusion.name: water not going where expected = PCB
commonConfusion.note: Physical/hydraulic/use causes come first. Only raise control/PCB once supply is good, passages are clear, the architecture is known and the expected valve/diverter isn't being operated.
wouldApplyIf: all physical causes excluded and the expected actuator isn't commanded

commonConfusion.name: auto-dose pump on a conventional machine
commonConfusion.note: Only propose an auto-dose pump/reservoir on machines whose architecture actually has automatic dosing. Establish conventional-drawer vs auto-dose first.
wouldApplyIf: the model is confirmed to have an automatic-dosing system

docs.secondaryQuestion: Is it only one compartment (like the conditioner section) or are all of them flushing poorly - and is it a conventional drawer or an automatic-dosing machine?
adviceBeforeReplacement: clean the drawer, the conditioner siphon cap/insert and the roof jets (soak removable parts in warm water; scrub the jet holes and channels)
check the conditioner/detergent isn't above the MAX line or too thick (dilute thick softener; don't exceed MAX)
check the correct compartment is used and any liquid-detergent insert/flap is fitted
if ALL compartments are weak, check the taps, inlet hose and inlet filter/strainer before the valve (cross-ref filling)
on an auto-dosing machine, check it's switched on and dosed, the reservoir has the right product and the concentration matches, and run a dispenser/self-clean
switch off/unplug and isolate the water before removing the inlet hose or filter to inspect

docs.label: Drum position / drum sensor fault
discriminators: Direct-drive drum/rotor position sensing => hall-sensor (rotor-position). Bearing noise/play => excessive-vibration / motor-drum. This node is an alignment/cross-link and a future consolidation candidate into hall-sensor.
ARCHITECTURE: no carbon brushes/belt on confirmed direct-drive.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is it a direct-drive machine, and does the drum turn freely by hand with the power off?

components.name: rotor/drum position sensing (direct-drive)
supports: confirmed direct-drive/brushless architecture
abnormal powered drum movement with a free drum by hand
against: brushed machine (=> tacho)
mechanical stiffness/rumble (=> bearing)

components.name: drum bearing (if the complaint is really noise/play)
supports: deep rumble/grumble on spin, drum play/drop
against: clean electronic position/speed fault with a free drum

commonConfusion.name: drum position sensor = a distinct fault family
commonConfusion.note: On direct-drive machines this IS the hall/rotor-position sensor - see hall-sensor. Bearing noise is excessive-vibration/motor-drum. Treated as an alignment/cross-link, not a separate route.
wouldApplyIf: genuine direct-drive rotor-position evidence => hall-sensor

docs.label: MEMS vibration sensor fault
discriminators: Rule out a genuinely unbalanced load and poor levelling before the vibration sensor.

commonConfusion.name: vibration-sensor code = replace the sensor
commonConfusion.note: A MEMS / vibration-sensor code (or a repeated spin-abort) is usually a genuinely unbalanced load or poor levelling rather than a failed sensor. Rule out load distribution, overloading and levelling/feet before the vibration sensor.
wouldApplyIf: load balanced and redistributed, machine level and not overloaded, yet the sensor fault / spin-abort still persists

Fault: MEMS vibration sensor fault
Customer phrases: vibration sensor; mems fault; 8e sensor
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- vibration-sensor code = replace the sensor: A MEMS / vibration-sensor code (or a repeated spin-abort) is usually a genuinely unbalanced load or poor levelling rather than a failed sensor. Rule out load distribution, overloading and levelling/feet before the vibration sensor.
   Only consider if: load balanced and redistributed, machine level and not overloaded, yet the sensor fault / spin-abort still persists.

Likely parts in order: load balance / levelling / installation (false imbalance), MEMS vibration sensor, sensor wiring / connector, main PCB

docs.label: Control panel / stuck button fault
symptoms: wont let me select a programme
screen is blank but it has power
some buttons work and others dont
lights are on but it wont respond
discriminators: FIRST distinguish COMPLETELY DEAD (no lights/display) => low-voltage/supply (true-dead path, PCB last) from POWERED-BUT-MISBEHAVING controls/display => control-panel.
CHECK control/child lock FIRST for 'buttons don't work' (padlock symbol; persists across power-off). Then a power-cycle/reset for a temporary glitch.

One control dead, rest fine => a stuck button/selector or the panel. Whole display blank/garbled but machine powered => UI/control board + ribbon. Display present but not talking to the board => comms/wiring.
Down-rank the main PCB: fascia/control input -> UI/control panel -> communications/wiring -> main PCB, by evidence.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is the display lit at all, and do some buttons work while others don't — or is the whole machine dead with no lights?

components.name: control lock / child lock engaged
supports: all buttons except power do nothing
a padlock/key symbol is shown
the lock stays on after switching off and on
a lock button was pressed by accident
against: the display is completely dead/blank too (=> power/board)

components.name: power state / reset
supports: a power-cycle at the wall clears a temporary glitch
recently interrupted mid-programme
against: display lit but a physical button is dead (=> panel)

components.name: stuck / dirty button or selector
supports: one control clearly dead while the rest of the UI works
a button physically stuck or a constant beep
a sticky or damaged fascia
against: the whole panel/display is unresponsive

components.name: user-interface / control panel board + ribbon
supports: display blank/partial/garbled but the machine otherwise has power
display segments missing
a moisture- or heat-corroded panel connector
against: the whole machine is completely dead with no lights (=> supply/main PCB)

components.name: communication / wiring panel to main board
supports: display present but not talking to the main board
a communication error shown
against: a single stuck button with the rest working

components.name: main control PCB / supply
supports: UI and wiring proven good
no response with power confirmed to the boards
against: a completely dead machine => supply/low-voltage first (property supply, lead, mains filter, wiring, PCB last)

commonConfusion.name: unresponsive = main PCB
commonConfusion.note: Down-rank the main PCB. Check control-lock, a reset, and a single stuck button / UI board before blaming the main board.
wouldApplyIf: control-lock excluded, a reset tried, and the UI board/ribbon evidenced faulty

commonConfusion.name: dead machine = control panel
commonConfusion.note: A COMPLETELY dead machine (no lights at all) is a SUPPLY/true-dead case (see low-voltage): property supply, lead, mains filter, wiring, PCB last — not the control panel.
wouldApplyIf: display and lights are alive but the controls/display misbehave

commonConfusion.name: buttons dead = faulty panel
commonConfusion.note: Control/child lock is the commonest cause of 'buttons don't work' — check it before a part.
wouldApplyIf: control-lock ruled out and a button is physically stuck or dead

docs.text:
Appliance: washing machine
Fault: Control panel / stuck button fault
Customer phrases: button stuck; keypad error; panel fault; buttons not working; panel not responding; controls not working; wont let me select a programme; touchpad not responding; display blank; display not working; display frozen; display garbled; screen is blank but it has power; some buttons work and others dont; keeps beeping; a button is stuck; lights are on but it wont respond
Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. control lock / child lock engaged [CHECK]
   More likely if: all buttons except power do nothing; a padlock/key symbol is shown; the lock stays on after switching off and on; a lock button was pressed by accident.
   Less likely if: the display is completely dead/blank too (=> power/board).
2. power state / reset [CHECK]
   More likely if: a power-cycle at the wall clears a temporary glitch; recently interrupted mid-programme.
   Less likely if: display lit but a physical button is dead (=> panel).
3. stuck / dirty button or selector [PART]
   More likely if: one control clearly dead while the rest of the UI works; a button physically stuck or a constant beep; a sticky or damaged fascia.
   Less likely if: the whole panel/display is unresponsive.
4. user-interface / control panel board + ribbon [PART]
   More likely if: display blank/partial/garbled but the machine otherwise has power; display segments missing; a moisture- or heat-corroded panel connector.
   Less likely if: the whole machine is completely dead with no lights (=> supply/main PCB).
5. communication / wiring panel to main board [CHECK]
   More likely if: display present but not talking to the main board; a communication error shown.
   Less likely if: a single stuck button with the rest working.
6. main control PCB / supply [PART]
   More likely if: UI and wiring proven good; no response with power confirmed to the boards.
   Less likely if: a completely dead machine => supply/low-voltage first (property supply, lead, mains filter, wiring, PCB last).
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- unresponsive = main PCB: Down-rank the main PCB. Check control-lock, a reset, and a single stuck button / UI board before blaming the main board.
   Only consider if: control-lock excluded, a reset tried, and the UI board/ribbon evidenced faulty.
- dead machine = control panel: A COMPLETELY dead machine (no lights at all) is a SUPPLY/true-dead case (see low-voltage): property supply, lead, mains filter, wiring, PCB last — not the control panel.
   Only consider if: display and lights are alive but the controls/display misbehave.
- buttons dead = faulty panel: Control/child lock is the commonest cause of 'buttons don't work' — check it before a part.
   Only consider if: control-lock ruled out and a button is physically stuck or dead.
Engineering notes: FIRST distinguish COMPLETELY DEAD (no lights/display) => low-voltage/supply (true-dead path, PCB last) from POWERED-BUT-MISBEHAVING controls/display => control-panel. CHECK control/child lock FIRST for 'buttons don't work' (padlock symbol; persists across power-off). Then a power-cycle/reset for a temporary glitch. One control dead, rest fine => a stuck button/selector or the panel. Whole display blank/garbled but machine powered => UI/control board + ribbon. Display present but not talking to the board => comms/wiring. Down-rank the main PCB: fascia/control input -> UI/control panel -> communications/wiring -> main PCB, by evidence.
Likely parts in order: control panel, control panel module, main pcb
Confused with: low-voltage, main-pcb, comms, door-lock
Advice before replacing parts: check for a child/control lock (padlock symbol) and turn it off; switch off at the wall for a minute and back on to clear a temporary glitch; check the plug/socket and that the machine has power before assuming a board
Best question to ask if unsure: Is the display lit at all, and do some buttons work while others don't — or is the whole machine dead with no lights?
Follow-up question if still unclear: Could a child/control lock be on, and does switching off at the wall for a minute help?

docs.label: Bangs / bounces / walks or vibrates violently on spin
symptoms: drum wobbles and catches the clothes
loose paddle rattling in the drum
discriminators: BRAND-NEW or just-installed machine banging/bouncing from the very first spin: almost always the transit (shipping) bolts have NOT been removed - they lock the drum for transport and bypass the suspension. Remove them from the back panel (keep them for future moves), then check the machine is level with all four feet firm and lock nuts tight, and not on a springy/loose floor. No spare part needed.
An OLDER machine that has GRADUALLY started bouncing/walking: worn shock absorbers or suspension springs (bouncing), or drum bearings if there's a grinding/rumbling as the drum spins.
Only happens when washing a single bulky item (bath mat, duvet, towels): that's an unbalanced load, not worn parts - redistribute the load (see unbalanced-load).

NOISE IS NOT ONE SYMPTOM - route by CHARACTER: violent banging/shaking => load/installation/transit first, then counterweight/suspension; heavy SOLID knock => counterweight/major suspension; deep GRUMBLING/RUMBLING/ROARING (worse with speed) + play => drum bearing (seal/support); LIGHT metallic tick/scrape once per rev => paddle or foreign object between tubs; DEEPER rhythmic tick/knock => pulley or worn belt (belt-driven only). Combine with timing/load/architecture, not as absolute acoustic labels.
NEW / RECENTLY MOVED + violent vibration => TRANSIT bolts/brackets + levelling FIRST; do not recommend suspension parts until excluded.
LOAD-SPECIFIC (bath mat/duvet/single heavy/very small/overloaded) => unbalanced-load CHECK (Story 11), not suspension/bearing parts. Fine with an ordinary load confirms this.
WALKS ACROSS THE FLOOR => level/feet/floor and stationary-rock check before parts.
BEARING + OILY MARKS ON CLOTHING (or dirty/oily leak) => drum bearing/seal is strong combined evidence (cross-ref Story-13).
DROPPED/WOBBLY DRUM => bearing AND drum spider/support are both candidates - don't collapse every dropped drum into 'bearings'.
ARCHITECTURE: offer drum pulley / drive belt only on belt-driven machines; on direct-drive there is neither (Story 11).
CAUSAL CHAINS: bearing/spider -> drum play/drop -> door seal ripped -> leak (Story 13); loose counterweight -> banging -> tub cracked -> major leak (Story 13/14). Address the underlying cause.
RETAINED WATER + won't spin (banging while trying to spin with water still in the drum) => drainage remains authoritative (Story 9), not vibration.
SAFETY: a big leak with violent banging, or a machine moving dangerously, is a stop-use situation, not continued operation.

DROPPED / WOBBLING DRUM that also catches or marks clothes = worn bearing / broken suspension (this fault or motor-drum), NOT damaging-clothes: the fabric damage is a CONSEQUENCE of the mechanical play, so fix the mechanical fault. A LOOSE paddle that rattles/knocks with movement is mechanical here; only a BROKEN paddle with a sharp edge that snags fabric (no drum movement) is damaging-clothes.

mediaInformation.description: Transit bolts hold the drum still for delivery and must be removed before use — a machine that bangs, walks or vibrates (especially when new or recently moved) often still has them fitted. They unscrew from the back of the machine. Typical layout — your machine may differ.

docs.label: Smells / mouldy (maintenance)
discriminators: Usually a maintenance issue, not a fault: bacteria/detergent residue build up in the door seal folds, the drawer and the filter. Wipe out the door-seal folds, clean the filter, and run a hot 90C maintenance wash (empty) with a washing-machine cleaner or soda crystals; leave the door and drawer ajar between washes.
If a strong drain smell remains after cleaning, check the drain hose/standpipe (see not-draining).
If the rubber door seal is torn or perished and holding mould, it may need replacing.

ROUTE BY SMELL CHARACTER, do not collapse. IMPORTANT: a BURNING/acrid/electrical smell or HOT RUBBER is NOT a hygiene problem — do NOT give cleaning/maintenance advice; treat as SAFETY (stop use/unplug) and route to the electrical/mechanical fault (motor-drum/tacho/hall-sensor, tripping-electrics, or a slipping belt). OILY + grinding/rumble => drum bearing (excessive-vibration/leak-flood). MUSTY/damp/earthy => hygiene/biofilm (advice); SEWAGE/sulphur strongest at the drain => waste plumbing (often NOT the appliance).
MUSTY vs SEWAGE: musty is earthy and eases with airing then returns; sewage is sharp sulphur, intensifies near the drain and after water use (dry/again-incorrect trap).
BURNING/ELECTRICAL: active burning, smoke, melting or severe overheating => STOP USE and unplug; cross-link mains filter/wiring/motor/brushes/heater; do NOT give live-testing instructions.
ARCHITECTURE: hot-rubber/belt smell only on belt-driven machines; never suggest a belt on confirmed direct-drive.
OILY + mechanical noise/marks => bearing (excessive-vibration/leak-flood) OUTRANKS generic hygiene odour.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: What kind of smell is it - musty/damp, like drains/sewage, or hot/burning - and when is it strongest?

components.name: musty/mouldy — biofilm hygiene (door seal, drawer, filter, drum)
supports: earthy musty/damp smell
visible black mould/slime in the door-seal folds, drawer or filter
frequent low-temperature or liquid-only washing
too much detergent
machine routinely left shut
smell eases with airing then returns
against: sharp sulphur smell strongest at the drain (=> plumbing)
hot/acrid burning smell (=> electrical/mechanical)

components.name: sewage/drain/sulphur — waste plumbing & installation
supports: sharp rotten-egg/sulphur smell
strongest near the standpipe/waste, or after water use
worse when unused (dry trap)
recent plumbing change / no U-bend or anti-siphon
drain hose pushed too far or no air gap
against: earthy musty that airing helps (=> hygiene)
smell only when heating/spinning (=> electrical/mechanical)

components.name: burning/electrical smell — SAFETY
supports: hot/acrid/electrical burning smell, especially on spin or heating
any smoke, melting or visible scorching
against: earthy musty (hygiene)
sulphur at the drain (plumbing)

components.name: hot rubber / friction — drive belt [belt-driven ONLY]
supports: rubbery burning smell on spin
belt-driven machine
drum stiff/slipping/restricted
against: confirmed direct-drive (no belt)
acrid electrical smell rather than rubbery

components.name: oily/greasy — bearing / drum seal
supports: oily/greasy smell with a grinding/rumble on spin
oily marks on the washing
against: no noise and no marks

commonConfusion.name: any smell = clean the machine
commonConfusion.note: Only the MUSTY/mouldy mode is a hygiene/advice issue. Drain smell is plumbing; burning is a safety/electrical stop-use; oily+noise is a bearing.
wouldApplyIf: earthy musty smell with visible mould, no burning and no drain sulphur

commonConfusion.name: smell = a failed appliance part
commonConfusion.note: Musty and sewage smells rarely need an appliance part - do not push replacements from weak hygiene/plumbing evidence.
wouldApplyIf: burning/electrical, or oily+mechanical noise, evidenced

commonConfusion.name: burning smell = just clean it
commonConfusion.note: NEVER treat a burning/electrical smell as hygiene. It is a stop-use safety situation; cross-link the electrical/mechanical cause.
wouldApplyIf: hot/acrid/electrical smell, smoke, melting or scorching

docs.secondaryQuestion: Is there visible black mould in the door-seal folds or drawer, and does it get worse after draining or when the machine has been shut up unused?
adviceBeforeReplacement: musty: wipe the door-seal folds, clean the drawer and the pump filter, run a hot 60-90C maintenance wash (empty) with a machine cleaner or soda crystals, and leave the door and drawer ajar between washes
drain smell: check the standpipe/U-bend/anti-siphon and the drain-hose installation and air gap (plumbing, not usually an appliance part)
burning/electrical smell: stop using it and unplug it - treat as an electrical/mechanical fault, not hygiene

Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. musty/mouldy — biofilm hygiene (door seal, drawer, filter, drum) [CHECK]
   More likely if: earthy musty/damp smell; visible black mould/slime in the door-seal folds, drawer or filter; frequent low-temperature or liquid-only washing; too much detergent; machine routinely left shut; smell eases with airing then returns.
   Less likely if: sharp sulphur smell strongest at the drain (=> plumbing); hot/acrid burning smell (=> electrical/mechanical).
2. sewage/drain/sulphur — waste plumbing & installation [CHECK]
   More likely if: sharp rotten-egg/sulphur smell; strongest near the standpipe/waste, or after water use; worse when unused (dry trap); recent plumbing change / no U-bend or anti-siphon; drain hose pushed too far or no air gap.
   Less likely if: earthy musty that airing helps (=> hygiene); smell only when heating/spinning (=> electrical/mechanical).
3. burning/electrical smell — SAFETY [CHECK]
   More likely if: hot/acrid/electrical burning smell, especially on spin or heating; any smoke, melting or visible scorching.
   Less likely if: earthy musty (hygiene); sulphur at the drain (plumbing).
4. hot rubber / friction — drive belt [belt-driven ONLY] [CHECK]
   More likely if: rubbery burning smell on spin; belt-driven machine; drum stiff/slipping/restricted.
   Less likely if: confirmed direct-drive (no belt); acrid electrical smell rather than rubbery.
5. oily/greasy — bearing / drum seal [CHECK]
   More likely if: oily/greasy smell with a grinding/rumble on spin; oily marks on the washing.
   Less likely if: no noise and no marks.
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- any smell = clean the machine: Only the MUSTY/mouldy mode is a hygiene/advice issue. Drain smell is plumbing; burning is a safety/electrical stop-use; oily+noise is a bearing.
   Only consider if: earthy musty smell with visible mould, no burning and no drain sulphur.
- smell = a failed appliance part: Musty and sewage smells rarely need an appliance part - do not push replacements from weak hygiene/plumbing evidence.
   Only consider if: burning/electrical, or oily+mechanical noise, evidenced.
- burning smell = just clean it: NEVER treat a burning/electrical smell as hygiene. It is a stop-use safety situation; cross-link the electrical/mechanical cause.
   Only consider if: hot/acrid/electrical smell, smoke, melting or scorching.
Engineering notes: Usually a maintenance issue, not a fault: bacteria/detergent residue build up in the door seal folds, the drawer and the filter. Wipe out the door-seal folds, clean the filter, and run a hot 90C maintenance wash (empty) with a washing-machine cleaner or soda crystals; leave the door and drawer ajar between washes. If a strong drain smell remains after cleaning, check the drain hose/standpipe (see not-draining). If the rubber door seal is torn or perished and holding mould, it may need replacing. ROUTE BY SMELL CHARACTER, do not collapse. IMPORTANT: a BURNING/acrid/electrical smell or HOT RUBBER is NOT a hygiene problem — do NOT give cleaning/maintenance advice; treat as SAFETY (stop use/unplug) and route to the electrical/mechanical fault (motor-drum/tacho/hall-sensor, tripping-electrics, or a slipping belt). OILY + grinding/rumble => drum bearing (excessive-vibration/leak-flood). MUSTY/damp/earthy => hygiene/biofilm (advice); SEWAGE/sulphur strongest at the drain => waste plumbing (often NOT the appliance). MUSTY vs SEWAGE: musty is earthy and eases with airing then returns; sewage is sharp sulphur, intensifies near the drain and after water use (dry/again-incorrect trap). BURNING/ELECTRICAL: active burning, smoke, melting or severe overheating => STOP USE and unplug; cross-link mains filter/wiring/motor/brushes/heater; do NOT give live-testing instructions. ARCHITECTURE: hot-rubber/belt smell only on belt-driven machines; never suggest a belt on confirmed direct-drive. OILY + mechanical noise/marks => bearing (excessive-vibration/leak-flood) OUTRANKS generic hygiene odour.
Confused with: poor-wash-results, not-draining, leak-flood, motor-drum, tripping-electrics, excessive-vibration
Advice before replacing parts: musty: wipe the door-seal folds, clean the drawer and the pump filter, run a hot 60-90C maintenance wash (empty) with a machine cleaner or soda crystals, and leave the door and drawer ajar between washes; drain smell: check the standpipe/U-bend/anti-siphon and the drain-hose installation and air gap (plumbing, not usually an appliance part); burning/electrical smell: stop using it and unplug it - treat as an electrical/mechanical fault, not hygiene
Best question to ask if unsure: What kind of smell is it - musty/damp, like drains/sewage, or hot/burning - and when is it strongest?
Follow-up question if still unclear: Is there visible black mould in the door-seal folds or drawer, and does it get worse after draining or when the machine has been shut up unused?

docs.label: Poor wash results (marks / powder left / not clean)
symptoms: clothes come out with powder on them
discriminators: Often not a fault: too much detergent, washing too cool, or overloading. Use less detergent, a hotter wash occasionally, and don't overfill.
Check water is actually flowing through the dispenser drawer and the drawer/jets aren't blocked; if little/no water reaches it, suspect the inlet valve or a blocked drawer.
Poor rinsing/marks can also follow a drainage problem (see not-draining).

BOUNDARY — decide FIRST: if the DRUM is not turning/agitating properly GROUND motor-drum; if the water never gets HOT on a hot wash GROUND heater/temperature-sensor; if there is heavy FOAM GROUND foam-suds; if product is left in the DRAWER GROUND dispenser. poor-wash-results is for wash-quality/rinse/residue when the machine otherwise fills, heats, agitates and drains normally.
Mostly CHECK/advice: reduce dose, dissolve powder or use liquid/tablets, don't overload, run an occasional hot maintenance wash, clean the drawer and seal. Rarely a part.
White/powdery residue => undissolved or over-dosed detergent, or hard water. Greasy/grey marks + musty smell => biofilm build-up (maintenance). Product left in the DRAWER => dispenser.
Poor rinse specifically => over-dosing + low water + overloading; cross-link foam-suds, dispenser and inlet-valve where evidence supports.

docs.label: Ripping / snagging clothes
discriminators: Most often a torn/perished door seal (boot) or a foreign object (coin, wire, bra underwire) trapped in the drum or behind the paddles - check those first.
A cracked/rough drum paddle (lifter) or a rough spot from failed drum bearings can also snag - listen for a grinding noise on spin.

BOUNDARY (Story-18 D-class #2) — decide FIRST: if the report includes ANY mechanical noise (rumble/grumble/grinding/knock on spin), a dropped or wobbly drum, or an oily/greasy leak or oily marks, GROUND the underlying MECHANICAL fault — drum bearing/support (motor-drum or excessive-vibration) or a leak (leak-flood) — NOT damaging-clothes. A ripped seal alongside a dropped/wobbly drum is consequential damage: the bearing/spider/drum-support failure wins.
damaging-clothes is only for PHYSICAL cuts/tears/snags/holes with NO mechanical noise and NO dropped drum: a torn seal lip, a broken paddle, a foreign object, or a drum burr.
Split by TYPE of damage: physical cuts/tears/snags => seal/paddle/foreign-object/burr; greasy/oily marks WITH noise => bearing/tub-seal; white/powder marks => poor-wash-results/dispenser.
Sudden onset + metallic scraping => a foreign object between the tubs (bra wire/coin) or through a drum perforation — inspect before parts.
Same spot/item every wash => a fixed snag: a broken paddle, a burr on the drum, or a split seal lip.
CHECK laundry/use (load size, open zips, underwired bras, bio detergent/bleach on delicates) before recommending any part.

DOWN-RANK GUARD: 'ripped/tearing/holes' ALONE does not make this the fault. If the SAME report has a dropped/sagging/wobbling drum, rumble/roar/grinding on spin, or greasy/black/oily marks, that mechanical fault (motor-drum / excessive-vibration) or a leak (leak-flood) WINS and this is only consequential damage. Choose damaging-clothes ONLY for fabric cuts/snags/holes with NO drum movement and NO mechanical noise: a split seal lip, a sharp broken paddle edge, a foreign object (coin/wire/bra underwire), a drum burr, or a stuck zip.

docs.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
symptoms: trips as soon as i turn it on
discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.
'Knocking the electrics out', 'flipping the fuse box', 'tripping the mains' all mean it trips the RCD/fuse - an earth fault.

Trips once it starts HEATING (fills then trips a few minutes in) = the HEATER ELEMENT leaking to earth (most common). Trips the instant it's switched on or as it fills = a wiring/short or a shorted DRAIN PUMP or mains lead. Water getting into wiring/connectors can also trip it.
Isolate by timing: which part of the cycle trips it (fill, heat, wash, spin)? That points to heater vs motor vs pump.

discriminators: If it stalls with WATER STILL IN the drum, investigate draining (filter/pump) and heating first - those commonly stall a programme. The door staying locked is a symptom of the stall, not the cause.

docs.label: Motor / drum fault
discriminators: NOISE BY TIMING: noise only while DRAINING = drain pump; motor heard but drum still = belt; grinding worse at high spin = bearings; drum jerks/struggles = motor/control.

A screech/squeal on spin = drum bearings or a glazed/slipping drive belt, NOT carbon brushes. A burning-rubber smell = a slipping/perished drive belt or a seized pump/motor - unplug it if the smell is strong.

Won't spin but drains fine: this is NOT a drain fault - carbon brushes (brushed motors), a snapped/slipped drive belt, or motor control. Won't spin because water is left in the drum: it's a drain fault first (not-draining), not the motor.

CALIBRATED PRECISION: prefer a drive/motor/control AREA diagnosis unless a specific observation points to one part (grinding-worse-on-spin = bearings; motor heard, drum still = belt; drum jerks/struggles to reach speed = motor/brushes/control). Do not name an exact internal part the customer's observations cannot single out.

Even for a brief 'won't spin at all', COMMIT to this motor/drum fault (usual causes: worn CARBON BRUSHES or the DRIVE BELT) and use the checks to refine - don't withhold a diagnosis. But weigh two things first: (1) WATER - it won't spin until drained, so no-spin with water left is a DRAIN fault (drain pump / blocked filter), not the motor. (2) LOAD - an unbalanced load (bathmat, one heavy item) makes it abort the spin; redistributing fixes it. If neither applies, it's a motor/drive fault (brushes/belt).

Identify the MOTOR TYPE first. A CARBON-BRUSH (universal) motor's speed is controlled by a module fast-switching a triac; no-spin here is usually WORN BRUSHES, and low brushes sparking can blow a MOTOR THERMAL FUSE - so it can be brushes and/or the fuse. Hand-spinning the drum and listening tells you if brushes are worn down.

An INDUCTION motor has NO brushes - it is capacitor-start (a START CAPACITOR gives a start winding ~90 degrees out of phase). No-spin/won't-start on a brushless machine points to the START CAPACITOR or windings, not brushes.
A snapped/slipped DRIVE BELT gives motor-running but drum-not-turning.

NOISY washer-dryer - tell by the KIND of noise: deep RUMBLING/grinding worse on spin = worn DRUM BEARINGS (grip the inner drum, up/down play confirms it). TICKING/knocking, or drum paddles snapping off = a FOREIGN OBJECT trapped (bra wire, coin). WHIPPING/slapping = worn DRIVE BELT. A cracked MOTOR PULLEY on the back of the drum also causes noise. The drain PUMP is rarely noisy - it tends to just jam - so treat the pump as the LAST suspect for a noise complaint.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is there still water in the drum, was it a big/uneven load, and can you hear the motor trying while the drum stays still?

docs.label: Drying heater fault (won't dry)
likelyComponents: thermal cut-out (may be tripped by airflow restriction)
symptoms: drum cold on the drying cycle
washes fine but clothes not drying
gets hot but clothes stay wet
dries small loads but not a big one
discriminators: WON'T DRY is NOT automatically the drying heater - differentiate first. (1) WATER ACTUALLY REMOVED? If the wash didn't SPIN/DRAIN properly the clothes start the dry soaking and never dry - that is a SPIN / DRAIN / unbalanced-load fault (see not-draining / unbalanced-load / motor-drum), NOT the drying heater. (2) HOT BUT STILL WET, or drying takes far too long, points to restricted AIRFLOW / CONDENSATION - a blocked lint FILTER or CONDENSER (and, on condenser designs that use cooling water, the water supply) - clean those FIRST, not the heater. (3) NO HEAT AT ALL (drum turns, air stays cold) points to the drying HEATER ELEMENT, its THERMOSTAT, or a tripped THERMAL CUT-OUT. (4) TOO BIG A DRY LOAD dries poorly with no fault at all.

THERMAL CUT-OUT gotcha: a tripped drying thermal cut-out is usually the SYMPTOM of earlier airflow restriction (blocked filter/condenser), not a random failure - clean the airflow path and look for a reset before condemning parts.

A washer-dryer dries a SMALLER load than it washes - a full wash load put straight onto dry, or an overloaded drum, gives poor drying with no failed part. Suggest a smaller dry load before replacing anything.

A BURNING / HOT / SCORCHING smell while DRYING is normally FLUFF & LINT scorching on the hot drying ELEMENT because airflow is restricted - clean the lint FILTER (and check the vent/condenser) FIRST; if the smell is strong, unplug it and let it cool. This is a drying-heater / airflow issue, NOT the cooling fan and NOT the wash side.

If airflow, spin/drain and load are all fine and it still won't heat or smells hot, suspect the drying HEATER ELEMENT or its THERMOSTAT / thermal cut-out. Route a burning-smell-on-dry to the drying heater/overheat side, not to a 'cooling' error.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does it get hot during drying but leave the clothes damp, or is there no heat at all - and were the clothes properly spun before the drying stage?

commonConfusion.name: won't dry / wet clothes = the drying heater
commonConfusion.note: Wet clothes after a dry cycle are NOT automatically a drying-heater fault. Rule out (a) water not removed by a poor spin/drain, (b) restricted airflow/condenser (hot-but-wet or slow drying), and (c) too large a dry load, before the drying element/thermostat. Only NO heat at all with airflow/spin/load fine points to the heater.
wouldApplyIf: the clothes were properly spun (not dripping) before drying, the lint filter/condenser are clean, the dry load is modest, and there is still NO heat during drying

commonConfusion.name: hot but still wet = the heater
commonConfusion.note: If it clearly gets HOT but clothes stay damp (or drying is very slow), the heater is working - the problem is AIRFLOW / CONDENSATION (blocked filter/condenser), not the heating element.
wouldApplyIf: it gets hot during drying yet clothes remain wet, or drying takes far longer than normal

adviceBeforeReplacement: clean the lint/fluff filter and (on condenser models) the condenser, and make sure the airflow path isn't restricted

docs.label: Leak / anti-flood triggered
discriminators: A DARK, greasy/oily leak (not clear water) usually means the DRUM BEARINGS have failed - the bearing seal lets water past and dark residue out - or an oil-filled shock absorber is leaking. Listen for a grinding/rumbling on spin (bearings). Do NOT tell the customer the machine has no oil; front-loaders do have greased bearings and oil-damped absorbers. Clear-water leaks are the door seal, sump hose, pump or inlet valve.

COMMIT-FIRST: an explicit report of external water pooling/escaping - 'leaking underneath', 'water/puddle on the floor', 'leaks water', 'water pouring out' - is enough on its own to COMMIT the leak-flood route; do not withhold the route or ask whether it is really a leak. (Water specifically from the DETERGENT DRAWER/soap dispenser still belongs to the dispenser route, not generic leak-flood.) THEN pin the source part by WHERE it leaks from and WHAT the water looks like - that pins the part far better than the word 'leak' alone. Use location + timing + water appearance ONLY to narrow the source component (door seal, sump hose, drain pump, dispenser, inlet valve, tub/bearing) as a follow-up refinement - not as a precondition for routing.

Leaking DOWN THE FRONT from the DETERGENT DRAWER = a blocked / gunged-up detergent dispenser: soap and softener build up and the incoming water backs up out of the drawer. Fix = clean the dispenser/drawer. Not a pump or seal.

Leaking FROM THE DOOR = the DOOR SEAL (boot). GOTCHA: many door-seal leaks are just a DIRTY/gunged seal fold or debris trapped across it (coin, wire, fabric) - clean the seal fold and clear debris FIRST; only replace the boot if it's actually split or perished.

Leaking ON SPIN or WHILE EMPTYING/DRAINING with CLEAN water = the DRAIN PUMP (or the sump hose to it): under drain/spin the pump is pressurised, so a cracked pump body, worn pump seal or split sump hose pushes clean water out. Top suspect for spin/empty leaks.

Leaking DIRTY water, especially with a NOISY / rumbling drum = worn DRUM BEARINGS / failed tub seal: water gets past the tub seal (so it looks dirty) and the bearings are failing. Dirty-water leak plus noise = bearings, not the pump.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Where does the water come from - down the front by the drawer, at the door, or underneath on spin - and is it clean or dirty?

docs.label: Unbalanced load (spin aborted / stops mid-cycle)
symptoms: keeps trying to spin then stops
discriminators: Started right after washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet, blanket): that's an unbalanced load, not a fault. The item soaks up water and sticks to one side, so the machine keeps trying to redistribute and won't spin up (can look 'stuck' or 'dead' mid-cycle). Pause, open the door, redistribute or add a few smaller items, then re-run - no part needed.
Happens on EVERY load with normal mixed washing, and the machine bangs/walks: then suspect worn shock absorbers or suspension, or (with a grinding/rumbling noise) drum bearings.
Won't spin AND water is left in the drum: that's a drain fault (see not-draining), not balance.

docs.label: Bangs / bounces / walks or vibrates violently on spin
discriminators: BRAND-NEW or just-installed machine banging/bouncing from the very first spin: almost always the transit (shipping) bolts have NOT been removed - they lock the drum for transport and bypass the suspension. Remove them from the back panel (keep them for future moves), then check the machine is level with all four feet firm and lock nuts tight, and not on a springy/loose floor. No spare part needed.
An OLDER machine that has GRADUALLY started bouncing/walking: worn shock absorbers or suspension springs (bouncing), or drum bearings if there's a grinding/rumbling as the drum spins.
Only happens when washing a single bulky item (bath mat, duvet, towels): that's an unbalanced load, not worn parts - redistribute the load (see unbalanced-load).
Violent movement on spin: first rule out transit bolts and a bad load, then dampers/springs, then bearings.

docs.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
likelyComponents: wash heater element leaking to earth
drying heater element leaking to earth
drain / wash pump leaking to earth
symptoms: trips as soon as i turn it on
trips when it starts to heat
trips after it has been drying a while
discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.

WHEN it trips localises the earth fault by PHASE (a washer-dryer has two heaters). Trips the instant it is switched on / as it fills = wiring/short, a shorted pump, the mains lead or the suppressor. Trips once the WASH water starts HEATING = the WASH heater element leaking to earth. Trips when the DRYING phase starts to heat = the DRYING heater element (or its wiring) leaking to earth. Water getting into wiring/connectors can trip it at any point.
Isolate by timing: which part of the cycle trips it (power-up, fill, wash-heat, spin, or when drying heats)? That points to wiring/pump vs the wash heater vs the drying heater.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: At what point does it trip - as soon as you switch it on, once the wash water starts heating, on spin, or when the drying phase begins?
adviceBeforeReplacement: do NOT keep resetting the RCD/breaker and re-running an appliance that repeatedly trips the supply - stop use where there is a credible electrical fault
note the timing of the trip (on power / on fill / when the wash heats / on spin / when drying heats) to localise the fault before replacing a part

docs.label: Not heating / clothes stay damp
symptoms: vented dryer runs but no heat
condenser dryer runs but clothes stay wet
discriminators: Tumbles but stays cold: heater element or thermal cutout (a tripped cutout is often caused by a blocked lint filter/condenser - clean first).

CLEAN THE FILTER FIRST (a CHECK, not a part). On vented and condenser dryers the lint/fluff filter (and the condenser filter) is user-cleanable and routinely neglected. A clogged filter restricts airflow, the dryer overheats and TRIPS THE THERMAL CUT-OUT (TOC), which kills the heat - so a blocked filter/vent is the cheapest and most common cause, rule it out before selling parts.

On a VENTED or CONDENSER dryer the STRONG FIRST hardware candidate for genuine no-heat is the heater ELEMENT: dryer heaters are relatively fragile and commonly fail OPEN (simply stop heating). When the element has failed, ALSO check/replace the THERMAL CUT-OUT and thermostat - they are cheap and commonly fail together, and the overheat that opened one often stresses the other. Note: unlike a built-in OVEN, earth-leakage is NOT the dominant dryer-heater failure mode, so do not copy the oven priors - a dryer heater usually just goes open-circuit and cold.

A HEAT-PUMP dryer is completely different and has NO conventional heating element - do NOT recommend an element/TOC for it. It dries with a sealed refrigeration circuit (a fridge in reverse). No-heat/not-drying on a heat-pump points to a blocked CONDENSER/EVAPORATOR FILTER first (cheap, common), then the refrigerant/heat-pump circuit or its sensors - a specialist repair. If the architecture is unknown and it changes the answer, establish vented/condenser/heat-pump before recommending a heater part.

mediaInformation.title: Tumble dryer runs but doesn't heat — what to check

docs.label: Overheating / thermal cut-out
symptoms: smoke coming out of the dryer
changed the thermal cutout and it went again
replaced the toc and it blew again
discriminators: A burning smell from a dryer is most often lint built up on/around the heater - a FIRE RISK, so clean the lint filter and vent first. A rubbery/mechanical burning smell with a squeal or grinding is the drive belt or motor. If it also cuts out once hot, the thermostat/thermal cut-out has tripped.
Heats then cuts out / trips after a while: overheating - clean the lint filter and condenser FIRST, then suspect the thermostat/thermal cutout.

Overheating and a tripped thermal cut-out are usually the EFFECT of restricted airflow, not the root cause. Work the causal order: fluff/lint filter, then the air path/vent, then the condenser/heat exchanger where fitted, then the BLOWER FAN operating, then the heater/thermostat control - and only THEN the TOC itself. Replacing a TOC without fixing the airflow leaves the real fault in place and it will trip again.
So 'I changed the thermal cutout and it has gone again' is a classic airflow/fan problem - investigate the filter, fan and air path, do not just fit another TOC.

A strong burning-LINT smell, smoke, scorching or repeated severe overheating is a FIRE RISK: STOP USING the dryer, unplug it at the wall, and do not run another cycle 'to see if it happens again'. Clean out the lint safely and get it checked; do not attempt live mains testing.

docs.label: Moisture / temperature sensor (AutoDry) fault
symptoms: autodry says dry but clothes damp
discriminators: AutoDry/sensor programmes infer dryness (moisture bars in the drum, and/or temperature/humidity in the airflow - the design varies by make and architecture, so don't assume one universal sensor). Ends too early / 'dry' but damp: check programme and load first, then the moisture/temperature sensing; PCB last. Never ends / runs for hours: usually weak heat or restricted airflow (clean filter/condenser), or clothes went in soaking - not automatically the sensor or PCB.

AutoDry/sensor drying infers dryness - depending on make and architecture it uses moisture bars in the drum, and/or temperature/humidity sensing in the airflow. Do NOT assume one universal sensor design; describe it as the moisture/temperature sensing system.

ENDS TOO EARLY ('dry' but still damp, or jumps to the end): CHECK the programme and load size first (a tiny load or a timed-vs-sensor difference is common), then wipe accessible moisture contacts, then the moisture/temperature sensing and its wiring. PCB LAST.

NEVER ENDS / runs for hours: usually the clothes are genuinely still wet - weak heat, restricted airflow (clean filter/condenser), or laundry that went in soaking. Consider the sensing only after heat and airflow are ruled out; do not blame the PCB first. If timed drying works fine but only the sensor programme misbehaves, that points to the sensing rather than heat/airflow.

docs.label: Condensate not emptying (condenser / heat-pump dryer)
symptoms: water in the bottom of the dryer
water sitting in the bottom of my condenser dryer
water in the base of a condenser dryer
water pooling in the bottom of the dryer
dries fine but the tank never fills
clothes dry but the water tank never fills
water container light stays on after emptying
water never reaches the top container
discriminators: Condenser/heat-pump dryer, water tank fills very fast or won't fill, damp clothes: condensate pump or the float switch (check the condenser is clean).

Follow the causal water path: moisture is condensed, drops to the lower sump, the pump lifts it to the top container (or a drain hose). A 'container full/empty' warning that won't clear does NOT by itself prove the pump - check the container is seated and its detection, the float/level, and whether the sump/path is blocked with fluff-sludge. Water sitting in the base means the sump or path is blocked or the pump/hose is not moving it.
Follow the causal water path: moisture is condensed, drops to the LOWER SUMP, the PUMP lifts it to the TOP CONTAINER (or a drain hose). Diagnose along that path rather than jumping to the pump.

A 'water container full/empty' WARNING that won't clear does NOT by itself prove the pump. Check the container is fully seated and its detection, the float/level switch, and whether the sump/path is blocked with fluff-sludge. 'Container stays empty' only implicates the pump once you've confirmed condensate is actually being produced and the path is blocked or the pump/float has failed.
Water sitting in the BASE usually means the sump or condensate path is blocked, or the pump/hose isn't moving it - find the blockage before replacing the pump.

docs.label: Drum drive / motor fault (drum not turning)
symptoms: motor runs but drum doesnt turn
motor sounds like its running but drum stationary
drum hard to turn by hand
discriminators: Build the drive diagnosis in causal order: drive BELT (snapped = motor runs, drum stationary; glazed/stretched = slips), then the JOCKEY/idler tension pulley, then the MOTOR and its START CAPACITOR (hums but won't turn = capacitor), then obstruction, and only then drum support/bearings. A genuinely SEIZED drum/bearing is RARE - do not make it the default. 'Hard to turn by hand' points to support rollers/bearings; 'turns freely by hand but motor just hums' points to the capacitor or belt.

Diagnose the drive in causal order and do NOT default to the motor or a seized drum. Motor RUNS but drum STATIONARY, or drum turns freely by hand = DRIVE BELT (snapped/off). Squeal/chirp or slipping while it still turns = JOCKEY/idler tension pulley or a glazed belt. Motor HUMS but won't turn (drum free by hand) = MOTOR START CAPACITOR, not a dead motor. Only when belt, pulley and capacitor are excluded consider the motor itself.

A genuinely SEIZED drum/bearing is RARE. 'Drum hard to turn by hand' with a rumble/grinding and drum play points to worn support rollers/pads (front) or the rear bearing/bush - not the motor. Do not make seized bearings the default answer to a non-turning drum.

Squeal/chirp (drum still turning) = jockey/idler tension pulley or a glazed belt - consider these before a motor or a seized drum. Rhythmic thump = drum support roller or a belt joint or the load. docs.label: Heat pump circuit underperforming
symptoms: heat pump takes longer than old vented
heat pump takes longer than my old dryer
heat pump runs cold never dries
heat pump trips after compressor starts
takes longer than my old vented dryer
discriminators: A heat-pump dryer is a refrigeration system (compressor + sealed refrigerant circuit), NOT a conventional heater. It NORMALLY runs at a lower temperature and a longer programme than an old vented dryer - 'only feels warm' and 'takes longer than my old dryer' are usually NORMAL characteristics, not a fault, so do not diagnose a hardware failure from those alone. Ground a fault only on worsening performance, genuinely COLD operation that never dries, error evidence, airflow restriction, sensor behaviour, or compressor/refrigeration evidence. Never recommend a conventional heater element for a heat-pump machine.

A heat-pump dryer is a REFRIGERATION system (compressor + sealed refrigerant circuit) used to recover heat - conceptually a fridge in reverse. It has NO conventional heating element, so NEVER recommend a heater element/TOC for a confirmed heat-pump machine.

NORMAL-BEHAVIOUR BOUNDARY: a heat-pump dryer normally runs at a LOWER drum temperature and a LONGER programme than an old vented dryer. So 'only feels warm rather than very hot' and 'takes longer than my old vented dryer' are usually NORMAL and must NOT by themselves produce a fault/part diagnosis. Reassure and, if anything, suggest cleaning the filters and reducing load.

Ground a hardware fault only on stronger evidence: worsening performance over time, genuinely COLD operation that never dries, abnormal cycle behaviour, error codes, airflow restriction, or sensor/compressor evidence. The cheap common cause of gradually poor drying is a blocked CONDENSER/EVAPORATOR filter (clean first); the sealed refrigerant circuit is a specialist/costly repair and the last resort.

docs.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
symptoms: trips as soon as it starts
discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.

Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a CONVENTIONAL vented/condenser dryer the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth - it typically trips only once the cycle reaches the HEATING stage; also consider the mains cable/plug, water sitting in the base, and less often the motor or mains suppressor. Tripping the INSTANT you switch on (before heating) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the motor/pump than the element.

On a confirmed HEAT-PUMP dryer there is no conventional element - trips that follow the COMPRESSOR starting point to the compressor/inverter drive electronics, wiring or motor/fans. Do not recommend a conventional heater element for a heat-pump machine.

SAFETY: never advise the customer to do live mains testing, insulation-resistance testing, bypassing protection, or repeatedly resetting the RCD and running it again. Repeated tripping with burning/smoke means STOP USE and get it checked.

docs.label: Tearing / snagging clothes
discriminators: A dryer that tears/snags clothes is usually a worn drum felt/rear seal (items slip into the gap) or a rough spot/crack in the drum edge.

Route by the damage type/evidence - do NOT default to the heater or motor. Most commonly a worn drum FELT/rear SEAL lets small items slip into a gap and catch, or a rough spot/crack/sharp edge on the drum snags fabric. Also check for a trapped foreign object (coin, bra underwire). Scorching/melting rather than tearing points to excessive heat (see overheating), not a mechanical snag.

docs.label: Not draining / standing water
symptoms: stops mid cycle with water in the bottom
discriminators: A dishwasher that stops mid-cycle and beeps/flashes is most often a drainage fault (blocked filter, pump or hose) - it can't pump out so it halts. Water standing in the bottom confirms it. (If it's bone dry and dead instead, look at the door switch or PCB.)
Standing water in the base that won't clear: drain pump or a blocked filter/sump; check the non-return valve.
Drains but leaves a little water each time: often normal, or a partial filter blockage.

Not draining is CHECK-FIRST: 1) twist out and clean the drain FILTER, 2) check the SUMP/impeller for a foreign object (glass, bone, label), 3) the DRAIN HOSE for kinks/blockage, 4) the waste/spigot connection (on a new install the sink-spigot blanking plug is often left in). Only then the drain pump.

Distinguish NO pump activity (silent => pump/supply/wiring) from PUMP HUMS but water stays (jam/blockage => clear it) from PUMP RUNS with the path obstructed (clear the obstruction). Humming is usually a jam, not a dead pump.
Water left with the machine stopping mid-cycle and beeping is usually a DRAIN issue (filter/blockage) - check the filter before anything electrical.

docs.label: Fill / no water fault
discriminators: Fill is CHECK-FIRST: property supply, isolation tap, inlet hose (kinks), inlet filter/strainer, and any anti-flood state. Then the inlet valve, flow/level sensing, and (on machines that have one) the side water matrix.
An inlet valve can fail PARTIALLY - opening but passing only a trickle. Don't treat fill as simply open or closed.
Controls are often in the door: an inlet valve that tests GOOD but is never POWERED points to the door wiring loom/harness, not the valve or (jumping ahead) the PCB.

[S24] COMMON CAUSE: hard-water area + gradually slower fill + weakening spray + worsening wash is more likely ONE progressively restricted water path (scale) than the inlet valve, circulation pump and both spray arms all failing at once. Ask 'is this several faults or one restricted path?' - do NOT shotgun valve + pump + arms + PCB.

[S24] PROGRESSIVE vs SUDDEN: gradual worsening favours scale/restriction/contamination; a sudden failure (worked yesterday, dead/completely different today) favours a discrete blockage, failed component, electrical fault or leak - not scale. Not absolute.

[S24] Keep the boundaries: several unrelated ELECTRICAL symptoms / intermittent controls / behaviour that changes with door position => DOOR LOOM, not scale. Water in the base + drain pump running => anti-flood, FIND THE LEAK, not scale.

check the machine isn't in an anti-flood state

docs.label: Heating fault (won't heat / cold wash)
symptoms: cold at the end of the cycle
cycle takes hours and dishes are cold
discriminators: Genuine NO-HEAT (dishes and wash water clearly COLD, wash also poor, cycle may run abnormally long waiting for temperature) points to the heater / flow-through heater assembly, the NTC temperature sensor or its wiring. Many modern machines (e.g. Bosch) have NO exposed element - heating is a flow-through heater built into the circulation-pump assembly. DISHES WET BUT HOT at the end is NOT a heating fault - that is poor-drying (rinse aid / programme / plastics).
Confirm genuine NO-HEAT first: wash water and dishes clearly COLD, washing also poor, and the cycle may run abnormally long waiting for temperature. HOT-but-wet dishes is poor-drying, not heating.

Architecture matters: older machines have an exposed base element; many modern machines (e.g. Bosch) use a FLOW-THROUGH heater integrated into the circulation-pump assembly (no separate element). Identify the model before recommending a part.
Order: element / flow-through assembly -> NTC temperature sensor -> heater wiring (and the door loom, since a good heater that's never powered mimics a heater fault) -> control/PCB last.

docs.label: Leak / anti-flood (Aquastop) triggered
symptoms: water from the bottom of the door
leaks from the bottom of the door
water under the machine no puddle
leaks from the side of the door
pump keeps running with an empty machine
keeps stopping with water in the bottom
leaks again after a few washes
discriminators: Water leaking FROM THE DOOR (especially the bottom) is usually the door seal/gasket, not the latch - route a door LEAK here, not to the door latch/switch fault.

Dishwasher leaks are diagnosed by WHERE the water appears. A leak from the SIDE or EDGE of the DOOR during washing is the classic one: a perished/dirty DOOR SEAL, a MISALIGNED/dropped door, or a SPLIT SPRAY ARM firing water at the door - check seal, alignment and spray arm before replacing anything.

Most dishwashers have a base tray with a float / anti-flood (Aquastop) switch that catches INTERNAL leaks (sump hose, pump seals, spray-arm feed, tub). An internal leak often shows as the machine STOPPING / anti-flood triggered / a leak error with NO water on the floor, rather than an obvious puddle.

REPAIR TRAP: draining/drying the base tray makes an anti-flood fault look fixed and it may run for a wash or two, but if the underlying leak is still there the tray refills and it triggers again. 'Emptied the tray and it worked' is NOT a repair - the leaking component still needs finding and fixing.

STRONG anti-flood / base-flood pattern: the tub looks EMPTY, the DRAIN PUMP RUNS CONTINUOUSLY and a normal programme won't start or fill => the float in the base has detected water and put the machine into a protective drain/lockout. Establish that the base is wet, then FIND THE LEAK (sump/pump seals, hoses, tub, spray arm, dispenser). The flood switch is responding correctly - it is NOT the fault unless the base is proven dry and the float is stuck.
Do not keep re-running a machine that keeps flooding its base - the leak remains and water damage continues.

docs.label: Door latch / door switch fault
symptoms: nothing happens when i press start
discriminators: A dishwasher that won't turn on/start: if it still has power/lights, the usual cause is the door catch/latch not confirming the door is shut (or the on/off switch). If it's completely dead with no lights, look at the mains/PCB (main-pcb) instead.
A door that drops/slams open (rather than a latch/catch problem) is worn door balance/support springs or the hinge cables.

Separate MECHANICAL from ELECTRICAL. Physically won't close => loading/rack/alignment, hinge, latch. Closes normally but won't start => latch/interlock, then the door switch wiring / DOOR LOOM, then control - PCB last.
If moving or pressing the door changes the symptom, raise alignment, latch and especially the loom/flex wiring.
Integrated (furniture-door) machines: check the furniture-door adjustment/balance before condemning an internal part.

docs.label: Wash / circulation pump fault
discriminators: Spray arm(s) not spinning is most often a BLOCKAGE first - clean the arm jets/holes and the filter. If the arms are clear and still don't turn, it's a weak/failed wash (circulation) pump or its motor.
A loud hum/drone while WASHING usually means the wash (circulation) pump or debris caught in it; a hum only while DRAINING points to the drain pump instead.

Weak/no spray: clear the spray arms and jets first, then confirm the tub fills to the correct level (underfill starves the arms - that's a fill/matrix problem, not the pump). Only then the circulation/wash pump (or debris jamming its impeller).
Noise by stage: a loud hum/drone while WASHING => the circulation pump or debris in it; a hum while DRAINING => the drain pump; a regular ticking => a spray arm hitting the dishes.

[S24] LOCAL vs SYSTEMIC: one arm / one rack / one group of jets favours a LOCAL spray-arm or distribution restriction; slow fill / low water level / ALL spray weak / whole machine washing poorly favours a COMMON water-delivery, level or circulation restriction. Don't diagnose several failed parts when one restricted water path fits better.

[S24] In hard-water areas, weak spray with a NORMAL fill level may be scaled spray-arm jets (local) rather than the pump; underfill points upstream to fill/matrix. Confirm the fill level and clear/descale the jets before the pump.

docs.label: Pressure switch / water level fault
discriminators: [S24] Hard water is EVIDENCE, not proof: a hard-water area PLUS progressive water-path symptoms PLUS visible scale/restriction raises a scale/restriction cause - hard-water location ALONE is never a diagnosis.

[S24] PROGRESSIVE vs SUDDEN: gradual worsening favours scale/restriction/contamination; a sudden failure (worked yesterday, dead/completely different today) favours a discrete blockage, failed component, electrical fault or leak - not scale. Not absolute.

docs.label: Poor cleaning results (dishes dirty / gritty / filmy)
discriminators: Clean and unblock the spray arms (clear the little jet holes) and the filter first - the commonest cause of poor results.
Make sure rinse aid and dishwasher salt are topped up and the water is getting hot enough; cloudy glasses are often hard-water/rinse-aid related.
If water isn't heating or the arms aren't spinning, suspect the heater element or the wash/circulation pump.

Rusty cutlery is usually not the machine: low/empty dishwasher salt (soft water protects cutlery), a loose salt-reservoir cap letting salt into the wash, or a chipped rack coating exposing bare metal - one rusting item can mark the rest. Top up salt, check the cap, and repair/replace chipped rack tips.

Even for a vague 'not cleaning properly', COMMIT to this poor-cleaning fault with the BLOCKED FILTER as the lead cause (by far the most common) and ask what residue is left to refine - don't withhold a diagnosis.

Diagnose a poor-wash by the RESIDUE and rank by likelihood. GRITTY/SANDY residue (like coffee grounds) = a BLOCKED FILTER recirculating dirty water - by far the most common (~60%). Twist out and rinse the bottom filter first.

GREASY/FILMY dishes that are still WET with NO steam/heat right after the cycle = genuine no-heat (heater/flow-through assembly) - next most common (~20%). But wet dishes that are HOT is drying (rinse aid), not heating.
ONE rack or corner consistently unwashed while the rest is clean = CLOGGED/blocked SPRAY ARMS or an arm not spinning - clear the holes (~15%).

Fills and drains but SILENT during the wash, or a loud continuous hum with no spray = the CIRCULATION/WASH PUMP (jammed impeller - e.g. broken glass - or failed motor) - least common (~5%). If the tub is UNDERFILLED, it's a fill problem starving the arms, not the pump.
A WHITE CHALKY film is hard-water/limescale or empty rinse-aid/salt (maintenance/settings), not a failed part - sort salt/rinse-aid and descale before replacing anything.

[S24] Hard water is EVIDENCE, not proof: a hard-water area PLUS progressive water-path symptoms PLUS visible scale/restriction raises a scale/restriction cause - hard-water location ALONE is never a diagnosis.

[S24] COMMON CAUSE: hard-water area + gradually slower fill + weakening spray + worsening wash is more likely ONE progressively restricted water path (scale) than the inlet valve, circulation pump and both spray arms all failing at once. Ask 'is this several faults or one restricted path?' - do NOT shotgun valve + pump + arms + PCB.

[S24] LOCAL vs SYSTEMIC: one arm / one rack / one group of jets favours a LOCAL spray-arm or distribution restriction; slow fill / low water level / ALL spray weak / whole machine washing poorly favours a COMMON water-delivery, level or circulation restriction. Don't diagnose several failed parts when one restricted water path fits better.

[S24] Keep the boundaries: several unrelated ELECTRICAL symptoms / intermittent controls / behaviour that changes with door position => DOOR LOOM, not scale. Water in the base + drain pump running => anti-flood, FIND THE LEAK, not scale.
