Customer phrases: dishes still dirty; gritty dishes; not cleaning; food left on dishes; cloudy glasses; film on glasses; dishes not clean; poor wash; rusty cutlery; rust on cutlery; rusty dishes; cutlery going rusty; hard water area; gradually getting worse; limescale build up; progressively worse washing; sandy residue; greasy film; filmy dishes; not washing properly; dishes come out wet; white film; chalky film; tablet not dissolving; undissolved tablet
Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. drain filter (clean first - gritty/sandy residue) [CHECK]
   More likely if: gritty or sandy residue like coffee grounds; food redeposited on the dishes; by far the most common poor-wash cause (~60%).
   Less likely if: the filter is proven clean.
2. spray arms / jets blocked or arm not spinning [CHECK]
   More likely if: one rack or corner consistently unwashed; scale or seeds blocking the jets.
   Less likely if: the arms are clear and spinning.
3. water level / underfill [CHECK]
   More likely if: all-over poor wash with a low water level.
   Less likely if: the tub fills to the correct level.
4. rinse aid / salt / hard water (white chalky film) [CHECK]
   More likely if: a white chalky film; cloudy glasses; empty rinse aid or salt, hard-water area.
   Less likely if: the residue is greasy or gritty, not chalky.
5. heater / flow-through assembly (greasy film + cold) [PART]
   More likely if: greasy/filmy dishes that are still WET, with NO steam/heat when you open the door right after the cycle; the wash is clearly cold.
   Less likely if: the wash is hot (film is rinse-aid/hard-water, not heat).
6. circulation / wash pump (silent wash / jammed impeller) [PART]
   More likely if: fills and drains but is SILENT during the wash (no sloshing/spraying); a loud continuous hum with no spray; broken glass jamming the impeller.
   Less likely if: the arms just need clearing.
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- tablet not dissolved = dispenser: An undissolved tablet with dirty dishes is a WASH problem (weak spray, underfill, blocked arms, low temperature) - not the dispenser, provided the flap opened.
   Only consider if: the flap opened but the tablet remains.
- white film = failed part: White chalky film is hard water / empty rinse-aid or salt (maintenance/settings), not a failed part - sort the salt and rinse aid and descale first.
   Only consider if: the film is white/chalky.
- [S24] gradual poor wash = several failed parts: Hard-water area + gradually slower fill + weakening spray + worsening wash is more likely ONE progressively restricted water path (scale) than the valve, pump and both arms all failing at once. Consider a common restriction before a multi-part diagnosis.
   Only consider if: a hard-water area with several gradually-worsening water symptoms.
Engineering notes: Clean and unblock the spray arms (clear the little jet holes) and the filter first - the commonest cause of poor results. Make sure rinse aid and dishwasher salt are topped up and the water is getting hot enough; cloudy glasses are often hard-water/rinse-aid related. If water isn't heating or the arms aren't spinning, suspect the heater element or the wash/circulation pump. Rusty cutlery is usually not the machine: low/empty dishwasher salt (soft water protects cutlery), a loose salt-reservoir cap letting salt into the wash, or a chipped rack coating exposing bare metal - one rusting item can mark the rest. Top up salt, check the cap, and repair/replace chipped rack tips. Even for a vague 'not cleaning properly', COMMIT to this poor-cleaning fault with the BLOCKED FILTER as the lead cause (by far the most common) and ask what residue is left to refine - don't withhold a diagnosis. Diagnose a poor-wash by the RESIDUE and rank by likelihood. GRITTY/SANDY residue (like coffee grounds) = a BLOCKED FILTER recirculating dirty water - by far the most common (~60%). Twist out and rinse the bottom filter first. GREASY/FILMY dishes that are still WET with NO steam/heat right after the cycle = genuine no-heat (heater/flow-through assembly) - next most common (~20%). But wet dishes that are HOT is drying (rinse aid), not heating. ONE rack or corner consistently unwashed while the rest is clean = CLOGGED/blocked SPRAY ARMS or an arm not spinning - clear the holes (~15%). Fills and drains but SILENT during the wash, or a loud continuous hum with no spray = the CIRCULATION/WASH PUMP (jammed impeller - e.g. broken glass - or failed motor) - least common (~5%). If the tub is UNDERFILLED, it's a fill problem starving the arms, not the pump. A WHITE CHALKY film is hard-water/limescale or empty rinse-aid/salt (maintenance/settings), not a failed part - sort salt/rinse-aid and descale before replacing anything. [S24] Hard water is EVIDENCE, not proof: a hard-water area PLUS progressive water-path symptoms PLUS visible scale/restriction raises a scale/restriction cause - hard-water location ALONE is never a diagnosis. [S24] COMMON CAUSE: hard-water area + gradually slower fill + weakening spray + worsening wash is more likely ONE progressively restricted water path (scale) than the inlet valve, circulation pump and both spray arms all failing at once. Ask 'is this several faults or one restricted path?' - do NOT shotgun valve + pump + arms + PCB. [S24] LOCAL vs SYSTEMIC: one arm / one rack / one group of jets favours a LOCAL spray-arm or distribution restriction; slow fill / low water level / ALL spray weak / whole machine washing poorly favours a COMMON water-delivery, level or circulation restriction. Don't diagnose several failed parts when one restricted water path fits better. [S24] Keep the boundaries: several unrelated ELECTRICAL symptoms / intermittent controls / behaviour that changes with door position => DOOR LOOM, not scale. Water in the base + drain pump running => anti-flood, FIND THE LEAK, not scale.
Likely parts in order: heater element, circulation pump
Confused with: heating, circulation-pump, spray-arm, detergent-dispenser, not-draining
Advice before replacing parts: twist out and rinse the bottom filter; clear the spray-arm jets and check the arms spin; top up salt and rinse aid and descale for chalky film; check the tub fills to the normal level
Best question to ask if unsure: What's left on the dishes - sandy grit, greasy film, or white chalky film - and is the machine hot/steamy and audibly spraying during the wash?

docs.label: Excess foam / suds (wrong detergent)
symptoms: foam coming out of the door
discriminators: Excess foam is almost always the wrong detergent (hand dishwashing liquid) or too much detergent — not a failed pump, heater, or seal. Stop or cancel the cycle, let the foam settle, scoop or wipe it, then run an empty rinse or drain using this dishwasher's own cancel or drain control. Do not recommend a part.
Foam escaping the door is a consequence of the suds, not a failed door seal.

docs.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
symptoms: trips when it starts to heat
discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.

Diagnose by WHEN it trips: power-on/immediate => mains filter / incoming wiring / severe short; when circulation starts => circulation pump/wiring; when heating starts or after => heater / flow-through assembly insulation leakage; when draining => drain pump/wiring; when the DOOR MOVES => a chafed/pinched door-loom conductor. Timing is evidence, not absolute proof.

SAFETY: repeated tripping => stop repeated operation; burning or exposed wiring => STOP USE and isolate. Do not tell the customer to insulation-test, expose live wiring, bypass the earth/RCD, or manipulate the loom while powered.

safetyInformation.text: An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
safetyInformation.hazard: Dangerous wiring or an insulation fault (repeated tripping, a burning smell or scorch marks); a dishwasher combines mains electrics with standing water and a wash heater, so water present around a fault raises the shock risk.
safetyInformation.applicability: Appliance repeatedly trips the electrics, or there is a burning smell / scorching.

docs.label: Spray arm fault (blocked jets / split / not spinning)
symptoms: spray arm leaking at the door
top rack not washing scaled jets
discriminators: Split the fault: ONE arm affected => that arm (blockage, split/damage, mounting/bearing) or a diverter where fitted. ALL spray weak => a common upstream cause (underfill/low water, restricted fill/matrix, or the circulation pump), not both arms failing independently.

A LEAK at the door during washing with a visibly SPLIT/CRACKED lower spray arm is caused by the arm firing water sideways at the door - raise the damaged spray arm as the source, not automatically the door seal.
Ticking/knocking/rattling in time with the wash is usually the arm catching a tall item or a loose/damaged arm, not a pump fault.

[S24] LOCAL vs SYSTEMIC: one arm / one rack / one group of jets favours a LOCAL spray-arm or distribution restriction; slow fill / low water level / ALL spray weak / whole machine washing poorly favours a COMMON water-delivery, level or circulation restriction. Don't diagnose several failed parts when one restricted water path fits better.

[S24] Mineral SCALE (as well as food debris) restricts spray-arm jets: reduced pressure, distorted pattern, poor rotation, one rack cleaning badly, progressively worse. UPPER arm jets scaled + top rack poor while the bottom rack is fine = a LOCAL upper spray-arm restriction, NOT the inlet valve, matrix or circulation pump. ALL spray weak points upstream (level/circulation), not the arms.

[S24] PROGRESSIVE vs SUDDEN: gradual worsening favours scale/restriction/contamination; a sudden failure (worked yesterday, dead/completely different today) favours a discrete blockage, failed component, electrical fault or leak - not scale. Not absolute.

docs.label: Door wiring loom / hinge flex wiring fault
symptoms: loses power when the door moves
cuts out when i move the door
works if i move the door
starts if i jiggle the door
says the door is open but it is shut
heating error then door error then dispenser
a part tests fine but gets no power
discriminators: The dishwasher has a large moving door; the wiring for the door-mounted controls, door switch, dispenser and often the heater/sensor sense runs down through the hinge/flex area and flexes on every open and close. Over years individual conductors fatigue, chafe, pinch or break, giving INTERMITTENT and apparently UNRELATED faults.

STRONGLY raise the door loom when: (a) several unrelated errors come and go, (b) the fault changes when the door is opened/closed/moved or the machine starts if the door is jiggled, or (c) a component tests good but is never being driven. In all three, suspect the LOOM BEFORE condemning the PCB or replacing several parts.

The point of the reasoning is not to name the exact broken conductor: repeated door flex -> a broken/chafed wire -> an apparently unrelated component or control symptom. A qualified engineer confirms with the power off.
Do NOT ask the customer to test or manipulate the loom while the machine is powered.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Do the faults come and go or change when you open, close or move the door - and is it several different errors rather than one steady fault?

components.name: what changes with door movement / how many different faults (identify first)
supports: the fault comes and goes when the door is opened, closed or moved
it starts if the door is jiggled or pressed
several unrelated errors that appear and clear on their own
against: one steady fault that never changes with door position

components.name: door wiring loom / hinge flex wiring
supports: intermittent behaviour that changes when the door is moved
multiple unrelated errors coming and going

docs.label: Side water matrix / heat exchanger (architecture-specific)
symptoms: big water reservoir down the side
fills with only a little water
small amount of water then weak spray
not enough water in the machine
big water container down the side
fills with only a small amount of water
discriminators: Some dishwashers (notably Bosch-group) use a tall side WATER MATRIX / LABYRINTH / HEAT EXCHANGER that stores and routes water and aids condensation drying and softening/regeneration. On those machines treat supply -> inlet valve -> inlet filter -> matrix/exchanger -> valves -> flow/level sensing -> tub fill as one connected water-delivery system.

UNDERFILL vs CIRCULATION: fills with only a small amount of water + weak spray => a FILL / matrix / flow-level problem, NOT automatically the circulation pump. A restricted matrix, partial inlet valve or flow/level fault starves the arms. Only suspect the circulation pump when the tub fills to the correct level but spray is still weak.

Matrix/exchanger faults are architecture-specific - confirm the machine actually has one (model/appearance) before recommending matrix parts. Error-code meaning stays manufacturer/model-specific (e.g. some Bosch codes relate to the heat exchanger only on relevant machines); do not universalise codes.

[S24] Hard water is EVIDENCE, not proof: a hard-water area PLUS progressive water-path symptoms PLUS visible scale/restriction raises a scale/restriction cause - hard-water location ALONE is never a diagnosis.

[S24] Narrow matrix/labyrinth waterways progressively accumulate scale/deposits in hard-water areas -> reduced/incorrect water delivery -> underfill -> weak spray -> poor wash (or abnormal fill/level behaviour). Visible heavy scaling in the side matrix + low water + weak spray strongly favours a restricted matrix/water-delivery path OVER the circulation pump. Architecture-first still applies: a machine with no side matrix cannot have a scaled one.

[S24] PROGRESSIVE vs SUDDEN: gradual worsening favours scale/restriction/contamination; a sudden failure (worked yesterday, dead/completely different today) favours a discrete blockage, failed component, electrical fault or leak - not scale. Not absolute.

docs.label: Poor drying (dishes wet at the end)
symptoms: water droplets left on the dishes
discriminators: Dishes that are WARM/HOT but still WET at the end is NOT a heating fault - it is drying/condensation: top up the rinse aid (it sheets water off so it runs away), avoid Eco/Quick programmes that skip the heated dry, don't open the door too soon, and remember plastics naturally stay wetter than glass/ceramic. If the dishes are STONE COLD at the end (wash also poor), that is a heating fault instead (see heating).

Diagnose drying by whether the wash is HOT. HOT but WET => a drying issue: top up rinse aid, check the programme (eco/quick dry little), expect plastics to hold water, and remember many machines dry passively/by condensation or via auto-door-open - do NOT push a heater. COLD everywhere + poor washing => genuine no-heat (see heating).
Rinse aid is the single biggest lever for drying - it makes water sheet off rather than sit in droplets; suggest topping it up first.

docs.label: Heating element / not heating
symptoms: grill works but fan oven doesnt heat
element glowing red in one spot
discriminators: Slow to reach temperature / weak heat = a partially failed element (often only glowing in parts) or a drifting oven thermostat/sensor. Uneven or one-side-only heat on a FAN oven is the fan motor instead (see uneven-heating).

Fan turning but no heat proves the fan MOTOR is working. The fan-oven element is then a strong diagnostic candidate, but it is not proven and is not automatically a purchase. Burnt wiring or connectors, the selector/function/main switch, thermostat/control path, and the supply to the element remain realistic. Distinguish a likely diagnostic component from a safe purchase recommendation.

A function that heats in one mode but not another can be the mode-specific element, OR the selector/function switch, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, thermostat/control path, wiring/connectors, or supply to that function. If the same heating system produces heat in another mode, that argues against a simple open element — it does not by itself prove the selector either. Give the discriminator (which cavity, which mode, whether it glows in grill vs heats in top-oven) and keep both directions open when remote evidence cannot tell them apart. Earth-leak behaviour belongs only when the customer reports tripping.

TOP OVEN vs GRILL (double-oven / two-cavity): the upper cavity commonly provides both top-oven cooking and grill. In top-oven mode the two element sections can be wired in SERIES so each sees roughly half mains — hot enough to cook, not necessarily glowing bright red. In grill mode the switching gives the relevant section(s) full mains so they can glow/toast. Therefore 'the element heats in top-oven mode' does not prove the complete grill function is healthy, and 'part of the grill works' does not automatically prove the element is the failed part. Compare behaviour across modes and reason about the mode-specific control/supply path as well as the element.

Engineer check order for complete no-heat (no mode producing heat): 1) the relevant element, 2) burnt element terminal connectors, 3) the selector/main switch (the commoned neutrals can burn a contact), 4) the oven thermostat (turn it and listen for the click). A function-split is not complete no-heat — do not apply this default there. Only suspect gas ignition on a GAS oven. Do not skip from a heating symptom to asking for the model to sell a part while mode, still-works, and programmer state are still open.

Reason cavity/function/mode first, then what still works, then programmer/control state, then the electrical/heating path that mode uses, then compare across modes. A plausible component hypothesis is not purchase grain.

FAN RUNNING + fan-oven mode + cavity COLD: the fan motor is proven good. The fan/rear RING ELEMENT is a strong diagnostic candidate, not proven. Also keep burnt wiring/connectors, selector/function/main switch, thermostat/control path, and supply. Do not turn this into an unconditional element diagnosis or a model-for-part request.

PRESERVED FUNCTION is diagnostic, not generic 'oven not heating'. Grill works / fan oven cold is a different path from grill-partly-works-in-grill-mode while the same heating system heats in top-oven mode. Do not collapse them.

TOP OVEN vs GRILL topology (two-cavity): top-oven mode can wire element sections in SERIES (~half mains, heats without glowing bright red). Grill mode switches to full mains so they can glow/toast. 'Heats in top-oven' does not prove the grill path is healthy. 'Part of the grill works' does not prove the element is the failed part. Cross-mode evidence must keep the mode-specific control/supply path (selector/function switch, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, wiring) as well as the element — without swapping 'always element' for 'always selector'.

POWER-CUT / FLASHING PROGRAMMER: oven appears dead + clock/programmer flashing + recent power interruption => the programmer is often in automatic/timed state. Return to MANUAL. This is a control-state/use-condition, NOT a parts recommendation. Do not surface parts until that has been ruled out.

Engineer check order for COMPLETE no-heat (no mode producing heat): 1) the relevant element, 2) burnt element terminal connectors, 3) the selector/main switch, 4) the oven thermostat. A function-split is not complete no-heat. PCB last. VISIBLE element damage (split, blistered, holed sheath) strongly supports that element as a hypothesis still short of automatic purchase unless the rest of the path is accounted for.

1. which function works (fan/grill/top/base) - identify first [CHECK]

Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- no heat = the fan motor: If the FAN IS TURNING, the fan motor is proven good. That does NOT automatically prove the fan/ring element has failed — wiring, selector contacts, thermostat/control and supply remain realistic. The motor is only the cause if the fan isn't turning or is noisy.
   Only consider if: the fan isn't turning or is noisy.
- no heat = PCB: Down-rank the PCB. For no-heat the element (which-function), selector contact, thermostat and (if dead) supply/terminal-block come first.
   Only consider if: element, selector, thermostat and supply all proven good.
- dead after a power cut = failed part: Control-state, not a part. After power loss many ovens leave the programmer in automatic/timed mode; heating is inhibited until MANUAL. Do not recommend a timer, PCB or element until that is ruled out.
   Only consider if: still won't heat once the clock is set correctly to MANUAL.
Engineering notes: Slow to reach temperature / weak heat = a partially failed element (often only glowing in parts) or a drifting oven thermostat/sensor. Uneven or one-side-only heat on a FAN oven is the fan motor instead (see uneven-heating). Fan turning but no heat proves the fan MOTOR is working. The fan-oven element is then a strong diagnostic candidate, but it is not proven and is not automatically a purchase. Burnt wiring or connectors, the selector/function/main switch, thermostat/control path, and the supply to the element remain realistic. Distinguish a likely diagnostic component from a safe purchase recommendation. A function that heats in one mode but not another can be the mode-specific element, OR the selector/function switch, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, thermostat/control path, wiring/connectors, or supply to that function. If the same heating system produces heat in another mode, that argues against a simple open element — it does not by itself prove the selector either. Give the discriminator (which cavity, which mode, whether it glows in grill vs heats in top-oven) and keep both directions open when remote evidence cannot tell them apart. Earth-leak behaviour belongs only when the customer reports tripping. TOP OVEN vs GRILL (double-oven / two-cavity): the upper cavity commonly provides both top-oven cooking and grill. In top-oven mode the two element sections can be wired in SERIES so each sees roughly half mains — hot enough to cook, not necessarily glowing bright red. In grill mode the switching gives the relevant section(s) full mains so they can glow/toast. Therefore 'the element heats in top-oven mode' does not prove the complete grill function is healthy, and 'part of the grill works' does not automatically prove the element is the failed part. Compare behaviour across modes and reason about the mode-specific control/supply path as well as the element. Engineer check order for complete no-heat (no mode producing heat): 1) the relevant element, 2) burnt element terminal connectors, 3) the selector/main switch (the commoned neutrals can burn a contact), 4) the oven thermostat (turn it and listen for the click). A function-split is not complete no-heat — do not apply this default there. Only suspect gas ignition on a GAS oven. Do not skip from a heating symptom to asking for the model to sell a part while mode, still-works, and programmer state are still open. Reason cavity/function/mode first, then what still works, then programmer/control state, then the electrical/heating path that mode uses, then compare across modes. A plausible component hypothesis is not purchase grain. FAN RUNNING + fan-oven mode + cavity COLD: the fan motor is proven good. The fan/rear RING ELEMENT is a strong diagnostic candidate, not proven. Also keep burnt wiring/connectors, selector/function/main switch, thermostat/control path, and supply. Do not turn this into an unconditional element diagnosis or a model-for-part request. PRESERVED FUNCTION is diagnostic, not generic 'oven not heating'. Grill works / fan oven cold is a different path from grill-partly-works-in-grill-mode while the same heating system heats in top-oven mode. Do not collapse them. TOP OVEN vs GRILL topology (two-cavity): top-oven mode can wire element sections in SERIES (~half mains, heats without glowing bright red). Grill mode switches to full mains so they can glow/toast. 'Heats in top-oven' does not prove the grill path is healthy. 'Part of the grill works' does not prove the element is the failed part. Cross-mode evidence must keep the mode-specific control/supply path (selector/function switch, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, wiring) as well as the element — without swapping 'always element' for 'always selector'. POWER-CUT / FLASHING PROGRAMMER: oven appears dead + clock/programmer flashing + recent power interruption => the programmer is often in automatic/timed state. Return to MANUAL. This is a control-state/use-condition, NOT a parts recommendation. Do not surface parts until that has been ruled out. Engineer check order for COMPLETE no-heat (no mode producing heat): 1) the relevant element, 2) burnt element terminal connectors, 3) the selector/main switch, 4) the oven thermostat. A function-split is not complete no-heat. PCB last. VISIBLE element damage (split, blistered, holed sheath) strongly supports that element as a hypothesis still short of automatic purchase unless the rest of the path is accounted for. Do NOT diagnose GAS ignition unless the oven is explicitly GAS or a flame/burner/pilot is mentioned (this is the electric-oven element path).
Likely parts in order: fan oven element, grill element, base element, top element, element connectors, selector switch, grill energy regulator
Confused with: fan-motor, thermostat, selector-switch, clock-timer, terminal-block, tripping-electrics, main-pcb
Advice before replacing parts: identify cavity, which function/mode is affected, and what still works; after a power cut, or if the clock is flashing, set the clock/timer to MANUAL and the correct time before anything else; a visibly split/blistered element can be identified by eye (power off)
Best question to ask if unsure: Which cavity and function is affected (fan oven, top oven, grill, base), what still works, and is the clock or programmer flashing or left on automatic after a power cut?
Follow-up question if still unclear: In the affected cavity, does the same heating system behave differently in top-oven mode versus grill mode?

docs.label: Control board / PCB / communication fault
discriminators: An oven/cooker that won't switch on at all, or where the clock/display and light are dead together, points to no power reaching the board - check the mains/fuse and cooker switch first, then the control board/PCB.

OVEN DEAD is ambiguous. 'My oven is dead', 'oven won't work' or 'nothing happens' is not a component diagnosis. First establish what dead means: display/clock state, whether the clock is flashing, whether fan/light works, whether any heating function works, and whether power was recently interrupted. Do not jump to the PCB or an element from the phrase alone.

A flashing clock/programmer after a power interruption is often a control-state/use-condition (the programmer left in automatic/timed mode) — not a board fault. Route that to the clock/timer advice path; do not recommend parts until manual operation has been restored or ruled out.
Customers call the control board the 'programmer', 'brain' or 'module' - all mean the main PCB. It is the LAST candidate.

OVEN DEAD is ambiguous: establish display/clock, flashing/AUTO, fan/light, any heating function, and recent power interruption before a board or element. COMPLETELY DEAD (no display, no light) => supply/isolator, then mains TERMINAL BLOCK, then wiring; PCB last. DISPLAY works but oven won't run, especially after a power cut => programmer AUTO — MANUAL first, not a board.

docs.label: Gas ignition / flame fault
discriminators: A GAS oven/burner that lights then goes out, won't stay lit, or won't heat at all (while the grill/hob still work) is most often the FLAME FAILURE DEVICE (FSD/FFD) - the safety that shuts the gas off when it doesn't sense a flame (its thermocouple/flame probe). That mapping applies ONLY when the customer reported stay-lit / lights-then-goes-out behaviour. Uncommanded ignition sparking is not a stay-lit report. Accessing or testing the FFD/thermocouple/gas valve is for a Gas Safe engineer, not a remote DIY instruction.
ONLY diagnose gas ignition when the oven is explicitly GAS, or a flame / burner / pilot / gas is mentioned. A plain electric 'no heat' with no gas cue is the ELEMENT, not ignition.

A GAS oven/burner that lights then goes out, won't stay lit, or won't heat at all (while the grill/hob still work) is most often the FLAME FAILURE DEVICE (FSD/FFD) - the safety that shuts the gas off when it doesn't sense a flame (via its thermocouple/flame probe). Check the FFD/thermocouple FIRST, then the oven ignitor/glowbar, then the gas valve.
This is a GAS fault, NOT an electric element.

symptoms: horrible noise from the back of the oven when the fan runs
discriminators: The cavity fan MOTOR is the culprit only when the fan is NOISY (scrape/rattle/rumble) or clearly NOT TURNING. docs.text:
Appliance: oven cooker
Fault: Fan oven motor fault
Customer phrases: fan not turning; uneven cooking; fan noise; fan oven fan isnt working; fan making a noise; fan noisy; fan rattling; fan grinding; fan scraping; fan slow; fan blade rubbing; horrible noise from the back of the oven when the fan runs
Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. obstruction / fan blade fouling the rear cover [CHECK]
   More likely if: scraping/ticking as the blade catches the rear cover/shroud; something fouling the blade.
   Less likely if: clear blade and a dead/silent fan.
2. fan blade (loose/distorted) [PART]
   More likely if: rattle or scraping from a loose/bent blade; blade contacting the cover.
   Less likely if: deep rumble from the bearing (motor).
3. cavity fan motor [PART]
   More likely if: fan doesn't turn at all in fan mode; rumbling/rough bearing noise; fan slow/intermittent with the blade free.
   Less likely if: the fan turns fine but there's no heat (=> fan element).
4. fan thermal cut-out / wiring [CHECK]
   More likely if: fan dead with a tripped thermal cutout or broken wiring.
   Less likely if: fan runs normally.
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- fan oven no heat = fan motor: If the fan IS TURNING, the motor is proven fine. That does not automatically make the fan/ring ELEMENT a purchase — wiring, selector and supply remain realistic. The motor is only the cause when the fan is noisy or not turning.
   Only consider if: the fan is noisy or clearly not turning.
- noisy fan = cooling fan: The cavity/cooking fan (behind the rear plate, circulates heat) is different from the cooling fan (cools the controls). Match the symptom to the right fan.
   Only consider if: controls getting hot / cuts-out-hot => cooling fan instead.
Engineering notes: The cavity fan MOTOR is the culprit only when the fan is NOISY (scrape/rattle/rumble) or clearly NOT TURNING. If the fan turns but there's no heat, the motor is proven good — the heating/supply path (element, connectors, selector, thermostat) is then in play; do not treat the element as an automatic purchase. Best question to ask if unsure: Is the fan noisy or not spinning, or is it spinning fine but the oven just isn't heating?
Follow-up question if still unclear: What does the noise sound like - scraping/ticking, a deep rumble, or a rattle?

docs.label: Thermostat fault
symptoms: cuts out after a few minutes
turns itself off after a while
shuts off when it gets hot
too hot even on a low setting
heats up then goes cold then hot again
cuts out after a few minutes without tripping
discriminators: Burns everything / runs too hot / food cooks too fast even on a low setting = the thermostat isn't regulating and the oven overshoots the set temperature (whole oven too hot). This is different from burning on ONE SIDE only (that's uneven-heating / the fan).

An oven that runs then cuts out after several minutes / once it's hot is usually the thermostat or a thermal overheat cut-out; on a FAN oven a failing fan motor (poor air circulation) can also trip the overheat.

Burns everything / runs too hot even on low / never cycles off => the temperature is NOT being regulated: mechanical dial-thermostat oven => oven thermostat (and its capillary/phial); electronic oven => temperature sensor + control. It is NOT an over-powerful element.

Cuts out / goes cold once hot WITHOUT tripping the electrics => thermostat or overheat thermal cutout - and consider the COOLING FAN (if it recovers when cool). If it TRIPS THE RCD, that's an element earth fault (tripping-electrics), not the thermostat.
ARCHITECTURE: don't recommend a mechanical thermostat on a sensor/electronic oven or vice-versa - identify the control type.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is it running much too hot (burning even on low), or does it go cold after a while - and does it trip the electrics when it does?

components.name: mechanical oven thermostat [dial/capillary ovens]
supports: burns everything / runs too hot on a dial-thermostat oven
never cycles off
the capillary/phial or thermostat not regulating
against: an electronic/sensor-controlled oven (=> temperature sensor/control)

components.name: oven temperature sensor + control [electronic ovens]
supports: electronic-control oven running too hot/cold
temperature bears little relation to the setting
against: a simple mechanical dial thermostat

components.name: safety/overheat thermal cut-out
supports: cuts out once hot WITHOUT tripping the electrics, recovers when cool
against: it TRIPS the RCD (=> element earth leakage)

commonConfusion.name: too hot = the element is too powerful
commonConfusion.note: The element receives power according to the control system - an oven running too hot is the THERMOSTAT/sensor/control not regulating, not an over-powerful element.
wouldApplyIf: temperature far above the setting, never cycling off

commonConfusion.name: cuts out when hot = thermostat
commonConfusion.note: Cuts out hot and recovers when cool can be the COOLING FAN / airflow / thermal cutout. Cuts out WITH an RCD trip is element earth leakage. Only a non-tripping thermal regulation fault is the thermostat.
wouldApplyIf: cuts out hot without tripping and without the cooling fan/airflow being implicated

docs.label: Function / selector switch fault
symptoms: top oven heats grill does not
discriminators: The main/function switch on a double oven commonly performs the switching between top-oven and grill operation (series vs full-mains). Cross-mode evidence is valuable: an element that behaves one way in top-oven mode but incorrectly in grill mode should keep the MODE-SPECIFIC CONTROL/SUPPLY PATH in play as well as the element.

Do not conclude 'element works in another mode therefore the selector is faulty', and do not conclude 'grill partly heats therefore the element is faulty'. Use the complete evidence: which cavity, which mode, what still works, whether the same heating system heats in top-oven, and whether glow/toast is missing only in grill.

Grill energy regulator / simmerstat, burnt selector contacts/terminals, and wiring/connections are legitimate causes of heating-function faults. The supply/control path must remain available when evidence warrants it — this does not mean always recommending the selector.

When only PARTICULAR functions/positions work, the MAIN SELECTOR/FUNCTION SWITCH is a candidate — it commonly performs the switching between top-oven (element sections in series, ~half mains) and grill (full mains). That is not a deterministic selector diagnosis.

Cross-mode evidence is valuable: heats in top-oven but grill glow/toast is incomplete => reason about the mode-specific control/supply path (selector, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, wiring) as well as the element. Do not conclude 'element works in another mode therefore selector' or 'grill partly heats therefore element'.
If the WHOLE oven will not run (especially after a power cut), the flashing-programmer / AUTO use-condition comes first — advice, not a selector.

A visibly open single element (other modes switching correctly) keeps the element in play; burnt selector contacts/terminals remain legitimate when evidence warrants them. Do not always recommend the selector.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Which functions/positions work and which don't - and does any affected element work via a different mode?

components.name: clock/timer AUTO (if the whole oven won't run)
supports: oven won't run at all after a power cut - set MANUAL first
against: specific functions fail while others work

components.name: main function / selector switch
supports: several loads fail only on particular selector positions
a component works via a different position that uses it
only certain positions work / intermittent with position
knob spins freely / doesn't engage
a function stuck on / won't switch off
against: a single element open with the selector switching other modes correctly

components.name: grill energy regulator / simmerstat
supports: grill-mode heat/glow incomplete while top-oven cooking on the same system is normal
grill control does not vary grill power as expected
against: every function dead
a visibly failed element with no mode-specific split

components.name: control PCB (last)
supports: selector proven good and functions still misbehave
against: classic selector-contact pattern not excluded

commonConfusion.name: function dead = that element is bad
commonConfusion.note: Not always, and not automatically the selector either. A selector can fail on individual contacts. If the SAME heating system behaves differently by mode (top-oven vs grill), keep the mode-specific control/supply path AND the element in play. Do not conclude 'works in another mode therefore selector' or 'grill partly heats therefore element'.
wouldApplyIf: the same element works via another position, or multiple loads fail on one selector position

docs.secondaryQuestion: Does the selector knob engage properly or spin freely?
adviceBeforeReplacement: check whether the same element works via another compatible mode/position
after a power cut, set the clock to MANUAL first

docs.label: Clock / timer / programmer state
symptoms: oven wont come on but the clock works
oven wont turn on since a power cut
wont start until the clock is set
discriminators: A flashing clock/programmer after a recent power interruption is a CONTROL-STATE / USE-CONDITION, not a parts recommendation. Many ovens default the programmer into automatic/timed operation after power loss; the oven may not heat until it is returned to MANUAL. Advise that check first. Do not surface a timer, PCB or element until manual operation has been restored or ruled out.

THIS IS ALMOST NEVER A FAULTY PART. Only if the oven still will not heat once in manual, or the clock genuinely cannot be set, is a timer/programmer component even a hypothesis — and that still is not automatically a purchase.

THIS IS A CONTROL-STATE / USE-CONDITION, NOT A PART. After a power interruption the clock/programmer often defaults into automatic/timed operation and the oven will not heat until returned to MANUAL. docs.label: Uneven heating / burning on one side
discriminators: On fan (fan-assisted) ovens the usual cause is a failing fan motor or a loose/damaged fan blade, so heat no longer circulates evenly - check the fan spins freely.
A partially failed element (visible break or only glowing in parts) or a drifting thermostat/temperature sensor can also cook unevenly.

Uneven/one-sided cooking is CHECK-first: loading/tray/airflow, then cavity FAN circulation (slow fan / distorted blade), then DOOR SEAL / alignment (heat escaping), then a missing element for that mode. Thermostat/sensor last.
One side CONSISTENTLY hotter/cooler regardless of loading points to circulation or a door-seal/alignment gap.

supports: overloaded, trays blocking airflow, food too close to one element
against: consistent one-sided pattern regardless of loading

supports: one side consistently under/over-cooked

against: conventional (non-fan) mode only

components.name: door seal / door alignment (heat escaping one side)
supports: heat escaping one side, visible seal damage or a door that doesn't sit flush
against: seal and door sound

components.name: a missing element in the selected mode
supports: one of the elements for that mode has failed so heat comes from one side
against: all elements for the mode working

components.name: thermostat/sensor (last for uneven)
supports: temperature control clearly off as well
against: temperature is about right overall, just uneven

commonConfusion.name: uneven = thermostat

inspect the door seal and that the door closes flush

docs.label: Broken / shattered door glass
discriminators: Only a CRACKED, CHIPPED, BROKEN or SHATTERED pane needs replacing. Dirt, grease, smears, marks or condensation trapped BETWEEN the panes with no crack/break is a CLEANING job (clean between the glass - see door-glass-dirty), NOT a replacement: do not recommend a replacement glass, invent breakage, or raise a shard/injury hazard for a cleaning issue.

Safety first ONLY when the glass is genuinely broken/shattered: stop using the oven and clear the glass carefully. Both the inner and outer door glass are usually replaceable parts - the exact glass is model-specific, so we need the model number.
If only the inner pane broke, the oven may still be usable briefly but should not be run until replaced.

Cracked/shattered oven door glass (inner or outer) is a direct replacement part - identify the correct glass, don't run a heating diagnosis. Advise careful clear-up of shattered glass and not using the oven until replaced.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is it the inner or outer door glass that's broken?

docs.label: Marks or condensation trapped between the oven door glass
symptoms: clean between the oven door glass
discriminators: This is a CLEANING / access job, NOT a replacement: dirt, grease, smears, marks or condensation trapped between the door panes means the glass is intact and just needs cleaning between the layers. Do not recommend a replacement door glass, and do not tell the customer to stop using it for shards - the glass is not broken.

On most ovens the inner door glass unclips, or the door can be split, to clean between the panes (exact technique varies by make/model). Only if a pane is actually CRACKED, CHIPPED, BROKEN or SHATTERED does the glass need replacing (see broken / shattered door glass).
Persistent condensation/misting between the panes that returns after cleaning can mean a perished door seal letting moisture in - check the door seal before assuming any glass part is faulty.

docs.label: Interior light not working
discriminators: Usually just a blown bulb - a cheap fix. Oven bulbs are special heat-resistant 300C types (often SES/E14), so use the correct one.
If a new bulb doesn't work, check the lamp holder/wiring or the door switch.
If ONLY the cavity lamp fails and the oven otherwise works => lamp, then holder/local wiring. A bulb that keeps blowing points to the holder/heat. Don't route a simple lamp failure to the PCB.

docs.label: Door won't close / stay shut
discriminators: Worn or broken door hinges/springs are the usual cause of a door that won't stay shut or drops open - they're replaceable parts.
A perished door seal (gasket) can also stop the door closing flush. Give us the model and we'll find the right hinges/seal.

A dropped/sagging door, a door that won't stay shut or springs open, or an obvious gap is usually a HINGE (or its receiver) or alignment - usually visually/mechanically obvious. Poor closure can cause apparent heating/cooking problems.

docs.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
symptoms: trips as soon as i turn it on
trips when the grill is on
discriminators: An oven/cooker that trips the RCD/fuse (immediately, intermittently, or only once it is hot / after a few minutes) is often a heating element leaking to earth. Neutrals and electrical paths can be shared across grill/top, fan-oven and base elements and switched through common/main switching, so an earth-leaking element elsewhere can trip when another function is selected. The selected function is evidence, NOT proof of which element is leaking. Do not confidently recommend replacing the selected function's element from the tripping symptom alone.

Electrical insulation/leakage diagnosis is competent-person territory. Do not instruct insulation-resistance tests, megger tests, live probing, earth disconnection, RCD bypass, or repeated resets to reproduce the fault. Stop use and isolate; a qualified electrician/engineer must identify the leaking path.

An oven that trips the RCD/fuse often has a HEATING ELEMENT leaking to earth. Insulation leakage can rise as an element heats, so 'starts then trips once hot' is useful timing evidence. It does not identify which element.

CRITICAL - SHARED ELECTRICAL PATHS: grill/top, fan-oven and base elements can share neutrals and be switched through common/main switching. The function that trips is evidence, NOT proof of which element is leaking. Do not confidently recommend replacing the selected function's element from the tripping symptom.

SAFETY: leakage diagnosis is competent-person territory. Repeated tripping (or any burning) => STOP USE. Do NOT instruct insulation-resistance / megger tests, live probing, energising exposed components, disconnecting earth, bypassing the RCD, or repeatedly resetting to reproduce the fault.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does it actually trip the electrics/RCD (versus just going cold), and does it trip straight away or only after it's been heating for a while?

docs.label: Oven door seal / gasket

rubber seal on the door damaged
discriminators: A perished/detached oven door seal (gasket) lets heat escape around the door - it's a straightforward replaceable part. (A door that won't shut/drops is the hinge; broken glass is the door glass.)

docs.label: Mains terminal block / burnt supply connection
symptoms: scorched connector where the cable comes in
burning smell from the back of the oven
burnt smell where the cable comes in
discriminators: The mains TERMINAL BLOCK where the fixed supply cable enters the oven commonly overheats and burns (high-resistance/loose connection, undersized, or an element shorting to its sheath). Signs: burning smell from the back, charred/melted/discoloured connector, white powdery residue, intermittent power or power lost under load, or completely dead with heat damage.
STRONG VISIBLE BURNING/MELTING => STOP USE and isolate the supply; do NOT keep operating it.
A failing element can burn its terminal - check the element as well as the block.
Completely dead with NO heat damage/burning => check the external supply/isolator first, then the block, wiring and control - do not assume the block without evidence.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is there a burning smell or visible melting/charring at the back where the mains cable connects, and is the oven completely dead or intermittent?

docs.label: Cooling fan (controls/cabinet cooling) fault
symptoms: oven cuts out when hot then works when cool
kitchen units above oven getting hot
oven cuts out when it gets hot then works again when cool
kitchen units above the oven getting warm
oven shuts off after a while when hot
discriminators: The COOLING fan (cools the controls/cabinet - a quiet whirring during/after cooking) is a DIFFERENT component from the CAVITY/COOKING fan (circulates heat around the food). Uneven cooking / fan-only-mode not turning => cavity fan (fan-motor); controls/fascia getting hot or cuts-out-when-hot-recovers-when-cool => cooling fan.

CAUSAL CHAIN: cooling fan fails => controls/electronics overheat => overheat thermal cutout operates => oven cuts out; often works again after cooling. Consider cooling fan / its thermostat / airflow / thermal cutout.
SAFETY: a failed cooling fan lets the controls, fascia and surrounding units overheat (distortion/fire risk) - advise stopping use until repaired.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does it cut out only once it's hot and work again after cooling, and are the controls or the fascia getting hot?

components.name: airflow / vents obstruction
supports: vents blocked / oven boxed in with poor airflow
against: airflow clear and the cooling fan still not running

components.name: cooling fan motor
supports: the quiet whirring cooling fan isn't running
controls/fascia/cabinetry getting hot
oven overheats and cuts out then recovers when cool
against: it's the cavity fan (uneven cooking / fan-only mode) not turning (=> fan motor)

components.name: cooling-fan thermostat / control
supports: cooling fan never starts even when hot
fan control/switch not energising the fan
against: fan motor itself proven seized/open

components.name: overheat thermal cut-out
supports: oven cuts out on overheat because cooling failed; may not reset
against: no overheating - a straight no-heat or trip

commonConfusion.name: cuts out when hot = thermostat
commonConfusion.note: If it cuts out when hot and RECOVERS when cool, suspect the COOLING fan / airflow / thermal cutout, not just the thermostat. If it TRIPS THE RCD, that's element earth leakage instead.

docs.text:
Appliance: oven cooker
Fault: Cooling fan (controls/cabinet cooling) fault
Customer phrases: controls getting hot; fascia getting hot; cooling fan not running; cooling fan noisy; oven cuts out when hot then works when cool; kitchen units above oven getting hot; cooling fan stopped; oven cuts out when it gets hot then works again when cool; kitchen units above the oven getting warm; quiet whirring stopped; oven shuts off after a while when hot
Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. airflow / vents obstruction [CHECK]
   More likely if: vents blocked / oven boxed in with poor airflow.
   Less likely if: airflow clear and the cooling fan still not running.
2. cooling fan motor [PART]
   More likely if: the quiet whirring cooling fan isn't running; controls/fascia/cabinetry getting hot; oven overheats and cuts out then recovers when cool.
   Less likely if: it's the cavity fan (uneven cooking / fan-only mode) not turning (=> fan motor).
3. cooling-fan thermostat / control [PART]
   More likely if: cooling fan never starts even when hot; fan control/switch not energising the fan.
   Less likely if: fan motor itself proven seized/open.
4. overheat thermal cut-out [PART]
   More likely if: oven cuts out on overheat because cooling failed; may not reset.
   Less likely if: no overheating - a straight no-heat or trip.
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- cuts out when hot = thermostat: If it cuts out when hot and RECOVERS when cool, suspect the COOLING fan / airflow / thermal cutout, not just the thermostat. If it TRIPS THE RCD, that's element earth leakage instead.
   Only consider if: cuts out hot and recovers when cool, no RCD trip.
- cooling fan = cooking fan: The cooling fan cools the controls/cabinet (quiet whirring, top/rear); the cavity/cooking fan circulates heat around the food. Different components and symptoms.
   Only consider if: uneven cooking / fan-only mode not turning => cavity fan (fan-motor).
Engineering notes: The COOLING fan (cools the controls/cabinet - a quiet whirring during/after cooking) is a DIFFERENT component from the CAVITY/COOKING fan (circulates heat around the food). Uneven cooking / fan-only-mode not turning => cavity fan (fan-motor); controls/fascia getting hot or cuts-out-when-hot-recovers-when-cool => cooling fan. CAUSAL CHAIN: cooling fan fails => controls/electronics overheat => overheat thermal cutout operates => oven cuts out; often works again after cooling. Consider cooling fan / its thermostat / airflow / thermal cutout. SAFETY: a failed cooling fan lets the controls, fascia and surrounding units overheat (distortion/fire risk) - advise stopping use until repaired.
Likely parts in order: cooling fan, cooling fan thermostat, thermal cut-out
Confused with: thermostat, fan-motor, tripping-electrics
Advice before replacing parts: work out which fan: cavity fan (uneven cooking) vs cooling fan (quiet whirring, controls getting hot); if the controls/fascia are getting hot, stop using the oven until the cooling fan is repaired
Best question to ask if unsure: Does it cut out only once it's hot and work again after cooling, and are the controls or the fascia getting hot?
Follow-up question if still unclear: Is it the quiet cooling fan (controls area) that's stopped, or the cavity fan that circulates heat around the food?

docs.label: Not cooling / warm inside
symptoms: fridge not cold but freezer is
discriminators: A warm fridge with a freezer that seems cold is a COOLING-DISTRIBUTION / AIRFLOW question first, not automatic proof of a failed evaporator fan, and it does not justify listing fan + heater + PCB + timer. Ask: is cooling actually being produced (compressor running; is the freezer objectively cold — a reported 'cold freezer' is not a measured temperature)? Is cold air reaching the fridge (vents, overpacking, hidden ice on the evaporator, damper)? Is the fan known to be running or silent? Hidden ice and restricted airflow are common and often need a defrost/observation check before any part. A sealed-system failure is engineer-only.
Both compartments warm, compressor not running: compressor start relay/overload or the compressor.
Icing up at the back of the freezer: defrost system (heater/thermostat/sensor).

Even for a bare 'fridge isn't cold / not cooling' with no other detail, COMMIT to this not-cooling fault (lead causes: door seal, thermostat, fan, or on a frost-free model the defrost/airflow) and ask whether the FREEZER is still cold to refine - don't withhold a diagnosis.

KEY PATTERN: a WARM FRIDGE with a still-COLD FREEZER on a frost-free fridge-freezer is almost always an AIRFLOW failure, NOT the thermostat or a low gas charge. Frost-free models have ONE evaporator coil in the freezer that cools both sections, so if the cold air can't move, the freezer stays cold and the fridge goes warm.

Most likely (~70%) it's the DEFROST SYSTEM: the defrost heater, defrost (bi-metal) thermostat or defrost timer/control fails, so frost never clears and builds into a solid block of ice over the evaporator coil that chokes off the airflow. The fan can be spinning perfectly but cannot push air through the ice. Check the defrost components FIRST.
Less commonly it's the EVAPORATOR FAN MOTOR: the fan seizes, burns out, or its blades jam on stray ice, so cold air isn't pushed into the fridge even though the coil isn't fully iced up.

TELL THEM APART (simple checks): (1) Open the freezer and press the door-light switch by hand - if you hear the fan whirr, the fan has power so a DEFROST blockage is likely; dead silence means the fan is dead or jammed by ice. (2) With the freezer shut, feel the fridge supply vent (top-back): fan audible but little/no air = iced-up coils (defrost). (3) Remove the rear freezer panel: a solid snow-packed block of ice = defrost failure; clear/lightly-frosted coils but a stationary fan = fan motor.

JUST MOVED / JUST DELIVERED and not getting cold? This may be nothing wrong at all: if the fridge was transported on its side/flat, compressor oil runs into the cooling pipes. Powering it on too soon traps oil in the capillary tubes, blocks the refrigerant and can permanently burn out the compressor. Advice: if it was laid flat, stand it upright ~24 hours before switching on; if moved upright, wait 2-4 hours. Don't diagnose a fault until it's stood and then had a few hours running.

OVER-DIAGNOSED THERMOSTAT: if the fridge RUNS CONSTANTLY and never gets cold enough, suspect dirty CONDENSER COILS (dusty coils at the back/underneath) or a poor DOOR SEAL rather than the thermostat - the stat is doing its job, it just can't reach temperature.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is the freezer still cold while the fridge is warm, and is there a thick block of ice on the back wall inside the freezer?

docs.label: Compressor fault
discriminators: A fridge that's warm all over with the compressor CLICKING or HUMMING every few minutes is trying to start but tripping its thermal OVERLOAD because it can't get going. The cheap, common culprit is the START RELAY / overload (a small plastic pack clipped onto the side of the compressor, ~£15) - check this FIRST: if it rattles when gently shaken or smells/looks burnt, replace the relay before ever condemning the compressor.

It's the COMPRESSOR itself (expensive) only when the relay is sound but it still just hums and clicks - i.e. a mechanical seizure - or when the windings test open/short to the frame. Don't jump to a new compressor (or blame the thermostat) on a click alone: the relay is far more often the fix.
Tie-breaker: if a known-good relay still gives only a hum and a click, the compressor is mechanically seized/dead.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is there a clicking/humming every few minutes from the black cylinder at the bottom-back, and does the relay on its side rattle or smell burnt?

docs.label: Thermostat fault
discriminators: BEFORE blaming the thermostat, rule out the far more common causes - a thermostat fault is over-diagnosed. Warm fridge + cold freezer = DEFROST system (timer/heater), not the stat. Clicking compressor that won't start = the cheap START RELAY, not the stat. Fresh-food warm while freezer freezes = a stuck AIR DAMPER or the evaporator FAN. Fridge RUNS CONSTANTLY and never shuts off = dirty CONDENSER COILS or a poor DOOR SEAL stopping it reaching temperature (the stat is doing its job) - clean the coils and check the seal first.
Treat it as the thermostat only once those are excluded: e.g. it never calls for cooling at all (stays warm with no compressor run) or won't stop on a mechanical stat with the sensor bulb intact.

docs.label: Defrost fault / frost build-up
symptoms: fridge warm freezer cold with ice
thick ice on the back panel
sheet of ice on the back
block of ice at the back
discriminators: Heavy/abnormal ice on the internal rear (evaporator) panel with a warm fridge but a still-cold freezer is a DEFROST-SYSTEM fault (defrost heater, defrost thermostat/thermal fuse, or defrost sensor) blocking airflow - the exact failed sub-component is model-specific, so lead with the defrost system as the area and confirm the part with the model. A manual defrost that temporarily restores cooling confirms the AREA but does not prove which sub-component failed.
Light, normal frost is not a fault; only a thick sheet/block of ice over the panel points here.

Frost-free defrost failure = frost never clears and builds into a solid block of ice over the evaporator coil, choking the airflow so the fridge goes warm while the freezer stays cold. The three defrost parts to check: the DEFROST HEATER (burns out), the DEFROST (bi-metal) THERMOSTAT (stuck open so the heater never fires), and the DEFROST TIMER/control (never calls a defrost cycle).

Confirming sign: fan audible but no air at the fridge vent, and a snow-packed ice block on the coils behind the rear freezer panel. Manually defrosting (unplug 24-48h) will temporarily restore cooling - but it WILL ice up again within days until the failed defrost part is replaced, so don't treat 'defrosted it and it worked' as the repair.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Behind the rear panel inside the freezer, are the coils a solid block of ice, or fairly clear?

docs.label: Internal (evaporator) fan fault
symptoms: no cold air reaching the fridge
cold air not getting to the fridge
discriminators: A warm fridge with a still-cold freezer, without a known silent fan or heavy ice, is NOT yet an evaporator-fan diagnosis. Treat it as cooling distribution: is cooling produced, is it reaching the fridge, is airflow restricted, is hidden ice plausible, is the fan actually heard or seen? Give a safe test plan (vents, listen/look for the fan, look for a sheet of ice on the rear panel, optional measured freezer temperature, a period unplugged to defrost) before naming a part. Do not dump fan + heater + PCB + timer.

FAN NOISE (rattling / knocking / grinding / buzzing) with a warm fridge and a still-cold freezer means the fan blade is striking a BUILD-UP OF ICE on the evaporator - a DEFROST-SYSTEM failure. LEAD with the defrost system (defrost heater / defrost thermostat / defrost timer) and clearing the ice; a genuinely failed fan MOTOR is usually SILENT or a steady hum, not a rattle. Only lead with the evaporator fan MOTOR when the fan is SILENT / not spinning and the coils are clear.

Warm fridge + cold freezer with NO abnormal ice and the fan silent/not spinning points to the evaporator fan motor; if there is heavy ice the fan may just be blocked by it (defrost system). Before a part, check the internal vents aren't packed with food.

The evaporator (internal) FAN pushes cold air from the freezer coil into the fridge. If it seizes, burns out, or its blades jam on stray ice, the fridge goes warm while the coil itself stays relatively clear of a full ice block.

Tell it from a defrost fault: press the freezer door switch - dead silence with CLEAR coils = fan motor; if you hear the fan but no air reaches the fridge and the coils are a block of ice, it's the DEFROST system, not the fan. A fan fouling on ice points back to a defrost problem too.

docs.label: Blocked defrost drain (water in base)
symptoms: water at the bottom of the fridge
discriminators: Water pooling under the salad/crisper drawers is overwhelmingly a BLOCKED DEFROST DRAIN: the small hole at the base of the rear (wet) wall clogs with food debris, gunk or ice, so defrost condensation can't run out to the evaporation tray and backs up into the cabinet. Clear the drain hole (cotton bud / flexible cleaner) and flush with warm water first.

If the drain is clear or the water returns fast, check the other causes: food/packaging pressed against the rear wet wall (moisture bridges past the channel); a worn/dirty DOOR SEAL letting warm damp air in (excess condensation); the fridge tilted slightly FORWARD (water misses the trough); or the hidden drain tube FROZEN into an ice block lower down even though the top of the hole looks clear.
This is usually a clean/level/seal fix, not a costly part - lead with clearing the drain and checking levelling and the seal.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is the water only under the salad drawers, and have you tried clearing the small drain hole at the bottom of the back wall?

docs.label: Noisy / buzzing / rattling
discriminators: A constant hum/buzz is usually the compressor or its start relay working; if it's unusually loud or the fridge isn't getting cold too, the relay or compressor may be failing.
A whirring/rattling that changes when you open the door is usually a fan (evaporator or condenser) - a blade catching ice, or a worn fan motor.
Buzzing only while it fills with water = the water inlet/ice-maker valve. A light rattle is often just pipework or a shelf touching the cabinet - reposition it (no part needed).

Split fridge noise three ways. FAN HITTING ICE = a rapid rhythmic ticking/clicking/buzz (like a card in bike spokes), from inside the freezer (evaporator fan) or bottom-rear (condenser fan). Verify: open the freezer door - if it STOPS, it's the evaporator fan (door switch cuts it); if the blades are fouling ice it points to a defrost problem or a warped blade.

COMPRESSOR noise = a continuous deep low hum/drone, or a metallic clunk on start/stop, low down at the back. Verify: it changes/stops when you briefly unplug. Cause is wear, perished mounting grommets, or a failing motor.

GENERAL RATTLE / PIPEWORK = an irregular buzzing/rattling that seems to come from everywhere. Verify: press firmly on the panels/back grille/drip tray - if it dampens, it's vibration: fridge not level, copper pipes touching, or a loose drip pan. This is a free fix (level it / separate the pipes / reseat the tray), not a part.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does the noise stop when you open the freezer door, when you unplug it briefly, or when you press on the cabinet panels?

docs.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when running
likelyComponents: STOP USE and isolate at the socket if there is burning, scorching or a smell of hot plastic (safety first)
compressor start relay / overload (electrical fault as it tries to start)
mains lead / plug / internal wiring or connector
symptoms: trips as soon as i plug it in
discriminators: A fridge-freezer that trips the RCD/fuse is an EARTH-LEAKAGE or short-circuit fault (mains lead, wiring, start relay or compressor windings), NOT a cooling-performance or refrigerant-charge question - do not lead with 'compressor failed' or 'needs re-gassing'. Timing is evidence: trips on plug-in => lead/plug/wiring or a dead short; trips when the compressor tries to start => start relay/overload or compressor windings to earth; trips after running => wiring or compressor insulation. Burning smell/scorching => STOP USE and isolate. No insulation testing, live probing, sealed-system/compressor-terminal work, earth/RCD bypass or repeated resetting by the customer.

A fridge-freezer that trips the electrics/RCD is an EARTH-LEAKAGE or short-circuit electrical fault - it is NOT a cooling-performance question, so do not lead with 'compressor failed' or 'needs re-gassing'. Use the TIMING as evidence, not proof: trips the INSTANT it is plugged in / switched on => mains lead, plug, incoming wiring or a dead short; trips when the COMPRESSOR tries to start (a click/hum every few minutes then a trip) => the start relay/overload or the compressor windings leaking to earth; trips after running a while => wiring/connector or compressor insulation breaking down as it warms.

A cold fridge that suddenly trips, with a burning or hot-plastic smell or visible scorching at the plug/socket or the back, is an electrical safety fault - STOP USE and isolate. Do not keep resetting the RCD to see if it holds.

SAFETY: do NOT tell the customer to insulation-test, energise or probe live components, open the sealed refrigeration system, work on the compressor terminals, bypass the earth or RCD, or repeatedly reset the trip. Sealed-system and live electrical work is for a qualified engineer only.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Does it trip the moment you plug it in, when the compressor tries to start (a click/hum every few minutes), or after it has been running a while - and is there any burning smell or scorching?

docs.label: Cookware not suitable / not detected (induction) - check the pan first
discriminators: Induction detects a pan only if the cookware is ferrous/magnetic, flat, and large enough to cover the zone - so 'won't recognise pans' is very often the COOKWARE, not the hob. Test with a magnet (it must stick firmly) and try a pan you KNOW works on the other zones. If that known-good pan also fails on this one zone, it points to the zone's coil/power (generator) module; if it works, the original pan was just unsuitable - no part needed.
A pan that is too small, warped/domed, or non-magnetic (aluminium, copper, some stainless) will not be detected on any induction zone - that is cookware, not a fault.

docs.label: Overheating protection triggered
discriminators: An error / 'E' shown on ALL zones at once points to a SYSTEM-WIDE cause - most commonly overheating protection (blocked vents or a failed cooling fan), or a supply / voltage problem, or the main power board - NOT a single zone's induction coil. Lead with the overheating / cooling / supply differential, do not confidently assert a dead PCB. If only ONE zone errors, that zone's coil / power module is the more likely cause.

A hob that cuts out under load, recovers when one zone is left off, or sits above an oven that is also running is a whole-hob thermal / cooling / supply path — not proof that a single zone element has failed. Unrelated co-occurring symptoms (an error code AND a separate grill fault) must not be merged into one diagnosis merely because they happened together.

The exact letter/number varies by make and generation, so an 'E' with no digits is ambiguous - give the strongest grounded differential and ask for the make/model and the full code to pin it, rather than inventing a specific meaning.

docs.label: Gas ignition fault
discriminators: Lights then goes out when you release the knob = the flame supervision device (FSD/FFD thermocouple) isn't sensing the flame to hold the gas valve open - that's the usual culprit for 'won't stay lit'. Won't spark at all = the ignition electrode/module.

Uncommanded clicking or sparking at an electrode is an ignition/control observation. It is NOT a report of flame-failure, a thermocouple, gas smell, overheating or burning — do not invent those symptoms. Accessible burner-cap and electrode cleaning without lifting the appliance or removing panels may be customer-safe; testing or replacing gas controls, thermocouples, ignition modules, or holding the knob to test a flame-failure device is for a Gas Safe engineer. If the next useful step is inside the gas path, stop remote diagnosis there. Naming an ignition area for an engineer is not the same as instructing the customer to access or replace it.
No spark on all burners = ignition switch/module; one burner = that electrode or a dirty/wet burner cap.

docs.label: Not heating (high-voltage heating circuit)
symptoms: cuts out after a few seconds
runs then stops with no heat
plate turns but food is cold
light and fan work but no heat
timer counts down but food stays cold
discriminators: MICROWAVE TYPE DECIDES THE PRIMARY PART. On an INVERTER model (all Panasonic, and any model badged 'inverter'), a cut-out after a fixed few seconds or 'runs but no heat' is the HV INVERTER BOARD first (the magnetron is the secondary suspect) - LEAD with the inverter board. On a CONVENTIONAL (transformer) model, lead with the MAGNETRON, then the HV diode and HV capacitor.

Cuts out after a FIXED few seconds (still lit) = the power circuit isn't drawing current: inverter board (inverter models) or magnetron - this is the H97/H98 fault shown as a symptom, NOT overheating (overheating cut-outs take minutes).
Stops the instant the door is nudged: door interlock / monitor switch (see door).

CALIBRATED, SAFE PRECISION: if it starts and runs normally (turntable turning, timer counting down) but produces no heat, the fault is in the high-voltage heating circuit - describe it as a high-voltage heating-circuit fault (the exact component - magnetron, HV diode, HV capacitor or inverter board - depends on the model and can only be confirmed by an engineer's test), do NOT name a single failed part or claim it is 'the magnetron'. NEVER tell the customer to remove the cover/casing, discharge the capacitor, or test the magnetron/diode/transformer - dangerous voltage can remain stored even when unplugged; this is an engineer diagnosis, not a DIY test.

SAFE DISCRIMINATOR FIRST: if it is unclear whether it runs normally or won't start / reacts to the door, ask that (runs-normally-but-cold vs won't-start / door-conditioned) before committing - a door/latch/interlock fault stops it heating too, and is a completely different (and often no-HV) repair (see door).

ARCHITECTURE FIRST: CONVENTIONAL = transformer + magnetron + HV capacitor + HV diode; INVERTER = inverter board + magnetron. NEVER recommend an HV transformer / conventional HV capacitor / conventional HV diode on a confirmed INVERTER machine, and never recommend an inverter board on a confirmed CONVENTIONAL machine. If architecture is unknown, do not assert architecture-specific parts - identify the model first.

HEAVY/ABNORMAL BUZZ + NO HEAT on a conventional machine strongly raises an HV DIODE short OR a magnetron fault/leakage to earth - much stronger than generic 'noisy'. It does not uniquely prove one component.
SMOKE / SEVERE BURNING / transformer-area overheating => STOP USE; do not tell the customer to run it again to reproduce the fault.
INTERNAL FUSE BLOWN on a conventional machine + heating/HV behaviour raises the HV CAPACITOR / HV circuit - but the fuse is EVIDENCE, not a diagnosis; keep alternatives.
INVERTER machine + repeatable ~3-second or ~28-second shutdown before cutting out is a strong inverter/magnetron/inverter-HV fingerprint (not a universal manufacturer-independent law).

HV DIODE DMM CAVEAT: a microwave HV diode needs a much higher forward voltage than an ordinary silicon diode; many ordinary digital multimeters cannot forward-bias it on their normal diode/ohms range, so 'my normal DMM reads the new HV diode open both ways' does NOT by itself prove the replacement diode faulty (a traditional test uses an analogue meter on a high range such as Rx10K with ~9V). Do not condemn a supplied diode on that evidence.
CHECK cookware / power level / mode and that the door latches BEFORE any HV part.

safetyInformation.text: Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.

safetyInformation.applicability: Any microwave internal-repair situation for this fault, independent of which internal part has failed.

docs.label: Door interlock / latch fault
likelyComponents: door interlock / monitor microswitch (electrical start path)
symptoms: button does nothing when i press it
acts like the door is open
wont start with the door closed
discriminators: SYMPTOM SPLIT: a door that physically WON'T OPEN/RELEASE is a MECHANICAL fault - lead with the release button/lever/linkage, then the latch/hook, the return spring, and alignment/hinge/obstruction. A door that CLOSES normally but the microwave WON'T START (beeps, acts like the door is open) is the ELECTRICAL interlock path - only then is the interlock/monitor microswitch a leading suspect. Do NOT lead with the interlock microswitch for a purely mechanical won't-open complaint.

BUTTON FEEL is the strongest discriminator: LOOSE/FLOPPY button = broken release button/lever/linkage or its spring/connection; NORMAL button but door still caught = latch/hook or alignment/binding further along; UNUSUALLY STIFF/JAMMED = binding latch/lever, an obstruction, or alignment. Use as evidence to re-rank, not as a guarantee.

TEMPORARY post-cooking sticking (hard to open just after cooking, releases normally shortly after) is a low-frequency pattern - do NOT treat it as a broken mechanical release; clarify before recommending a part.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: When you press the door-release button, does it feel normal, loose/floppy, or unusually stiff?

components.name: door release button / lever / linkage
supports: the button moves but doesn't release the door
the button feels loose or floppy
the button resistance has suddenly changed
the button has excessive travel
pressing at a particular angle sometimes releases the door
the release action disappeared suddenly
against: the release button feels mechanically normal
the button/lever clearly operates the latch mechanism
the symptom is electrical rather than physical (door closes fine but won't start)

components.name: door latch / hook mechanism
supports: the release button feels reasonably normal but the door stays caught
the door had become progressively harder to open
the door needs movement/lifting/pressure before it releases
the latch/hook appears damaged, worn or misaligned
an abnormal mechanical click or feel around the latch
against: the release button/linkage is obviously loose, broken or not transmitting movement
the door physically opens and closes normally and the real complaint is that it won't operate

components.name: button / latch return spring
supports: the button doesn't return normally
the button stays depressed
the mechanism feels unusually slack
the release behaviour changed suddenly
against: the button returns with normal resistance and movement
the evidence points to the latch/hook binding further along the mechanism

components.name: door alignment / hinge / accessible obstruction
supports: the door needs lifting or moving to release
the door appears dropped or misaligned
the problem became progressively worse
visible debris or grease around the accessible latch area
the door became increasingly difficult to open before eventually sticking
against: sudden failure together with a loose/floppy release button
an obviously broken release linkage

components.name: door interlock / monitor microswitch (electrical start path)
supports: the door CLOSES normally but the microwave WON'T START (beeps / acts as though the door is open)
intermittent start when the door is nudged
the latch engages but the switch isn't being made
against: the door physically WON'T OPEN/RELEASE (mechanical)
the release button feels loose/floppy or the handle is broken (mechanical)

docs.secondaryQuestion: Did it become harder to open over time, or did it suddenly stop opening?
adviceBeforeReplacement: the customer can visually inspect the accessible latch area
accessible crumbs/debris/grease around the latch can be gently cleaned
do not force or pry the door open
do not remove the microwave casing
do not test internal interlock switches and never bypass an interlock
