Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed):
1. door release button / lever / linkage
   More likely if: the button moves but doesn't release the door; the button feels loose or floppy; the button resistance has suddenly changed; the button has excessive travel; pressing at a particular angle sometimes releases the door; the release action disappeared suddenly.
   Less likely if: the release button feels mechanically normal; the button/lever clearly operates the latch mechanism; the symptom is electrical rather than physical (door closes fine but won't start).
2. door latch / hook mechanism
   More likely if: the release button feels reasonably normal but the door stays caught; the door had become progressively harder to open; the door needs movement/lifting/pressure before it releases; the latch/hook appears damaged, worn or misaligned; an abnormal mechanical click or feel around the latch.
   Less likely if: the release button/linkage is obviously loose, broken or not transmitting movement; the door physically opens and closes normally and the real complaint is that it won't operate.

   More likely if: the button doesn't return normally; the button stays depressed; the mechanism feels unusually slack; the release behaviour changed suddenly.
   Less likely if: the button returns with normal resistance and movement; the evidence points to the latch/hook binding further along the mechanism.
4. door alignment / hinge / accessible obstruction
   More likely if: the door needs lifting or moving to release; the door appears dropped or misaligned; the problem became progressively worse; visible debris or grease around the accessible latch area; the door became increasingly difficult to open before eventually sticking.
   Less likely if: sudden failure together with a loose/floppy release button; an obviously broken release linkage.
5. door interlock / monitor microswitch (electrical start path)
   More likely if: the door CLOSES normally but the microwave WON'T START (beeps / acts as though the door is open); intermittent start when the door is nudged; the latch engages but the switch isn't being made.
   Less likely if: the door physically WON'T OPEN/RELEASE (mechanical); the release button feels loose/floppy or the handle is broken (mechanical).

TEMPORARY post-cooking sticking (hard to open just after cooking, releases normally shortly after) is a low-frequency pattern - do NOT treat it as a broken mechanical release; clarify before recommending a part.
Likely parts in order: door release button / lever / linkage, door latch / hook mechanism, button / latch return spring, door alignment / hinge / accessible obstruction, door interlock / monitor microswitch (electrical start path)
Confused with: not-heating, low-voltage
Advice before replacing parts: the customer can visually inspect the accessible latch area; accessible crumbs/debris/grease around the latch can be gently cleaned; do not force or pry the door open; do not remove the microwave casing; do not test internal interlock switches and never bypass an interlock

Follow-up question if still unclear: Did it become harder to open over time, or did it suddenly stop opening?

docs.label: Turntable not turning
discriminators: CHECK the tray is seated on the coupler/rollers, clear of obstruction, and the roller ring is intact/clean FIRST. Then distinguish MOTOR NOT DRIVING (nothing moves, motor silent) from COUPLER NOT TRANSMITTING (motor turns/hums but the plate doesn't). Don't jump to the PCB.
A SMASHED/CRACKED glass plate is a direct accessory (glass turntable), NOT a fault-diagnosis - identify the replacement tray, don't run a motor diagnosis.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: When it should turn, does the motor hum/try to turn while the plate stays still, or is there no movement or sound at all - or is the glass plate actually broken?

components.name: tray seated correctly / obstruction
supports: tray not sitting on the coupler/rollers properly
something jamming the plate
food/debris under the tray
against: tray correctly seated and clear, still won't turn

components.name: roller ring / support wheels
supports: worn/dirty roller wheels
the ring dislodged or clogged
against: roller ring clean and intact

components.name: turntable coupler
supports: the motor turns/hums but the plate doesn't (drive not transmitted)
a stripped/split coupler
against: nothing moves at all and the motor is silent

components.name: turntable motor
supports: no movement at all and the motor is silent/dead with the tray removed
the coupler is intact but nothing drives it
against: the motor clearly turns but the plate doesn't (=> coupler)

components.name: glass turntable plate (if smashed)
supports: the glass plate/tray is smashed or cracked - a direct replacement accessory
against: the plate is intact but won't turn (=> coupler/motor/roller)

commonConfusion.name: turntable fault = main PCB
commonConfusion.note: Don't jump to the PCB. Check seating/obstruction/roller, then the coupler, then the motor.
wouldApplyIf: seating, roller, coupler and motor all proven good

commonConfusion.name: smashed glass = motor diagnosis
commonConfusion.note: A broken glass tray is a direct accessory purchase (glass turntable), not a motor fault - don't send it through the motor path.
wouldApplyIf: the customer says the glass plate is smashed/broken

docs.secondaryQuestion: Is the tray seated properly on the coupler and rollers, with nothing jamming it?
adviceBeforeReplacement: reseat the tray on the coupler/rollers and clear any obstruction
check the roller ring/wheels are clean and intact
if the glass plate is smashed, that's just a replacement tray
docs.text:
Appliance: microwave
Fault: Turntable not turning
Customer phrases: plate not spinning; turntable stuck; tray won't rotate; turntable not turning; tray wont rotate; glass plate not going round; dish not spinning; glass turntable smashed; glass plate broken; need a new glass tray; broken glass turntable
Candidate causes in initial diagnostic order (re-rank by the evidence below, do not treat the order as fixed). CHECK = a condition to inspect/clean/clear first, not automatically a part to sell; PART = a replacement component:
1. tray seated correctly / obstruction [CHECK]
   More likely if: tray not sitting on the coupler/rollers properly; something jamming the plate; food/debris under the tray.
   Less likely if: tray correctly seated and clear, still won't turn.
2. roller ring / support wheels [CHECK]
   More likely if: worn/dirty roller wheels; the ring dislodged or clogged.
   Less likely if: roller ring clean and intact.
3. turntable coupler [PART]
   More likely if: the motor turns/hums but the plate doesn't (drive not transmitted); a stripped/split coupler.
   Less likely if: nothing moves at all and the motor is silent.
4. turntable motor [PART]
   More likely if: no movement at all and the motor is silent/dead with the tray removed; the coupler is intact but nothing drives it.
   Less likely if: the motor clearly turns but the plate doesn't (=> coupler).
5. glass turntable plate (if smashed) [PART]
   More likely if: the glass plate/tray is smashed or cracked - a direct replacement accessory.
   Less likely if: the plate is intact but won't turn (=> coupler/motor/roller).
Common confusion — semantically related but NOT a leading cause for this symptom unless the stated evidence is present; do not surface these first without it:
- turntable fault = main PCB: Don't jump to the PCB. Check seating/obstruction/roller, then the coupler, then the motor.
   Only consider if: seating, roller, coupler and motor all proven good.
- smashed glass = motor diagnosis: A broken glass tray is a direct accessory purchase (glass turntable), not a motor fault - don't send it through the motor path.
   Only consider if: the customer says the glass plate is smashed/broken.
Engineering notes: CHECK the tray is seated on the coupler/rollers, clear of obstruction, and the roller ring is intact/clean FIRST. Then distinguish MOTOR NOT DRIVING (nothing moves, motor silent) from COUPLER NOT TRANSMITTING (motor turns/hums but the plate doesn't). Don't jump to the PCB. A SMASHED/CRACKED glass plate is a direct accessory (glass turntable), NOT a fault-diagnosis - identify the replacement tray, don't run a motor diagnosis.
Likely parts in order: turntable coupler, turntable motor, glass turntable
Confused with: noisy, main-pcb
Advice before replacing parts: reseat the tray on the coupler/rollers and clear any obstruction; check the roller ring/wheels are clean and intact; if the glass plate is smashed, that's just a replacement tray
Best question to ask if unsure: When it should turn, does the motor hum/try to turn while the plate stays still, or is there no movement or sound at all - or is the glass plate actually broken?
Follow-up question if still unclear: Is the tray seated properly on the coupler and rollers, with nothing jamming it?

docs.label: Sparking / arcing inside
symptoms: the little cardboard bit is sparking
paper bit on the side is sparking
little plate on the side wall sparking
burnt square on the side wall
that thing on the side wall is arcing
discriminators: FIRST determine WHERE the sparking is and WHAT was in the cavity. A metal object / foil / metallic-trimmed dish anywhere => remove it FIRST (user cause); this LEADS whenever the customer says something metallic was inside. Arcing at the mica/waveguide cover with burning or carbon marks => the waveguide cover (clean or replace). Chipped paint / bare metal => cavity coating. Only a clean cavity + intact cover + no metal raises the magnetron.

LOCATION is the highest-value discriminator: arcing at a SPOT ON THE SIDE/ROOF PANEL => the waveguide (mica) cover; arcing at the CAVITY FLOOR/WALL => contamination / coating damage / exposed metal / a foreign object; arcing at the DOOR EDGE / around the door frame => contamination or damage at the door face/choke/front frame (clean food/carbon debris there; a genuinely damaged door needs professional attention). If the LOCATION is unknown, advise a safe visual inspection (unplugged) before naming a part.

DO NOT lead with a 'door seal / gasket' for arcing INSIDE the cavity: a domestic microwave has no user-serviceable door seal, and cavity arcing (side/roof/floor) points to the waveguide cover / contamination / metal - only DOOR-EDGE-located arcing raises the door face/choke/perimeter.
STOP USE if the arcing is violent/repeated, or there is burning or visible cavity/cover damage - do not keep running it to 'see if it clears'.

commonConfusion.note: Usually metal in the cavity or a burnt/dirty waveguide (mica) cover. Do NOT jump to the magnetron - it is the last suspect after the cavity/cover are cleared.

commonConfusion.note: A domestic microwave has NO user-serviceable door seal/gasket. Arcing INSIDE the cavity (side/roof panel or floor) is the waveguide (mica) cover, food/metal contamination, or a metal object - never lead with a 'door seal'. docs.secondaryQuestion: Is the mica cover on the side/roof burnt, blackened or holed?

docs.label: Control board (PCB) fault
symptoms: display dead but it still works
discriminators: KEYPAD-ONLY (some buttons dead, display fine) => keypad/membrane. DISPLAY-ONLY (blank/garbled but the machine runs) => display/UI module. Check a control/child lock first. COMPLETELY DEAD => low-voltage. DOOR prevents start / beeps => door. Main PCB is the LAST suspect.
A stuck single button or specific unresponsive digits point to the membrane, not the whole board.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is the display still lit and working while only some buttons fail, or is the display itself blank/garbled - or is the whole machine dead?

components.name: control lock / demo mode
supports: all buttons locked out
a lock/child-lock symbol shown
a reset/power-cycle restores it
against: only certain buttons dead while others work

components.name: keypad / membrane / touchpad
supports: some buttons work and others don't
specific digits/functions unresponsive
sticky or damaged membrane, display otherwise fine
against: the whole panel and display are dead (=> supply)

components.name: control panel / fascia
supports: fascia/selector physically damaged
a rotary/selector control fault
against: a flat membrane keypad issue with a good fascia

components.name: display / UI module
supports: display blank/partial/garbled but the machine otherwise runs
against: a keypad-only issue with a good display

components.name: main control PCB
supports: keypad, fascia and display proven good and it still won't respond
against: cheaper causes (lock/keypad/display) not excluded

commonConfusion.name: controls = main PCB
commonConfusion.note: Down-rank the PCB. A dead/partial keypad is usually the membrane; a blank/garbled display is usually the display module. The main PCB is the last suspect.
wouldApplyIf: keypad, membrane and display module proven good

commonConfusion.name: unresponsive = broken
commonConfusion.note: Completely dead (no lights) => low-voltage/supply; door-prevents-start/beeps => door. Not every control problem is the control board.
wouldApplyIf: completely dead => low-voltage; beeps/won't start => door

docs.secondaryQuestion: Do some buttons still work, and does a power-cycle at the wall change anything?
adviceBeforeReplacement: check for a control/child lock and try a power-cycle reset
note whether it's some buttons (membrane) or the display (module) or completely dead (supply)

docs.label: Power supply / fuse fault
discriminators: COMPLETELY DEAD (no lights/display) is almost always a blown internal line fuse - but the fuse is EVIDENCE, not the diagnosis: find what blew it. List the likely causes to check: the property supply / plug fuse, the mains lead, the door monitor / interlock microswitch (the classic culprit), a worn door catch that mistimes that switch, the oven lamp / bulb (a shorted lamp takes out the fuse), and on a conventional machine a downstream HV short (HV capacitor / HV diode / magnetron); the control board only once the cheaper causes are excluded.
REPEATEDLY BLOWS THE INTERNAL FUSE => the same downstream causes (door monitor-switch, HV capacitor / HV diode / magnetron on a conventional machine) - the fuse is EVIDENCE, not the diagnosis.
Do NOT encode 'replace fuse = fixed' - a repeatedly blowing fuse means an upstream/downstream fault to find.
POWERED but WON'T START (display alive) is NOT this node => door/interlock/control.
docs.clarifyingQuestion: Is the microwave completely dead with no lights or display, or does it power up but blow the fuse (or refuse to start)?

components.name: property supply / socket / plug fuse
supports: completely dead, no lights
test the socket with another appliance
house circuit tripped
against: socket proven live and the machine still dead

components.name: mains lead / internal line fuse (evidence)
supports: completely dead
internal line fuse found blown
against: display lights up (=> not a dead-power fault)

components.name: downstream HV short - HV capacitor / HV diode / magnetron [CONVENTIONAL]
supports: REPEATEDLY blows the internal fuse, especially on start/heat
conventional machine
against: simply dead with no repeated fuse blowing
confirmed inverter architecture

components.name: door monitor / interlock microswitch (a mis-timed or failed monitor switch is the classic cause of a blown line fuse)
supports: dead after the door was slammed or the fuse blew on opening/closing
monitor-switch design where a mis-timed interlock blows the fuse
against: no door-correlated failure

components.name: door catch / latch (a worn catch mis-aligns the door and mistimes the monitor switch, blowing the fuse)
supports: door feels loose, rattles, or does not latch cleanly
went dead after the catch became worn or loose
against: door latches firmly and squarely

components.name: oven lamp / bulb (a lamp that fails short commonly takes out the line fuse)
supports: went completely dead around the time the internal lamp failed
against: lamp still works or is not on the fused circuit

components.name: control / power board
supports: dead with supply proven good and the line fuse intact
against: cheaper causes (supply/lead/fuse) not excluded

commonConfusion.name: replace the fuse = fixed
commonConfusion.note: The fuse is a SYMPTOM. A fuse that blows again means a fault - find WHY it blew (downstream HV short or a monitor-switch fault). Do not just keep replacing the fuse.
wouldApplyIf: the fuse blows again after replacement

commonConfusion.name: powered but won't start = dead
commonConfusion.note: If the display works but it won't start, that is the door/interlock/control path, NOT a dead-power fault.
wouldApplyIf: display/lights work but it won't start

docs.secondaryQuestion: If it blows the fuse, does it do so as soon as you switch on, or only when it starts to heat?
adviceBeforeReplacement: check the wall socket with another appliance and the plug fuse where fitted
if the internal fuse blows again, the cause is elsewhere - do not keep replacing it
do NOT open the casing or touch HV components - stored charge is lethal

docs.label: Noisy / loud when running
discriminators: A grinding/whirring from underneath as the plate turns = the turntable motor; a loud rushing/rattle = the cooling fan or a loose cover.
A loud HUM or buzz together with poor/no heating points to the magnetron or HV components on their way out (see not-heating).
